### policy.json is still an un-migrated Bedrock IAM policy, and the README's raw-CLI deploy path attaches it — producing a role that cannot read the API key at all

`lambda/tutor/policy.json:5-13` — `f3f0cf48a` · low · confirmed · correctness · ran locally · SPLIT VERDICT · re-raised from `fd41306fa` · fix plan 10

**Claim.** policy.json grants exactly `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream` on four hardcoded Bedrock ARNs plus logs. The handler makes no Bedrock call; it reads `{apiKey}` from Secrets Manager on first model call (index.mjs:539-542) and, when metering is on, calls DynamoDB GetItem/UpdateItem. The policy grants neither. README.md:100-109 still documents the raw-CLI fallback as `aws iam put-role-policy --policy-document file://lambda/tutor/policy.json` followed by `create-function ... --environment "Variables={SECRET_ID=quantum-tutor}"`.

**Correction.** Two impact claims are wrong. (1) "recoverable only via the tutorError alarm" is false for the path in question: TutorErrorMetricFilter/TutorErrorAlarm/AlertsTopic are template.yaml resources (lambda/tutor/template.yaml:255-283), so a raw-CLI deploy creates no metric filter, no alarm and no SNS topic — there is no recovery signal at all on that path, which makes the impact worse than described, not differently observable. (2) "fails GetSecretValue with AccessDenied on every single request" overstates: the out-of-scope gate, the over-long-body gate and the refused paid-model path all return without calling anthropic(), exactly as the deferred-fetch comment at index.mjs:530-537 states. Only requests that reach the model fail. The DynamoDB half of the claim is technically true but inert — WALLET_TABLE is unset and metering is off, so secretsmanager is the only load-bearing omission.

**Impact.** Anyone following the documented fallback path deploys a function that fails GetSecretValue with AccessDenied on every single request. Because the response is committed as 200 before the model call, the symptom is 100% of learners receiving the in-band error sentinel while HTTP status and Lambda Errors stay clean — recoverable only via the tutorError alarm. It also hardcodes production account $PROD_ACCOUNT into a public repo (one of only two tracked files that do), pinned to an application-inference-profile the migration abandoned.

**Evidence.** policy.json:7 `"Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream"]`; :9 `"arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:application-inference-profile/q050egz0q4mb"`. index.mjs:538-542 `const sm = new SecretsManagerClient({}); const secret = await sm.send(new GetSecretValueCommand({ SecretId: process.env.SECRET_ID }));`. template.yaml:160-165 grants `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` scoped to `${SecretId}-??????`, which policy.json has no equivalent of. `git grep -l $PROD_ACCOUNT` returns only this file and scripts/founding-credit/cohort-2026-08.json.

**Split verdict.** reproduces: confirmed · correct as written: partly true. Published at the more severe reading.

**Verification — reproduces** (confirmed, low, ran locally). Reproduces on every load-bearing point.

POLICY CONTENT (`cat -n lambda/tutor/policy.json`): exactly two statements — `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream` on four ARNs (line 9 is `arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:application-inference-profile/q050egz0q4mb`) plus `logs:*`. A node enumeration over the parsed document printed: `services granted by policy.json: bedrock, logs` / `grants any secrets-manager read? false` / `grants any dynamodb action? false`.

IAM'S OWN SIMULATOR AGREES (read-only, no state change):
`aws iam simulate-custom-policy --policy-input-list "$(cat lambda/tutor/policy.json)" --action-names dynamodb:GetItem dynamodb:UpdateItem bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream logs:PutLogEvents --resource-arns arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:table/quantum-stripe-wallet` → all four `implicitDeny`. Against the profile ARN the granted action returns `allowed`:
`aws iam simulate-custom-policy --policy-input-list "$(cat lambda/tutor/policy.json)" --action-names bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream --resource-arns arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:application-inference-profile/q050egz0q4mb` → `allowed`. I tried the same call with `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` in --action-names; this machine's secret-safety hook blocked it on keyword match (the simulator returns no secret value, but I did not evade the guard), so default-deny is proved structurally instead — the simulator cannot return anything but implicitDeny for a service the document never names.

TUTOR_ROSTER[wallet.tier] ?? TUTOR_ROSTER.free : null;`; :258 `const metered = Boolean(models && authToken);`. **Verification — reproduces** (partly true, low, observed live). Mechanically the claim reproduces exactly; the scope and impact do not.

Reproduced (read + executed):
- `grep -rn "AskTutor" web/src web/__tests__ web/e2e` returns one render site, `web/src/app/layout.tsx:111` `<AskTutor />`, with no props. `web/src/components/ask-tutor.tsx:114` makes `models` null and `:258` makes `metered` false whenever `wallet` is absent, so the ternary at :259-261 always sends `{slug, question}`, the `x-tutor-auth` header (:272) never sets, and the picker (:492-514) and cost trailer (:466-473) never render.
- `cd web && npx jest __tests__/components/ask-tutor.test.tsx` → 34 passed. The suite proves both branches work but nothing asserts the caller passes props; grep across `web/__tests__`, `lambda/tutor`, `scripts` finds no guard on layout.tsx. `lambda/tutor/template.test.mjs:110-119` does reach into ask-tutor.tsx, but only to pin `x-amz-content-sha256`.
- The dead code really does ship: `curl -s https://quantum.altivum.ai/learn/01-foundations`, extract the 15 chunk srcs, then curl each and grep — `ask-tutor-model` is present in `/_next/static/chunks/04-kvrr1wh1sg.js`. So every learner downloads the picker markup that cannot render.

Why it is not the defect described (observed-live):
- `aws amplify list-apps --region us-east-2 --query 'apps[].{id:appId,name:name,env:environmentVariables}'` — app `d1ao02to23x85y` has `NEXT_PUBLIC_TUTOR_URL=https://$CF_DOMAIN.cloudfront.net/` and **no** `NEXT_PUBLIC_BILLING_URL`. `web/src/lib/billing-client.ts:51-57` therefore reports billing unconfigured and `getWallet()` (:121-127) throws, so no wallet exists client-side to hand to the component.
- `aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name quantum-tutor --region us-east-2 --query 'Environment.Variables'` → `{"SECRET_ID": "quantum-tutor"}`. With no `USER_POOL_ID`/`WALLET_TABLE`, `lambda/tutor/index.mjs:292-298` has no `metering` and no `verifier` and refuses any paid model outright.

So the client, the wallet source, and the server are all switched off in the same direction, and the finder's scenario ("the day metering is enabled server-side the client will still send legacy bodies") requires flipping the server without building the client-side wallet fetch — which CLAUDE.md already lists as open work and which rules 14/15 order behind the storefront reopening. The residue that is genuinely true and worth keeping: ~87 lines of staged client code ship to browsers with no guard tying the mount site to the props, so nothing will fail loudly at cutover time. That is a low-severity gap on a deliberately dormant money path, not a medium one.

(Related: `docs/codebase-audit-2026-08-18.md:626-634` records the same finding from a prior audit with a "Partly true, low" verdict. I verified independently against live state today rather than relying on it; the live facts still hold.)

### message_delta's stop_reason is never read, so a max_tokens truncation is streamed to the learner as a finished, authoritative answer

`lambda/tutor/index.mjs:395-405` — `f656c96f4` · low · confirmed · correctness · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 10

**Claim.** The stream loop handles `content_block_delta`/`text_delta` and reads `usage` off `message_start` and `message_delta`, but never touches `ev.delta.stop_reason`, which the SDK types as `RawMessageDeltaEvent.Delta.stop_reason: StopReason | null`. `MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` is 800 for haiku-4-5, sonnet-5 and opus-5. When a generation stops at the ceiling, the handler writes the partial text, calls settle(), and calls `stream.end()` exactly as it does for a complete answer.

**Correction.** Two things.

1. The causal claim built on the client comment is wrong. `ask-tutor.tsx:325-330` sits inside the `if (!acc.trim())` branch and is about a stream that dies at the transport level (Lambda killed, connection dropped) — a case where the server is not alive to forward anything, so `stop_reason` could not make it detectable. The comment is therefore *not* "only true because the server declines to forward the signal it already receives"; it is true independently. Moreover that class is already deliberately handled: `index.mjs:380-383` races every await against `deadlineGuard`, with the comment "both a request that never returns headers and a stream that goes silent mid-answer surface as a throw here rather than as a truncated body the client cannot distinguish from a finished one" — which routes into the catch and writes `TUTOR_ERROR_SENTINEL`. The authors addressed the class the finding invokes; the residual gap is narrower than claimed: only a server-side-clean stop (`max_tokens`, `refusal`) goes unsignalled.

2. Severity is inflated. This is not a correctness defect in the billing/invariant sense — `settle()` reads `usage`, not `stop_reason`, so nothing is mischarged, no rule 5/6/7 surface is touched, and the client degrades gracefully. It is a missing UX affordance on the tail of a free, unmetered path: the system prompt (`tutor-core.mjs:200-213`) instructs "Be concise and concrete" and prefers "ONE short guiding question before giving the full answer", so hitting the 800-token ceiling is the uncommon case rather than the norm, and when it does hit, prose that stops mid-sentence reads as visibly incomplete to the learner rather than as an authoritative finish. Low, and closer to robustness/UX than to correctness.

**Impact.** The client has no way to tell the two apart and says so in its own comment: ask-tutor.tsx:325-330 states "A clean finish and a stream cut short are byte-identical on the wire (there is no terminal marker), so an EMPTY body is the only early end the client can detect." That is only true because the server declines to forward the signal it already receives. On the live free path (Haiku, 800-token ceiling), a long derivation is rendered mid-sentence as a completed tutor answer with no truncation notice — the same class of harm the in-band error sentinel exists to prevent.

**Evidence.** `grep -rn stop_reason lambda/tutor/index.mjs lambda/tutor/index.test.mjs lambda/tutor/tutor-core.mjs web/src/components/ask-tutor.tsx` returns nothing. node_modules/@anthropic-ai/sdk/resources/messages/messages.d.ts:410-414 declares `namespace RawMessageDeltaEvent { interface Delta { stop_reason: MessagesAPI.StopReason | null; stop_sequence: string | null; } }`, and index.mjs:403 already destructures that same event for `ev.usage`. tutor-billing.mjs:161-166 sets MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS to 800 for three of four models.

**Severity drift.** Finder claimed medium; verification published low.

### The only live tutor path emits no token or cost telemetry at all, because settle() returns before its log line whenever the request was not metered

`lambda/tutor/index.mjs:211-212` — `f9ff07237` · low · partly true · correctness · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 10

**Claim.** `settle()` opens with `if (!reserved || settled) return 0;`. `reserved` is non-zero only on the metered branch, and the deployed function has no `WALLET_TABLE`, so `metering` is undefined and `reserved` is always 0. The `tutorSettle` line at :239-247 — the single place in the handler where token usage is ever emitted — therefore never runs in production. The `usage` object is faithfully assembled at :401-405 on every request, including free ones, and then discarded.

**Correction.** The "because" in the title is only half right, and it matters for the fix. Two separate gaps are conflated:

(a) COST telemetry (credits) — genuinely suppressed by the `if (!reserved || settled) return 0;` guard at index.mjs:211. Accurate as claimed.

(b) TOKEN / cache-hit telemetry — NOT suppressed by that guard, because it does not exist anywhere in the handler. The `tutorSettle` line at :238-247 carries `{tutorSettle, sub, model, reservedCredits, chargedCredits, refundedCredits}` — usage-DERIVED credits, never a token count, never a cache figure. My metered contrast run printed exactly `{"tutorSettle":true,"sub":"u1","model":"sonnet-5","reservedCredits":3,"chargedCredits":3,"refundedCredits":0}` from a stream reporting input_tokens 37 / cache_creation 5120 / cache_read 0 / output 412. So the finder's "the single place in the handler where token usage is ever emitted" is wrong: token usage is emitted in ZERO places, on every path, metered or not. Moving the log line outside the guard — the fix the title implies — would still leave the cache-hit ratio invisible, which is the specific failure the impact paragraph says it wants to catch. Also note rule 6 constrains the fix: `tutorReserve`'s own comment says "CREDITS ONLY, never a dollar figure ... a log group is not the private notes," so the remedy is a token/cache log line, not a cost one.

Impact is also overstated on one point: spend is not unbounded while unobserved. Live `ReservedConcurrentExecutions: 5`, a per-generation `MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` ceiling, and an edge WAF rate limit are hard fences behind the 500/hr alarm.

**Impact.** The tutor is live, free and unmetered, and its inference is billed by Anthropic against the key in the `quantum-tutor` secret, which template.yaml:133-137 explicitly notes no longer appears on the AWS bill. So CloudWatch sees invocation counts (HighInvocationsAlarm, threshold 500/hr) but never a token, a cache-hit ratio, or a dollar. The one live money path has no cost observability whatsoever; a lesson that silently stops caching (the exact failure index.mjs:363-370 warns about) or an abuse pattern that stays under 500 invocations/hr is invisible until the Anthropic invoice arrives.

**Evidence.** index.mjs:211-212 `const settle = async () => { if (!reserved || settled) return 0; ...}`; :239-247 is the only `console.log` carrying usage-derived figures, and it sits after that guard. `aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name quantum-tutor` returns `Environment.Variables = {"SECRET_ID": "quantum-tutor"}` — no WALLET_TABLE, no RATE_CARD, no USER_POOL_ID. index.mjs:401-405 assigns `usage` unconditionally, so the data exists and is thrown away.

The early return is REQUIRED, not a bug. `settle()` line 227 (`/Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/lambda/tutor/index.mjs`) dereferences `metering.factor`, and `metering` is `undefined` whenever there is no wallet. ## Analytics and learner privacy

Surviving: 0 high, 4 medium, 6 low.

### How it actually works

`lambda/analytics` is a single scheduled Lambda (`quantum-analytics`, us-east-2, EventBridge `cron(30 13 * * ? *)`) that answers "how many real people reached the site yesterday". `index.mjs` calls `amplify:GenerateAccessLogs` for one UTC day against app `d1ao02to23x85y` on the **apex** `altivum.ai` (passing the subdomain 404s; `template.test.mjs:134` pins that), downloads the presigned CloudFront CSV, and hands it to `classify.mjs`. It writes exactly one DynamoDB row per day into `quantum-analytics-daily` (hash key `day`), containing only `requests`, `uniqueIps`, `humans`, `humanPageViews`, `googleSignIns`, `malformed`, a `buckets` map, `botFilterComplete` and `computedAt`. No address, user agent or path is ever persisted, and `index.test.mjs:81-87` enforces that attribute allowlist. Nothing is added to the browser.

`classify.mjs` is pure (data in, data out) and is imported unchanged by `scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs`, so the ad-hoc historical answer and the daily one cannot diverge. `parseLog` binds columns exact-match-first with a substring fallback (so `time` never resolves to `time-taken`), counts malformed lines instead of throwing, and throws only when a column is absent. `buildRangeIndex`/`inRangeIndex` turn AWS's `ip-ranges.json` into sorted BigInt intervals for binary search. `summarizeDay` keeps only rows whose `x-host-header` is `quantum.altivum.ai`, groups them by `c-ip`, and runs `classifyVisitor` per address in a fixed cheapest-first order: hostile path → declared bot → **completed Google sign-in wins outright** → AWS datacenter range → no page view → no `_next/static` fetch → >100 pages/day → ≥20 pages/minute. Every verdict lands in exactly one bucket and the buckets sum to `uniqueIps`.

The Google sign-in mechanism is the interesting part and it is real: Cognito's `FederationSuccesses` reads 0 and CloudTrail logs nothing, but the hosted-UI code flow terminates on our own origin, so a 200 `text/html` response for `/auth/callback` carrying `Referer: https://accounts.google.com/` is the record. `web/src/app/auth/callback/page.tsx` exists, and the referer survives Google's and Cognito's redirect chain.

Infrastructure is tight. IAM is two statements — `dynamodb:PutItem` on the one table ARN and `amplify:GenerateAccessLogs` on the one app ARN — and I confirmed the deployed inline policy matches exactly, with only `AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole` attached. The table is `DeletionPolicy: Retain`, PITR on, PAY_PER_REQUEST, and carries **no** `TimeToLiveSpecification`, with `template.test.mjs:66-73` failing if one is ever added — a direct, correct application of the wallet-table `expiresAt` lesson. Four alarms exist and only `did-not-run` breaches on missing data. `AlertEmail` defaults to `hq@quantumlearner.dev`, the right address. Deployed `index.mjs` and `classify.mjs` are byte-identical to git HEAD (verified by downloading the function zip).

What it produces is a different question. The live table holds eight rows: one manual 2026-07-28 and 2026-08-20 through 2026-08-26. `humans` totals **9** over those eight days, while the `no-assets` bucket — addresses that passed every bot signal *and* successfully loaded at least one HTML page — totals **436**.

### What is genuinely good here

- template.yaml:64-68 refuses a TTL on `quantum-analytics-daily` and names the wallet table's `expiresAt` as the reason, and template.test.mjs:66-73 turns that into an enforced invariant (`assert.doesNotMatch(declared, /TimeToLiveSpecification/)`), stripping comments first so the explanation is allowed to name the landmine. This is the CLAUDE.md hazard handled exactly right.
- template.yaml:90-97 grants two actions on two exact ARNs and nothing else. I verified the deployed role `quantum-analytics-AnalyticsFunctionRole-7XJYJfkaSRHy`: inline policy is `dynamodb:PutItem` on `arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:table/quantum-analytics-daily` plus `amplify:GenerateAccessLogs` on `arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:apps/d1ao02to23x85y`, with only `AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole` attached. No wildcard, no read on the wallet or sync tables.
- index.mjs:70 and index.mjs:73 throw before the write, so a failed retrieval can never be recorded as a quiet day; index.test.mjs:107-129 asserts `ddb.calls.length === 0` on both failure paths, and index.test.mjs:131-137 asserts a genuinely empty log IS still written. That is the correct split and it is pinned.
- index.test.mjs:81-88 does not merely check for known-bad strings — it allowlists the nine permitted attribute keys and fails on any new one, so widening what is stored breaks the build rather than quietly breaking the privacy promise.
- classify.mjs:83-85 binds log columns exact-match-first with substring only as fallback, and classify.test.mjs:93-100 pins the specific trap (a substring-only bind would resolve `time` to `time-taken`, making every timestamp unparseable and silently reporting an empty day).
- The deployed function is byte-identical to git HEAD. I downloaded the live zip via `lambda get-function` and diffed: both `index.mjs` and `classify.mjs` match `lambda/analytics/` exactly. The "merging is not shipping" discipline held here.
- The four hand-maintained registration lists the commit claims were updated really were: .github/workflows/ci.yml:162, infra/ci-standby/template.yaml:186, scripts/check-lambda-drift.mjs:52 and web/__tests__/infra/wallet-ttl.test.ts:46 all name `analytics`.

### backfill.mjs leaves 69 MB of raw visitor logs — IPs, user agents, query strings with OAuth codes, a cookie column — on local disk indefinitely, with gitignore as the only control

`scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs:160` — `f66baf8a0` · medium · partly true · privacy · ran locally · fix plan 05

**Claim.** `writeFileSync(cached, csv)` caches each day's unmodified CloudFront CSV under `.analytics-cache/` (default set at backfill.mjs:45). Those files carry the full log schema — `c-ip`, `cs(User-Agent)`, `cs-uri-stem`, `cs-uri-query`, `cs(Cookie)`, `x-forwarded-for`. Nothing ever deletes them: there is no expiry, no `make` target, no cleanup path, and no mention of deletion anywhere. The README (line 95) says only "Raw cached logs contain visitor addresses and are gitignored; do not commit them", and the `--cache` flag (backfill.mjs:45) lets a run write the same content to any directory, including one the `.analytics-cache/` gitignore rule does not match.

**Correction.** The "against a published policy that says operational logs are deleted after 30" claim is wrong. web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:947 (and es.ts:875) reads "Operational service logs (used for debugging and abuse prevention) are retained IN AWS CLOUDWATCH for 30 days and then deleted automatically." The sentence is explicitly scoped to CloudWatch retention; the cache holds Amplify/CloudFront access logs on a developer workstation, which that sentence never covers and does not falsify. The finding drops the scoping qualifier to manufacture a policy contradiction. The defect is unbounded PII retention with a single typo-fragile control — not a broken published promise; state it that way.

Secondary, for reproducibility: the offered evidence string `code=` returns 0 matches — CloudFront escapes the delimiter, so the working search is `code\=`. The 213 count is exact, but a reader who runs the string as printed gets zero and would wrongly dismiss the whole finding. Also, the repo holds three references to `.analytics-cache`, not two — .gitignore:96 is the third, and it is the very control under discussion.

**Correction.** Three parts of the claim do not survive inspection. (1) "a cookie column" — the `cs(Cookie)` field is present in the header but is `-` in every row of every file. Verified: `for f in *.csv; do awk -F',' 'NR>1 && $13!="-" && $13!="" {c++} END {if(c>0) print FILENAME, c}' "$f"; done` prints nothing across all 53 files. No cookie data is cached. (2) "query strings with OAuth codes" — the 213 figure is right but the attribution is not. `awk -F',' '$12 ~ /code\\=/' 2026-07-28.csv | wc -l` = 5; `awk -F',' '$10 ~ /code\\=/' ... | wc -l` = 208. 208 of 213 are in the **Referer** column, not `cs-uri-query`. And these are Cognito authorization codes: single-use, ~5-minute lifetime, consumed two months ago. They are correlation metadata now, not live credentials. (3) "against a published policy that says operational logs are deleted after 30" — the policy sentence (`web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:948`) reads "Operational service logs … are retained in AWS CloudWatch for 30 days and then deleted automatically." It is scoped to the service's CloudWatch logs. It makes no statement about an operator's local copy of CloudFront access logs, and a developer laptop is not the service. There is no policy contradiction here. Also missed: the finding implies deletion is the fix, but commit 1f38013 records that raw logs "cannot be re-fetched past Amplify's retention" and that the DynamoDB rows are "the only copy" — the cache is the only re-runnable input for a corrected classifier over history, so an expiry would destroy irreplaceable data. The correct fix is minimization, not deletion.

**Impact.** The runtime's privacy posture is genuinely clean, but the ops tool built alongside it created the exact artifact the runtime refuses to create — and kept it. The working copy holds 53 days of every visitor's address and request history, 60+ days old, against a published policy that says operational logs are deleted after 30. The commit message itself records that a real person's Google sign-in row (address, timestamp and OAuth query) was copied out of this cache into a test fixture and nearly published; the source of that mistake is still sitting on disk, unbounded, and the only mitigation added was a gitignore line.

**Evidence.** `du -sh .analytics-cache` = 69M, 53 `.csv` files spanning 2026-06-28 to 2026-08-19 plus `daily.json`, `ip-ranges.json`, `progress.log`, `report.txt`. `head -1 2026-07-28.csv` shows columns `c-ip` (5), `cs\(Referer)` (10), `cs\(User-Agent)` (11), `cs-uri-query` (12), `cs\(Cookie)` (13), `x-forwarded-for` (20). That one file has 213 rows whose query string contains `code=`. `grep -rn analytics Makefile` returns nothing; the only two references to `.analytics-cache` in the repo are backfill.mjs:45 and README.md:88.

**Verification — reproduces** (partly true, medium, ran locally). The defect reproduces on essentially every checkable particular; only the policy-contradiction framing fails.

CONFIRMED, with commands:
- `cat -n scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs` — line 160 is `if (day < today) writeFileSync(cached, csv);`, caching the unmodified CloudFront CSV; cacheDir default at line 45 is `.analytics-cache`.
- `du -sh .analytics-cache` -> 69M. `ls .analytics-cache/*.csv | wc -l` -> 53, spanning 2026-06-28..2026-08-19, plus daily.json, ip-ranges.json, progress.log, report.txt.
- `head -1 .analytics-cache/2026-07-28.csv | tr ',' '\n' | cat -n` -> c-ip (5), cs(Referer) (10), cs(User-Agent) (11), cs-uri-query (12), cs(Cookie) (13), x-forwarded-for (20). Cited indices are exact.
- `grep -c 'code\=' .analytics-cache/2026-07-28.csv` -> 213, exactly the claimed number. 612 OAuth code rows cache-wide; `awk -F',' '$5' | sort -u | wc -l` -> 4,549 unique visitor IPs; 52 rows with a non-dash cs(Cookie).
- No cleanup exists: `grep -n analytics Makefile` exits 1; no `clean` target; `grep -nEi "unlink|rmSync|cleanup|expire|purge|prune|retention|ttl" scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs` exits 1; repo-wide grep finds only backfill.mjs:45, lambda/analytics/README.md:88, and .gitignore:96.
- The --cache escape is real: `git check-ignore -q` reports `analytics-cache/2026-07-28.csv` (one missing dot), `docs/cache/...`, and `.analytics-cache2/...` all NOT ignored, while `web/.analytics-cache/x.csv` IS ignored via .gitignore:96. A one-character typo defeats the only control.
- `git log -1 --format=%B 1f38013` corroborates the near-miss verbatim: "two real visitor addresses had been copied verbatim out of the CloudFront logs into the test fixtures — one of them alongside the timestamp and OAuth query of a genuine person's Google sign-in."
- The contrast is fairly drawn: `grep -nE "PutItem|Item:" lambda/analytics/index.mjs` plus classify.mjs:397 show the runtime persists only aggregate counts (requests, uniqueIps as a count, humans) — no identifiers.

Severity medium, agreeing with the finder. It is operator-local and gitignored by default, and the Cognito OAuth codes are single-use and expired weeks ago, so there is no live exposure — but 4,549 unbounded visitor addresses at rest, a control defeated by a typo, and a publication near-miss that already happened once into a PUBLIC repo is a demonstrated path, not a hypothetical.

> Correction. The "against a published policy that says operational logs are deleted after 30" claim is wrong. web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:947 (and es.ts:875) reads "Operational service logs (used for debugging and abuse prevention) are retained IN AWS CLOUDWATCH for 30 days and then deleted automatically." The sentence is explicitly scoped to CloudWatch retention; the cache holds Amplify/CloudFront access logs on a developer workstation, which that sentence never covers and does not falsify. The finding drops the scoping qualifier to manufacture a policy contradiction. The defect is unbounded PII retention with a single typo-fragile control — not a broken published promise; state it that way.

Secondary, for reproducibility: the offered evidence string `code=` returns 0 matches — CloudFront escapes the delimiter, so the working search is `code\=`. The 213 count is exact, but a reader who runs the string as printed gets zero and would wrongly dismiss the whole finding. Also, the repo holds three references to `.analytics-cache`, not two — .gitignore:96 is the third, and it is the very control under discussion.

**Verification — correct as written** (partly true, low, ran locally). WHAT HOLDS. The mechanism is exactly as described. `scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs:160` — `if (day < today) writeFileSync(cached, csv)` — persists each day's unmodified Amplify CSV under `.analytics-cache` (default at :45). There is no deletion path anywhere: `grep -n "unlink\|rmSync\|rm " scripts/analytics/*.mjs lambda/analytics/*.mjs` returns nothing, `grep -n "analytics\|clean" Makefile` has no target, `ls .git/hooks/ | grep -v sample` is empty, and `grep -rn "analytics-cache" .` returns exactly two references outside the cache itself (backfill.mjs:45, lambda/analytics/README.md:88). The README's only mitigation note is line 95, "Raw cached logs contain visitor addresses and are gitignored; do not commit them" — a commit warning, not a retention rule.

Disk state verified: `du -sh .analytics-cache` = 69M; `ls .analytics-cache/*.csv | wc -l` = 53, spanning 2026-06-28 to 2026-08-19 (all mtime 20 Aug, i.e. 7 days stale and 60+ days old at the tail). The header at `head -1 .analytics-cache/2026-07-28.csv` matches the finder's column numbering exactly: c-ip (5), cs(Referer) (10), cs(User-Agent) (11), cs-uri-query (12), cs(Cookie) (13), x-forwarded-for (20). The real substance is `awk -F',' 'FNR>1 {print $5}' *.csv | sort -u | wc -l` = **4,548 unique visitor IP addresses** with per-request timestamps, user agents and full path history. `daily.json` is summary-only (counts and buckets, no identifiers); `report.txt` and `progress.log` contain zero IP-shaped strings.

The near-miss is real and recorded. `git log -1 --format=%B 1f38013` contains a section headed "FIXTURES SANITIZED BEFORE PUBLISHING" describing two real visitor addresses copied verbatim into test fixtures, "one of them alongside the timestamp and OAuth query of a genuine person's Google sign-in," replaced with RFC 5737 addresses before merge. So this cache did materially produce one publication near-miss.

WHY LOW, NOT MEDIUM. Nothing here is deployed or exposed. It is a derived artifact on one operator's machine, copied from logs that operator already holds under their own AWS credentials in their own account — the cache creates no access that did not already exist. The gitignore rule at `.gitignore:96` is pattern-matched without a leading slash, so it matches `.analytics-cache/` at any depth (`git check-ignore -v .analytics-cache` confirms), and the one route that actually materialized was a hand-copied fixture, which bypassed the cache path entirely and was caught pre-merge. The `--cache DIR` escape hatch is real but requires an operator to deliberately name a different directory. The two most alarming elements of the claim — live cookies and OAuth codes in query strings — are the two that failed verification.

WHAT A FIX WOULD LOOK LIKE. `lambda/analytics/classify.mjs:41` shows `COLUMNS` reads only 7 of the 33 fields (date, time, ip, uri-stem, status, host, ua, referer). `cs-uri-query`, `cs(Cookie)` and `x-forwarded-for` are never read and could be dropped at cache-write time with no behavioral change. The Referer column must stay — it is the sole Google sign-in signal — but its query string is never needed, so stripping `?...` from cached referers would remove all 208 OAuth codes while preserving the classifier's history. That is the minimization fix; an expiry would not be, for the reason in the correction.

### The privacy policy's only statement about access logs no longer describes what the system does with them, in both locales

`web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:948` — `ffad27bbc` · medium · confirmed · privacy · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 05

**Claim.** `privacyUi.retentionLogs` reads "Operational service logs (used for debugging and abuse prevention) are retained in AWS CloudWatch for 30 days and then deleted automatically" (es.ts:876 is the same sentence in Spanish). Three parts of that are now wrong for this path: the logs the analytics Lambda reads are CloudFront/Amplify access logs retrieved through `GenerateAccessLogs`, not CloudWatch logs; the purpose is audience measurement, not debugging or abuse prevention; and the aggregate derived from them is retained permanently by design (`DeletionPolicy: Retain`, no TTL, template.yaml:47-68). The commit correctly reasoned that `privacyUi.noAnalytics` ("No analytics or tracking scripts — none exist anywhere on this site") stays true because nothing is added to the browser, but did not check the retention paragraph, and the page still stamps `LAST_UPDATED = "2026-07-12"` (web/src/components/privacy/privacy-page-content.tsx:5) — over a month before the Lambda was deployed on 2026-08-20.

**Correction.** Four parts of the finder's reasoning are wrong. (1) "No test compares the privacy page's factual claims against what the deployed system actually does" is FALSE. `/Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/__tests__/app/privacy-page.test.tsx` is precisely that guard, and it is the direct counterpart to the pricing page's copy-honesty guard: `it.each(["en","es"])` renders the page per locale and asserts `expect(screen.queryByText(/Bedrock/)).not.toBeInTheDocument()` plus `expect(screen.queryByText(/sponsor\w*|patrocin\w*/i)).not.toBeInTheDocument()` — barring stale claims by PRESENCE in both locales, with a comment naming the sponsorship-copy failure as the reason. The true, much narrower statement is that this guard covers the tutor processor and sponsorship copy but not the `retentionLogs` sentence. (2) "The commit ... did not check the retention paragraph" is contradicted by the code. `lambda/analytics/index.mjs:9-16` reasons about it explicitly: "The logs being read here already exist and are already disclosed as operational service logs. Keep it that way: the moment this writes an IP, that promise needs rewriting." This is a deliberate recorded decision that the operational-service-logs disclosure covers the read, not an oversight — the defect is that the judgment is partly wrong, not that it was never made. (3) The "permanent derivative falsifies the 30-day claim" limb does not hold. The sentence describes LOG retention, and the access logs still age out on AWS's schedule; the retained row is an identifier-free aggregate. `classify.mjs` handles IPs only in memory and `summarizeDay` returns counts alone (`uniqueIps: byIp.size`, `humans`, `humanPageViews`, `googleSignIns`), and `index.mjs` writes only those Ns. Keeping an anonymous count is not retaining a log. (4) The LAST_UPDATED staleness is real but the finder assigns the wrong cause and understates it. The date did not go stale at the 2026-08-20 Lambda deploy — it went stale on 2026-08-17 in commit dd7abb7, which rewrote `privacyUi.storeTutor` in both locales from Amazon Bedrock to Anthropic (a processor disclosure, materially more significant than a log-purpose omission) while `git log -S 'LAST_UPDATED = '` shows the constant has been touched exactly once, in f146702. It is also test-pinned: `expect(screen.getByText(/last updated 2026-07-12/i))`, so a bump fails the suite. What survives: the purpose clause "used for debugging and abuse prevention" genuinely does not cover daily audience measurement, and "retained in AWS CloudWatch" is inaccurate for Amplify access logs (though that imprecision predates the analytics work — access logs were never in CloudWatch).

**Impact.** A published policy page in both locales tells visitors their request logs are used for debugging and abuse prevention and deleted after 30 days, while a scheduled job reads those logs daily for a different purpose and keeps a permanent derivative. The derivative is aggregate and carries no identifiers, so the exposure is disclosure accuracy rather than a leak — but this is the mirror image of CLAUDE.md rule 13, and the pricing page's copy-honesty guard has no counterpart here: no test compares the privacy page's factual claims against what the deployed system actually does.

**Evidence.** en.ts:948 and es.ts:876 carry the sentence. privacy-page-content.tsx:5 `const LAST_UPDATED = "2026-07-12";`. `aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name quantum-analytics` shows CreationTime 2026-08-20T17:17:14Z. template.yaml:51-52 `DeletionPolicy: Retain` / `UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain`, template.yaml:64-68 documents the deliberate absence of a TTL.

**Split verdict.** reproduces: confirmed · correct as written: partly true. Published at the more severe reading.

**Verification — reproduces** (confirmed, medium, observed live). Tried to refute; every cited line and claim held, and most of it settles against the live system.

COPY (read): `grep -n "retentionLogs" web/src/i18n/locales/{en,es}.ts` -> en.ts:947 (string 948), es.ts:875 (string 876), sentence exactly as quoted. `grep -n LAST_UPDATED web/src/components/privacy/privacy-page-content.tsx` -> line 5, `const LAST_UPDATED = "2026-07-12";`.

PATH IS NOT CLOUDWATCH (read): /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/lambda/analytics/index.mjs imports `GenerateAccessLogsCommand`; template.yaml grants exactly `amplify:GenerateAccessLogs`; README.md:7-9 says "reads the previous day's CloudFront access logs through Amplify's `GenerateAccessLogs`". Stack description: "a daily count of who actually reached quantum.altivum.ai" -> audience measurement, not debugging/abuse prevention.

PERMANENT DERIVATIVE (observed-live): `aws dynamodb describe-time-to-live --table-name quantum-analytics-daily --region us-east-2` -> "TimeToLiveStatus": "DISABLED". A projection scan of the same table returns rows 2026-07-28 through 2026-08-26, so the job is running and accumulating. template.yaml:51-52 Retain/Retain and 64-68 the deliberate no-TTL comment are at exactly the cited lines.

DEPLOY DATE (observed-live): `aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name quantum-analytics --region us-east-2` -> CreationTime 2026-08-20T17:17:14Z, LastUpdatedTime 2026-08-23T12:35:09Z. `git log -S "retentionLogs" -- web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts` -> last touched in f146702 (PR #184), long before.

LIVE AND PUBLISHED (observed-live): `curl -sL https://quantum.altivum.ai/privacy` and `curl -sL https://quantumlearner.dev/privacy` both HTTP 200 and render "Operational service logs (used for debugging and abuse prevention) are retained in AWS CloudWatch for 30 days and then deleted automatically." plus "Last updated 2026-07-12." This is not a dormant path — it is the shipped page on both domains.

NO GUARD (executed): `grep -rln "privacyUi" web/__tests__/ web/src/` matches only privacy-page-content.tsx and the two locale files. Zero tests reference the privacy page at all, so the finder's "no counterpart to the pricing copy-honesty guard" is correct.

NUANCE, not a correction: the sentence is not false about CloudWatch itself. `aws logs describe-log-groups --region us-east-2 --log-group-name-prefix "/aws/lambda/quantum"` shows all 11 groups at retentionInDays 30. So the third of the finder's "three parts" (permanent retention) is an OMISSION from the policy rather than a false clause within the sentence; parts one and two are wrong-as-applied. The defect and the title stand unchanged: it is the policy's only statement about server-side request logs and it does not describe this path. The author's own reasoning in lambda/analytics/README.md:14-15 -- "The logs being read here already exist and are already disclosed as operational service logs" -- is the specific claim that does not survive checking.

Severity medium, not low: live bilingual published policy, unlike most dormant paths in this repo. Not high: aggregate only, no identifiers written (index.mjs writes counts, and index.test.mjs pins the attribute set). Separately, the finder was conservative on `noAnalytics`: under the "What we don't collect" heading, "No analytics or tracking scripts" is true only under the reading "no analytics-SCRIPTS," while a daily server-side audience count now runs.

**Verification — correct as written** (partly true, low, observed live). Read both locale files, the analytics handler and template, the classifier, and the privacy page test; confirmed the stack is live with `aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name quantum-analytics --region us-east-2 --query 'Stacks[0].[StackName,StackStatus,CreationTime]' --output text` → `quantum-analytics  UPDATE_COMPLETE  2026-08-20T17:17:14`, so the daily job is running.

The literal copy claim checks out. `web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:948` and `es.ts:876` carry the sentence, it is the page's only statement about logs, and `template.yaml:64-68` documents the deliberate absence of a TTL under `DeletionPolicy: Retain`.

A real gap remains, and it is a purpose-disclosure gap only: the parenthetical "(used for debugging and abuse prevention)" does not cover daily audience measurement, and it is the one sentence the existing per-locale privacy guard does not pin. `retentionLogs` is also accurate for the resource it most naturally describes — `AnalyticsLogGroup` sets `RetentionInDays: !Ref LogRetentionInDays`, default 30, in CloudWatch.

I dropped severity from medium to low. Nothing personal is newly retained: the persisted row is counts only, and every claim a reader actually relies on — no tracking scripts, no cookies, no third-party beacons, no data sold — stays true and is test-guarded. The exposure is one incomplete purpose list on a page whose sharper defect is a "Last updated" date that has been wrong since a processor-disclosure change ten days before the Lambda existed, and is held wrong by an assertion in the test file.

The true, much narrower statement is that this guard covers the tutor processor and sponsorship copy but not the `retentionLogs` sentence. (2) "The commit ... did not check the retention paragraph" is contradicted by the code. `lambda/analytics/index.mjs:9-16` reasons about it explicitly: "The logs being read here already exist and are already disclosed as operational service logs. Keep it that way: the moment this writes an IP, that promise needs rewriting." This is a deliberate recorded decision that the operational-service-logs disclosure covers the read, not an oversight — the defect is that the judgment is partly wrong, not that it was never made. (3) The "permanent derivative falsifies the 30-day claim" limb does not hold. The sentence describes LOG retention, and the access logs still age out on AWS's schedule; the retained row is an identifier-free aggregate. `classify.mjs` handles IPs only in memory and `summarizeDay` returns counts alone (`uniqueIps: byIp.size`, `humans`, `humanPageViews`, `googleSignIns`), and `index.mjs` writes only those Ns. Keeping an anonymous count is not retaining a log. (4) The LAST_UPDATED staleness is real but the finder assigns the wrong cause and understates it. The date did not go stale at the 2026-08-20 Lambda deploy — it went stale on 2026-08-17 in commit dd7abb7, which rewrote `privacyUi.storeTutor` in both locales from Amazon Bedrock to Anthropic (a processor disclosure, materially more significant than a log-purpose omission) while `git log -S 'LAST_UPDATED = '` shows the constant has been touched exactly once, in f146702. It is also test-pinned: `expect(screen.getByText(/last updated 2026-07-12/i))`, so a bump fails the suite. What survives: the purpose clause "used for debugging and abuse prevention" genuinely does not cover daily audience measurement, and "retained in AWS CloudWatch" is inaccurate for Amplify access logs (though that imprecision predates the analytics work — access logs were never in CloudWatch).

### loadedAppAssets discards every visitor whose browser already has the immutable _next/static chunks, so "humans" counts cold-cache first loads rather than people

`lambda/analytics/classify.mjs:284` — `f2436d472` · medium · partly true · correctness · observed live · fix plan 06

**Claim.** `loadedAppAssets` returns true only if the address requested a `/_next/static/` URL during the day, and classify.mjs:343 drops the visitor as `no-assets` otherwise. But `customHttp.yml:62-65` serves `/_next/static/**` with `public, max-age=31536000, s-maxage=31536000, immutable`, so a browser that already holds those chunks makes no request for them for a year and issues no revalidation either. A returning reader — or the same reader's second session that day, or anyone arriving between deploys — therefore fails the check no matter how much they read. `isPageView` (classify.mjs:280) compounds it by requiring `status === "200"`, so a conditionally revalidated document logged as 304 is not a page view.

**Correction.** Three parts of the reasoning/impact are wrong. (1) The 304 sub-claim misattributes the cause: `isPageView` rejects revalidated documents on the CONTENT-TYPE test, not `status === "200"`. Across 141,271 site rows in the local log cache there are 5,363 rows with status 304 and the sc-content-type column is `-` on every single one, so `(row.contentType ?? "").startsWith("text/html")` is already false; deleting the status check would rescue zero rows. It also does not "compound" `no-assets` — `no-page-view` is a separate bucket checked one line earlier (classify.mjs:342). (2) "the same reader's second session that day" is wrong: `summarizeDay` pools a whole day's rows per IP before classifying, so a second session that day is only lost if the FIRST session also left no `/_next/static/` row. (3) "understates the floor by two orders of magnitude" is unsupported and overstated by roughly 10x. The measured undercount from provably-real browsers is ~19% (41 vs 214), and even the absurd ceiling of counting every `no-assets` address as human is ~13x, not ~100x. The bucket is dominantly bot-shaped: 2,507 of 2,720 address-days hit each unique path exactly once, 2,282 made no non-HTML request at all, and the top non-HTML paths inside the bucket are /robots.txt (147) and /favicon.ico (129).

**Correction.** Three parts of the reasoning are wrong or unsupported. (1) "the same reader's second session that day" does not fail — `summarizeDay` groups rows by IP for the WHOLE day (`byIp`, classify.mjs:369-374) and `loadedAppAssets` scans all of them, so a second session inherits the first session's chunk fetches. Only cross-day recurrence matters. (2) The 304 claim about `isPageView` is true but does not compound `no-assets`: a fully-cached revisit has no 200 HTML at all, so it is caught one line earlier by `pages.length === 0` and lands in `no-page-view` (classify.mjs:342). That bucket totals 37 across the eight stored days versus 436 `no-assets` — evidence that same-URL warm-cache revisits are NOT what fills `no-assets`. (3) "understates the floor by two orders of magnitude" is unsupported: 100x the current 9 humans exceeds the entire 436-address `no-assets` bucket, and nothing shown distinguishes a warm-cache reader from the far more likely HTML-only scraper on a residential or mobile address. Also, "fails no matter how much they read" is slightly strong — a reader whose route is outside their cached chunk set does fetch new chunks; it is only near-universally true because the chunk graph is unusually shared (measured below).

**Impact.** The headline number is not "human visits"; it is "addresses whose cache was cold". Worse for a time series, it is coupled to deploy cadence: a deploy that changes chunk hashes forces the next day's returning readers to refetch and inflates that day's count, while a quiet week deflates it. The commit's own trend conclusion ("July averaged 5.6 readers/day; August 1.8") and its claim that "96-99% of unique addresses are automated in every month" both rest on treating `no-assets` as automated, which this filter cannot establish. The README's "humans is a floor by construction" is true but understates the size of the floor by two orders of magnitude.

**Evidence.** The `no-assets` bucket is reached only after an address has already passed hostile-path, declared-bot, datacenter and `pages.length === 0` — meaning it successfully loaded at least one 200 text/html page and tripped no bot signal. Live table (`aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-analytics-daily`): over the eight stored days, `no-assets` totals 436 addresses against `humans` totalling 9. On 2026-08-26 alone: uniqueIps 212, no-assets 81, humans 3. `humans` is 0 on 2026-08-20, 2026-08-21 and 2026-08-25 (the last with 7,141 requests).

**Verification — reproduces** (partly true, medium, observed live). The defect is real and I reproduced the mechanism end to end on the live site and on real logs.

LIVE HEADERS (`curl -s -o /dev/null -D - https://quantum.altivum.ai/` and `... /_next/static/chunks/11kjbcysxu.nd.css`): the document returns `cache-control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=31536000` with an ETag, and the chunk returns `public, max-age=31536000, s-maxage=31536000, immutable`. So the HTML is re-fetched on every navigation while the chunks are never re-requested for a year — exactly the split the finding describes. A conditional GET (`curl -H 'If-None-Match: "75d1..."'`) returns HTTP/2 304, confirming documents do revalidate.

NO ESCAPE HATCH. I compared the static-asset sets of two different routes:
`comm -13 <(curl -s https://quantum.altivum.ai/ | grep -o '/_next/static/[^"]*' | sort -u) <(curl -s https://quantum.altivum.ai/learn/01-foundations/ | grep -o '/_next/static/[^"]*' | sort -u)`
returns 0 lines — home and lesson pages reference an identical 30-URL chunk set. There is no per-route chunk that would rescue a returning reader, so once a browser has loaded ANY page it needs zero `/_next/static/` requests until a deploy changes a hash. The failure is total, not partial.

REPRODUCED ON REAL LOGS. `.analytics-cache/` holds 53 days of raw CloudFront logs (2026-06-28..2026-08-19). I ran the real `classifyVisitor` over them (scratchpad scripts probe2/probe3/probe4.mjs, importing `lambda/analytics/classify.mjs` unmodified). Result: 214 `human` address-days vs 2,720 `no-assets`. Of the `no-assets` bucket, **41 address-days fetched Next.js RSC payloads (`/review/__next._tree.txt`, `/credentials/__next._tree.txt`, etc.) across 21 distinct days** — requests only a browser executing the app's JS bundle emits, which is precisely a warm-cache reader doing client-side navigation. Those are real people the filter discards, a ≥19% undercount against a base of 214, and a strict floor since a warm-cache reader who does no client-side navigation leaves no trace at all. Ten addresses flip between `human` and `no-assets` on different days (e.g. one address: 2026-07-05 human, 27 pages/90 reqs; 2026-07-06 no-assets, 8 pages/8 reqs; 2026-07-30 human again) — the signature of cache warming and busting, and the concrete form of the deploy-cadence coupling the finding predicts.

LIVE TABLE (`aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-analytics-daily`) confirms the cited row: 2026-08-26 uniqueIps 212, no-assets 81, humans 3. My own recomputation reproduces the commit's trend figures exactly (July 175 humans / 31 days = 5.6/day; August 34 / 19 = 1.8/day), so the finding's target for that conclusion is correctly identified.

Severity medium, not higher: nothing user-facing, financial, or rule-governed depends on this; the README already labels `humans` a floor. What earns medium rather than low is that the bias is not a constant offset — it is coupled to whether a deploy busted the chunk hashes, so day-over-day comparisons in a table whose whole purpose is a time series are not comparable. MECHANISM CONFIRMED LIVE. `curl -sSI https://quantum.altivum.ai/_next/static/chunks/03edqrb4zdj~g.js` returns `cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, s-maxage=31536000, immutable`, matching /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/customHttp.yml:61-65. THE ATTACK THAT SHOULD HAVE REFUTED IT — and did not. My best refutation was that Next.js emits per-route chunks, so a returning reader opening a page they have not seen would fetch a new chunk and pass. It fails on this build's actual shape. Over the 126 pages in /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/out:
  find . -name '*.html' -exec grep -o '/_next/static/chunks/[a-zA-Z0-9_~.-]*\.js' {} \; | sort -u | wc -l   -> 37 distinct chunk URLs site-wide
  per-page chunk-set md5, uniq -c  -> 89 of 126 pages share ONE identical set
`learn/00-prereqs.html` and `learn/01-foundations.html` have byte-identical chunk sets (comm shows zero difference). So a returning reader can read every lesson in the curriculum and issue zero `/_next/static/` requests. Their HTML fetches are still 200 (new URLs, not in browser cache), so `pages.length > 0` and they land squarely in `no-assets`. That is the finding's scenario, and it is real.

I also checked the buildId escape hatch: `_next/static/Phb5hfHXna9Nx3mOyRF6A/_buildManifest.js` exists but is only referenced inside the RSC flight payload as `"b":"Phb5..."`, not as a script src, so it is not fetched per page load and does not rescue the check. The deploy-cadence coupling therefore rests on chunk rehashing, which does hold for the shared set on any code change. `git log --since=2026-07-25 --date=short` shows 15 distinct commit days with gaps of 11 days (Aug 5 to Aug 16) and 5 days (Aug 19 to Aug 24) — consistent with, though not proof of, the July-vs-August drop the commit message attributes to readership.

LIVE DATA REPRODUCED EXACTLY. `aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-analytics-daily --region us-east-2` (read-only): totals over 8 days are no-assets 436, human 9, no-page-view 37, declared-bot 636, scanner 101, datacenter 58, high-rate 17. 2026-08-26: uniqueIps 212, no-assets 81, humans 3. Humans 0 on 2026-08-20, 08-21 and 08-25 (7,141 requests). Every figure the finder cited checks out.

The 304 sub-claim is independently true: `curl -H "If-None-Match: <etag>" https://quantum.altivum.ai/` returns HTTP 304, and HTML is served `max-age=0, s-maxage=31536000`.

NOT A DOCUMENTED DECISION. classify.mjs's header documents the direction ("Fail toward NOT counting… a floor") and lambda/analytics/README.md:55 repeats it, but nothing anywhere records the cache interaction. The README's rejected-approaches table lists "Did it load app assets?" only for its false-POSITIVE failure (six bots that fetched chunks); the false-negative side is unmodelled. `grep -rn "no-assets\|loadedAppAssets"` finds five sites, and classify.test.mjs:246-249 asserts only the intended positive. So this is an unmodelled interaction, not an accepted tradeoff.

SEVERITY — I judge the finder's "medium" mildly inflated; I set low. This is a live daily path, not a dormant one, and the bias falls on exactly the population the metric most wants (returning readers), which is what keeps it from being trivial. But it stores no identifiers, touches no money, breaks no monetization rule, harms no learner, and the classifier's stated contract is already "a floor, never an inflated headline" with every bucket persisted for auditing — an operator reading 436 no-assets against 9 humans can see the filter is aggressive. The real cost is a wrong internal traffic read, and the commit message's "July 5.6 / August 1.8 readers/day" and "96-99% automated" conclusions do inherit it. Medium is defensible; I would not go above it.

### The quantum-analytics SNS topic has zero subscriptions in production, so all four alarms — including did-not-run — notify nobody

`lambda/analytics/template.yaml:115-122` — `f000d0bae` · medium · confirmed · correctness · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 06

**Claim.** `AlertsTopic` declares an email subscription to `!Ref AlertEmail`, and the deployed stack carries `AlertEmail=hq@quantumlearner.dev`. The live topic has no subscriptions at all — not even a `PendingConfirmation` one. Every alarm in the stack points its `AlarmActions` at that topic, so none of them can reach a human today. The stack was created 2026-08-20 and updated 2026-08-23 (which is when CLAUDE.md records the move to `hq@`); SNS deletes an unconfirmed email subscription after roughly three days, and 2026-08-23 + 3 days lands before today.

**Correction.** Three parts of the reasoning are wrong. (1) THE CAUSAL STORY: the finder frames this as the 2026-08-23 hq@ migration replacing a working subscription which then expired. CloudTrail shows the ORIGINAL 2026-08-20 subscription was never confirmed either — both Subscribe calls returned {"subscriptionArn": "pending confirmation"} and there is no ConfirmSubscription event at any point. The alarms have been inert since the stack was created on 2026-08-20, not since 2026-08-23. This makes the finding's own framing understate the duration. (2) THE THREE-DAY FIGURE: AWS's Subscribe API reference and the SNS FAQ both state confirmation tokens are valid for TWO days, not three (an older SDK-for-PHP guide page says three; AWS's docs are self-inconsistent), and AWS's troubleshooting doc says pending subscriptions normally persist in Pending Confirmation rather than being auto-removed — so the stated expiry mechanism is speculation presented as fact, even though the observed end state matches. (3) LOCATION/CATEGORY: the code at template.yaml:115-122 is correct as written — it declares the email subscription properly, and lambda/analytics/README.md:106 already documents "Confirm the SNS email subscription from the inbox once, or no alarm will ever reach a human." This is a deployed-state/ops gap, not a code defect, so category "correctness" against that line is mislabeled. Minor: list-subscriptions-by-topic is not "the only way to see it" — CloudTrail carries the full subscription history. Severity high -> medium: the collector is currently healthy with no data lost (Invocations=1 for every day 2026-08-19..26; quantum-analytics-daily has a row for each), so harm requires a second failure first, and the blast radius is visitor-count telemetry, not money, privacy, or learner-facing behavior.

**Impact.** The observability design the README calls out as load-bearing is inert. `quantum-analytics-did-not-run` is described in template.yaml:170-173 as guarding "the one failure this stack must never produce" — a collector that silently stops looking exactly like a site with no visitors — and it currently fires into a topic with no subscribers. The same is true for `errors`, whose description warns that a missed day's raw logs age out of Amplify's retention and become unrecoverable. This is a live instance of the exact hazard CLAUDE.md records ("An SNS email subscription delivers NOTHING until it is confirmed"), one step worse: the subscription is not pending, it is gone, so re-deploying the stack will not recreate it (the topic resource is unchanged) and `list-subscriptions-by-topic` is the only way to see it.

**Evidence.** `aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic --topic-arn arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:quantum-analytics-alerts --region us-east-2` returns `{"Subscriptions": []}`. Every other quantum topic in the same region has a confirmed subscription (quantum-stripe-alerts, quantum-qpu-alerts, quantum-tutor-alerts, quantum-workspace-sync-alerts all list christian.perez@altivum.io). `aws cloudformation get-template --stack-name quantum-analytics` shows `AlertsTopic.Properties.Subscription` = `[{Protocol: email, Endpoint: {Ref: AlertEmail}}]`, and `describe-stacks` shows `AlertEmail = hq@quantumlearner.dev`, `LastUpdatedTime = 2026-08-23T12:35:09Z`. All four alarms report `AlarmActions: [arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:quantum-analytics-alerts]` and `StateValue: OK`.

**Split verdict.** reproduces: confirmed · correct as written: partly true. Published at the more severe reading.

**Severity drift.** Finder claimed high; verification published medium.

**Verification — reproduces** (confirmed, medium, observed live). Reproduced end to end against account $PROD_ACCOUNT (verified via `aws sts get-caller-identity`), all read-only.

1. The topic is genuinely empty. `aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic --topic-arn arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:quantum-analytics-alerts --region us-east-2` returns `{"Subscriptions": []}`. Corroborated by `aws sns get-topic-attributes --topic-arn ... --region us-east-2`, which reports `SubscriptionsConfirmed: "0"`, `SubscriptionsPending: "0"`, `SubscriptionsDeleted: "0"` — so there is not even a PendingConfirmation entry, exactly as claimed.

2. The siblings differ. Looping `list-subscriptions-by-topic` over `quantum-stripe-alerts`, `quantum-qpu-alerts`, `quantum-tutor-alerts`, `quantum-workspace-sync-alerts` returns one confirmed `email` subscription to `christian.perez@altivum.io` on each. quantum-analytics is the lone outlier.

3. The template really does rely on the inline subscription. `aws cloudformation get-template --stack-name quantum-analytics --region us-east-2` returns `AlertsTopic.Properties.Subscription = [{Protocol: email, Endpoint: {Ref: AlertEmail}}]`, matching /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/lambda/analytics/template.yaml:115-122. `describe-stacks` gives `AlertEmail = hq@quantumlearner.dev`, `CreationTime = 2026-08-20T17:17:14Z`, `LastUpdatedTime = 2026-08-23T12:35:09Z`.

4. All four alarms are armed and point at the dead topic. `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-name-prefix quantum-analytics --region us-east-2` shows `quantum-analytics-{errors,throttles,did-not-run,slow}`, each `ActionsEnabled: true`, `StateValue: OK`, `AlarmActions: ["arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:quantum-analytics-alerts"]`.

5. The mechanism story holds up. `aws cloudformation describe-stack-events --stack-name quantum-analytics` shows `AlertsTopic UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS` at 2026-08-23T12:35:11Z → `UPDATE_COMPLETE` at 12:35:29Z — CFN did re-create the subscription against the new `hq@` endpoint on 08-23, and 08-23 + ~3 days of unconfirmed life lands before today (08-27).

6. This is not a dormant path. `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/Lambda --metric-name Invocations --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=quantum-analytics --period 86400 --statistics Sum` shows exactly 1 invocation on each of the last 8 days. The collector is alive; only its ability to page a human is gone. I grepped lambda/analytics for any second notification path (`grep -rn "AlertsTopic\|AlertEmail\|Subscription" lambda/analytics/template.yaml`) — the four AlarmActions are the only consumers, and README.md:106 states the requirement in the stack's own words ("Confirm the SNS email subscription from the inbox once, or no alarm will ever reach a human").

Two caveats on the finder's reasoning, neither of which changes the verdict. (a) `SubscriptionsDeleted: "0"` means SNS's own counter records no deletion, so "SNS aged out the unconfirmed subscription" is a well-supported inference from the timeline rather than something the API confirms; the observed end state — zero subscriptions of any kind — is what is directly proven, and it is what the finding turns on. (b) "re-deploying will not recreate it" is correct CFN semantics (an unchanged `AlertsTopic` resource is a no-op on update) but I could not execute a deploy to demonstrate it, so that one line is read-level reasoning.

Severity: I judge medium, not the finder's high. It is live, current, and correctly identified, but the exposure is observability-only — no learner-facing surface, no money, no data corruption, and the collector it guards is verified healthy today. What it costs is detection latency on a future outage (and, downstream, Amplify access logs aging out unrecovered). Fix is a one-liner (`aws sns subscribe` + confirm from the hq@ inbox), and the topic attributes make it cheap to add to `make drift` so it cannot recur silently.

**Verification — correct as written** (partly true, medium, observed live). Tried to refute; the core claim survives every angle I checked. VERIFIED LIVE: `aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic --topic-arn arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:quantum-analytics-alerts --region us-east-2` -> {"Subscriptions": []} (not even a PendingConfirmation row). `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names quantum-analytics-errors quantum-analytics-throttles quantum-analytics-did-not-run quantum-analytics-slow` -> all four State=OK, AlarmActions=[the analytics topic] and, importantly, OKActions=[] and InsufficientDataActions=[] — so there is no alternate notification path. `aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name quantum-analytics` -> AlertEmail=hq@quantumlearner.dev, Created 2026-08-20T17:17:14Z, Updated 2026-08-23T12:35:09Z, UPDATE_COMPLETE. REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT FAILED: no second alert channel (OKActions/InsufficientDataActions both empty); no repo-side guard (grep for list-subscriptions-by-topic / PendingConfirmation / sns across Makefile, scripts/, .github/workflows/ returns nothing, so `make drift` cannot catch this); the only repo test, lambda/analytics/template.test.mjs:124, asserts `Endpoint: !Ref AlertEmail` is present in the template text and by construction cannot see live state — the same blind spot CLAUDE.md records for the Stripe Dashboard parity checks.

ROOT CAUSE, established rather than assumed: `aws cloudtrail lookup-events --region us-east-2 --start-time 2026-08-18T00:00:00Z --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=Subscribe` returns exactly two events — 2026-08-20T12:17:28-05:00 and 2026-08-23T07:35:18-05:00, both protocol=email, both with responseElements {"subscriptionArn": "pending confirmation"}. ### A single failed ip-ranges fetch is cached for the container's lifetime, so the failure persists rather than the data

`lambda/analytics/index.mjs:46-56` — `ffc402c3f` · low · confirmed · correctness · ran locally · fix plan 06

**Claim.** `ranges()` assigns the failure result to `cachedRanges` (index.mjs:53) and index.mjs:47 returns it unconditionally on every later call. There is no retry and no distinction between "cached because it worked" and "cached because it did not". A transient network error therefore pins that warm container to `complete: false` for as long as it lives.

**Impact.** Small today because the schedule is once daily and the container is almost always cold, but it becomes real for any manual gap re-run that invokes the function several times in a row: the first failure poisons the rest of the batch, and every row those runs write is stamped `botFilterComplete: false` with an inflated `humans`. Caching only the success would cost one line.

**Evidence.** index.mjs:47 `if (cachedRanges) return cachedRanges;` and index.mjs:52-54 `catch (err) { cachedRanges = { index: buildRangeIndex([]), complete: false, why: err.message }; }`. index.test.mjs:90-97 exercises the single-invocation case only.

**Verification — reproduces** (confirmed, low, ran locally). Reproduced. Line citations are exact: index.mjs:47 `if (cachedRanges) return cachedRanges;` and index.mjs:53 assigns the FAILURE object (truthy) to the same variable, so line 47 cannot distinguish the two. `createAnalyticsCore` is called once at module scope (index.mjs:97), making `cachedRanges` per-container.

REPRO (executed): wrote a scratchpad harness importing the real `createAnalyticsCore` with a `fetchImpl` whose ip-ranges call fails ONLY on the first attempt, then invoked ONE core three times — `node /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-cperez-dev-altivum-inc-quantum/b7fc46e5-3806-4423-bbf8-8ccaa78ee81d/scratchpad/repro2.mjs`:
  ALL FETCHES OK:    humans=1/complete=true   humans=1/complete=true   humans=1/complete=true   fetchAttempts=1
  FIRST FETCH FAILS: humans=2/complete=false  humans=2/complete=false  humans=2/complete=false  fetchAttempts=1
One transient error pins every later invocation to complete=false, never re-fetches (1 attempt for 3 invocations), and inflates `humans` (2 vs the correct 1 — the 10.0.0.0/8 visitor stops being filtered). Both halves of the claim hold.

TEST-COVERAGE CLAIM VERIFIED: `grep -n "await core(" lambda/analytics/index.test.mjs | wc -l` -> 6, each in a separate test with its own `makeCore()`; no test invokes a core twice, so the suite structurally cannot catch this. The cited test is at index.test.mjs:90-97 as stated. The `{day}` override that the gap-re-run impact argument depends on is real (index.test.mjs:63).

SCOPING NOTE (does not contradict the finding): the historical backfill path /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs does NOT share the bug — its own `loadRanges()` re-fetches per process and falls back to a disk cache. Exposure is confined to repeated warm-container Lambda invokes.

SEVERITY: low, agreeing with the finder. Once-daily schedule means containers are nearly always cold, and the row is stamped honestly (botFilterComplete:false + botFilterNote), so the module's stated goal — never presenting an inflated count as real — survives. The cost is a batch of rows that must be re-run, not silent bad data. Fix is one line: only assign `cachedRanges` in the try.

**Verification — correct as written** (confirmed, low, ran locally). I tried hard to refute this and could not.

Code as claimed (/Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/lambda/analytics/index.mjs): `cachedRanges` is a closure variable created once inside `createAnalyticsCore`; line 47 `if (cachedRanges) return cachedRanges;` returns whatever is stored, and line 53 stores the FAILURE object `{ index: buildRangeIndex([]), complete: false, why }`. The module builds exactly one `core` at load (lines 101-108) and `handler` (line 110) just calls it, so the closure — and any poisoned cache — lives for the execution environment's lifetime.

Refutations I checked and eliminated:
- No retry, no success/failure distinction anywhere else in the file; `ranges()` is called from exactly one place (line 76), once per invocation, so the cache serves no within-invocation purpose at all — its only function is cross-invocation reuse, which is precisely the case it gets wrong. Not a deliberate decision: the comment at lines 39-45 records only the degrade-rather-than-fail choice, nothing about pinning a failure.
- The ops script is a separate implementation and is NOT affected — /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs has its own `loadRanges()` (lines 117-133) with a disk fallback, and imports only from classify.mjs. The finder did not claim otherwise.
- No test covers it: every one of the 8 `core(...)` calls in index.test.mjs runs against a freshly built core. The cited lines 90-97 are exactly the single-invocation degraded-run test.
- The multi-invoke path the finder names is real and documented: lambda/analytics/README.md:128-133 tells the operator to re-run missed days with `aws lambda invoke --payload '{"day":"..."}'`, and successive invokes land on the same warm environment.

Executed proof (read-only; scratch script, no repo files touched):
`node /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-cperez-dev-altivum-inc-quantum/b7fc46e5-3806-4423-bbf8-8ccaa78ee81d/scratchpad/poison.mjs` — a `fetchImpl` whose ip-ranges call fails ONLY on the first attempt, then three sequential `core({day})` calls on one core. Output:
  2026-08-19  complete=false  humans=2  datacenterBucket=0
  2026-08-18  complete=false  humans=2  datacenterBucket=0
  2026-08-17  complete=false  humans=2  datacenterBucket=0
  ip-ranges fetch attempts made across 3 invocations: 1
  rows written, botFilterComplete flags: false,false,false
`humans=2` is the inflation: the 10.0.0.0/8 address is counted as a person because the datacenter filter never loaded, and the ranges were never re-fetched even though the network had recovered.

On severity — low is right, not inflated, and I would not raise it. Two things cap it: the poisoned rows are honestly stamped `botFilterComplete: false` with `botFilterNote`, which is the whole point of that stamp, and `day` is the table's HASH key (template.yaml:56-61), so a later re-run PutItem overwrites the bad row cleanly. It needs a transient ip-ranges failure to coincide with a multi-day manual backfill, and it is fully recoverable when it happens. The one-line fix the finder proposes (assign `cachedRanges` only on success) is correct.

### A systematically broken parse or a failed range fetch is recorded on the row but alarms on nothing, so it does masquerade as a quiet day

`lambda/analytics/index.mjs:86-93` — `f4743df2a` · low · partly true · correctness · observed live · fix plan 06

**Claim.** classify.mjs:69-70 justifies returning `malformed` on the grounds that "the count is surfaced so a systematically broken parse cannot masquerade as a quiet day", and index.mjs:88-90 justifies `botFilterComplete` as recorded "so a later reader is not misled". Both are written to the row and neither is watched. If a download truncates and most lines fail the field-count check, the run succeeds, writes `requests` near zero with a large `malformed`, and no alarm fires — `AnalyticsErrorsAlarm` needs a throw and `AnalyticsSilentAlarm` needs an absent invocation. The same holds when the AWS ranges fetch fails: `humans` is written inflated with `botFilterComplete: false`, no alarm.

**Correction.** The named trigger is wrong. A truncated download does NOT make "most lines fail the field-count check" — a CSV cut mid-stream clips only its final line. I ran the real `core()` against a body sliced to 50%: it returned `requests=1498, malformed=1`. That is a ~50% silent UNDERCOUNT that `malformed` does not flag at all, so the caveat field the finding relies on would not even be elevated. (A truly severed stream more often rejects inside `res.text()`, which does throw and does trip `AnalyticsErrorsAlarm`.) The mass-malformed zero-day the finding describes is real but arrives by a different route: a systematic parse break — a CloudFront date/time format change (every `Date.parse` NaN) or a column-count drift in the data rows. Both of those I reproduced at `malformed=3000, requests=0`. Note also that a header-level column change throws at classify.mjs:88 and IS alarmed; only the per-row failures are silent.

**Correction.** Three parts of the reasoning are wrong. (a) The truncation example is mechanically wrong: a truncated download leaves a valid prefix plus one partial trailing line, so malformed=1 and `requests` is silently short — the named scenario is one the malformed counter does NOT flag, not one it flags unwatched. (b) Most mass-corruption modes are already covered: parseLog throws on any missing column (classify.mjs:87-89), so gzip garbage, an HTML error body, or a renamed/removed column all fire AnalyticsErrorsAlarm. The unwatched window is narrow — a header retaining all nine column needles while data lines change field count. (c) "A row that nobody scans" overstates it: the table's only intended consumer IS a human scan (template.yaml Outputs prints `aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-analytics-daily`), both caveats sit on the same row as the numbers they qualify, core() returns them in the invoke output, and backfill.mjs:216-217 prints the malformed count. index.mjs:88-90's stated purpose ("a later reader is not misled") is delivered; only classify.mjs:69-70's stronger "cannot masquerade as a quiet day" overreaches, and only for an unattended run. Category should be observability, not correctness — nothing computes incorrectly, and index.test.mjs pins the record-rather-than-inflate behavior as intended.

**Impact.** The stack's stated worst case is "a collector that silently stops looks exactly like a site with no visitors". A collector that keeps running and produces zeros is the same failure with none of the coverage, and it is the more likely one because a running Lambda emits Invocations. Recording a caveat on a row that nobody scans is not detection. Both would be a metric filter or a `PutMetricData` call away.

**Evidence.** index.mjs:86 writes `malformed`, index.mjs:90 writes `botFilterComplete`, index.mjs:93 writes `botFilterNote`. `grep -n 'Metric\|Alarm' lambda/analytics/index.mjs` returns nothing — the handler emits no custom metric. template.yaml:124-209 defines four alarms, all on `AWS/Lambda` built-ins (Errors, Throttles, Invocations, Duration); none reads a value the handler produces.

**Verification — reproduces** (partly true, low, observed live). The defect stands: both caveat fields are written to the row, nothing watches either, and a run that produces zeros exits 0.

Reproduced by driving the real `createAnalyticsCore` from lambda/analytics/index.mjs with stubbed amplify/ddb/fetch (`node /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-cperez-dev-altivum-inc-quantum/b7fc46e5-3806-4423-bbf8-8ccaa78ee81d/scratchpad/repro.mjs`), 3000 synthetic rows on the verbatim CloudFront header:
- A (date/time format change, every `Date.parse` NaN): wrote `requests=0 humans=0 malformed=3000`, one PutItem, no throw.
- B (one extra field per data row): wrote `requests=0 humans=0 malformed=3000`, no throw.
- D (body sliced to 50%): `requests=1498 malformed=1` — see correction.
- Ranges path (`repro2.mjs`, same real module): with ranges `humans=1`; with the ip-ranges fetch throwing, `humans=4 botFilterComplete=false`, run succeeds. Inflated 4x, no throw, so `AnalyticsErrorsAlarm` cannot see it.

The alarm half checks out too, live not just on paper. `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-name-prefix quantum-analytics --region us-east-2` returns exactly four alarms — quantum-analytics-errors (Errors), -throttles (Throttles), -did-not-run (Invocations), -slow (Duration) — all Namespace `AWS/Lambda`, all OK. None reads a value the handler produces. `grep -rn "PutMetricData|CloudWatchClient|MetricFilter" lambda infra scripts .github` returns hits only under lambda/qpu (four MetricFilters there, e.g. QpuRefundFailureMetricFilter) and none under lambda/analytics — so the log-metric-filter pattern is established in this repo and simply was not applied here. index.mjs and classify.mjs contain no `console.*` at all, so there is not even a log line a filter could match. The only reader of these fields is scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs (manual ops script) and the template's own Output, which tells the operator to `aws dynamodb scan` by hand.

`AnalyticsSilentAlarm` genuinely cannot cover this — the Lambda runs and emits Invocations, so `Sum >= 1` and the alarm stays OK, which is the finding's central point and it is correct.

Severity low, agreeing with the finder: this is an observability gap on an internal traffic collector — no money, no learner-facing surface, no privacy promise at risk (the row still stores counts only). A manual scan of the table would show `malformed: 3000` beside `requests: 0`, so the caveat is legible, just unalarmed — except in the truncation case, where nothing on the row is anomalous at all.
