### Only AWS prefixes are loaded in production, though the test file names a Google Cloud address that already slipped through

`lambda/analytics/index.mjs:49` — `faa878913` · low · partly true · correctness · observed live · fix plan 06

**Claim.** `ranges()` fetches only `AWS_RANGES_URL` (index.mjs:27). `buildRangeIndex` is variadic and accepts bare CIDR arrays specifically so a second provider needs no new code path (classify.mjs:169-179), and classify.test.mjs:147-153 exercises it with the comment "34.122.x.x is the Google Cloud address that slipped through when only AWS ranges were checked during the investigation". Production still passes one source.

**Correction.** The last sentence of the finding — "the mechanism to fix it already exists and is already tested; only the call site is missing" — is wrong. `inRangeIndex` binary-searches a list sorted by range START, which is only correct for non-overlapping ranges, and AWS's own list contains 3,021 adjacent overlaps. Probing the midpoint of every v4 range in the AWS-only index, the binary search disagrees with a linear scan on 267 of 10,516 addresses that really are inside an AWS prefix. Worse, adding a second source perturbs which addresses are missed: `3.94.1.1` (a real AWS address) is `true` under `buildRangeIndex(aws)` and `false` under `buildRangeIndex(aws, gcpCidrs)` — i.e. wiring in Google Cloud through the "already tested" variadic path would silently reclassify some AWS datacenter traffic as human while catching Google. The two-disjoint-prefix test at classify.test.mjs:147-153 cannot see this. A fix must coalesce overlapping ranges (or search by predecessor-start with a running max end), not just add a fetch. Also minor: the finder's "humans is a floor by construction" objection is a fair caveat but slightly strong — the README already frames the floor as "uncertain visitors are dropped", never as a proof of zero false positives.

**Correction.** Two parts of the reasoning are wrong. (1) "The mechanism to fix it already exists and is already tested; only the call site is missing" is false for the very provider named. Google publishes its prefixes at https://www.gstatic.com/ipranges/cloud.json under the keys `ipv4Prefix`/`ipv6Prefix`, not AWS's `ip_prefix`/`ipv6_prefix`. `buildRangeIndex` reads `src.prefixes` and then `p.ip_prefix`, so the Google document parses to ZERO ranges — silently, no throw, and the row would still be stamped `botFilterComplete: true`. Verified by execution (below): naive size 0, adapted size 1092. The fix therefore needs a per-provider shape adapter (new code, plus a test that the adapter yields a non-zero size), not a second URL at the call site. The same holds for the other providers listed: Azure publishes Service Tags in a third shape, DigitalOcean a CSV, and Hetzner/OVH publish no prefix document at all (ASN/BGP only). There is also a structural trap: `ranges()` wraps its one fetch in a single try/catch that discards ALL ranges on failure, so bolting a second fetch into that block would let a Google outage zero the AWS index too. (2) "The README's 'humans is a floor by construction' is not quite true" is overreach. That sentence describes the design's failure direction (uncertain -> dropped); it can never be a literal floor against a headless browser on a residential proxy or any unlisted host, so adding GCP prefixes narrows the gap without making the statement true or false. A cloud-hosted agent still has to clear four other filters, which is precisely the "asset-loading alone fails" case the module documents.

**Impact.** Datacenter traffic from Google Cloud, Azure, DigitalOcean, Hetzner and OVH — the usual homes of scrapers — is not caught by the datacenter rule and must be caught, if at all, by the weaker downstream signals. This pushes in the opposite direction from every other bias in the classifier, so the README's "humans is a floor by construction" is not quite true: the count can include cloud-hosted agents that fetch assets and read slowly. The mechanism to fix it already exists and is already tested; only the call site is missing.

**Evidence.** index.mjs:49 `const res = await fetchImpl(AWS_RANGES_URL);` — one source, no second fetch. classify.test.mjs:147-153 documents the known miss. Live rows show the `datacenter` bucket at 3-10 addresses per day against 105-212 unique addresses.

**Verification — reproduces** (partly true, low, observed live). The core defect reproduces exactly as claimed. Verified three ways.

1) READ: `lambda/analytics/index.mjs:49` fetches only `AWS_RANGES_URL` (`index.mjs:27`); `grep -rn "ip-ranges|RANGES_URL|buildRangeIndex" --include="*.mjs" lambda scripts web/src docs` shows no second provider anywhere — `scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs:36` is AWS-only too, so the historical path has the same gap. `classify.mjs:169-179` is variadic and accepts bare CIDR arrays, and `classify.test.mjs:147-153` carries the cited "34.122.x.x is the Google Cloud address that slipped through" comment.

2) EXECUTED — reproduction against the REAL public prefix lists (`curl https://ip-ranges.amazonaws.com/ip-ranges.json` and `curl https://www.gstatic.com/ipranges/cloud.json`, then `node /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-cperez-dev-altivum-inc-quantum/b7fc46e5-3806-4423-bbf8-8ccaa78ee81d/scratchpad/repro.mjs`, which imports the production `createAnalyticsCore` with a URL-recording `fetchImpl`). Output: the core fetched exactly two URLs — the presigned log and `ip-ranges.amazonaws.com` — one prefix-list fetch. Against a synthetic day holding four identical slow, asset-loading crawlers (20 pages each, one per hour, real Chrome UA) on 34.122.55.1 (GCP), 20.36.44.10 (Azure), 165.227.0.10 (DigitalOcean) and 3.94.1.1 (AWS), the deployed classifier returned `{"humans":3,"buckets":{"datacenter":1,...,"human":3}}` — only the AWS one was convicted. Direct index probes: `inRangeIndex(awsIdx, "34.122.55.1") === false`, `inRangeIndex(buildRangeIndex(aws, gcpCidrs), "34.122.55.1") === true`. So the gap is real and the datacenter rule (`classify.mjs:339`) is the only place a cloud host is caught.

3) OBSERVED-LIVE — `aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-analytics-daily` (read-only) returns 8 rows; the finder's figures are accurate: datacenter 3-10/day against uniqueIps 105-212 (e.g. 2026-08-26: uniqueIps 212, datacenter 7, humans 3; 2026-08-21: 143 / 10 / 0). `botFilterComplete` is true on every row, so the AWS fetch is succeeding and the small datacenter bucket is the true AWS-only yield, not a fetch failure.

Severity stays low: this inflates an internal, non-customer-facing daily counter whose human values are 0-3/day, touches no money and no rule in CLAUDE.md. But see the correction — the suggested one-line fix is not safe as described, and the overlap bug in `inRangeIndex` (classify.mjs:200-217) is arguably the more interesting defect in this file since it already produces ~2.5% false negatives on AWS's own overlapping list today.

> Correction. Two parts of the reasoning are wrong. (1) "The mechanism to fix it already exists and is already tested; only the call site is missing" is false for the very provider named. Google publishes its prefixes at https://www.gstatic.com/ipranges/cloud.json under the keys `ipv4Prefix`/`ipv6Prefix`, not AWS's `ip_prefix`/`ipv6_prefix`. `buildRangeIndex` reads `src.prefixes` and then `p.ip_prefix`, so the Google document parses to ZERO ranges — silently, no throw, and the row would still be stamped `botFilterComplete: true`. Verified by execution (below): naive size 0, adapted size 1092. The fix therefore needs a per-provider shape adapter (new code, plus a test that the adapter yields a non-zero size), not a second URL at the call site. The same holds for the other providers listed: Azure publishes Service Tags in a third shape, DigitalOcean a CSV, and Hetzner/OVH publish no prefix document at all (ASN/BGP only). There is also a structural trap: `ranges()` wraps its one fetch in a single try/catch that discards ALL ranges on failure, so bolting a second fetch into that block would let a Google outage zero the AWS index too. (2) "The README's 'humans is a floor by construction' is not quite true" is overreach. That sentence describes the design's failure direction (uncertain -> dropped); it can never be a literal floor against a headless browser on a residential proxy or any unlisted host, so adding GCP prefixes narrows the gap without making the statement true or false. A cloud-hosted agent still has to clear four other filters, which is precisely the "asset-loading alone fails" case the module documents.

### HOSTILE_PATH's /shell rule matches three paths the site actually serves, and the guard test cannot see them because it only walks web/src/app

`lambda/analytics/classify.test.mjs:266-289` — `fa3dabafa` · low · confirmed · correctness · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 06

**Claim.** The test "no route this site serves is classified hostile" walks `web/src/app/` for directories containing `page.tsx`. The site serves far more than that from the same host: 789 files under `web/public` (the JupyterLite lab, the staged Monaco tree, Pyodide, welcome imagery), and three of them match `HOSTILE_PATH` today via the `\/shell\b` alternative — `/monaco/0.55.1/vs/shell-ClXCKCEW.js`, `/lab/build/schemas/@jupyter-notebook/application-extension/shell.json` and `/lab/build/schemas/@jupyterlab/application-extension/shell.json`. The test also misses routes defined by anything other than `page.tsx` and the root route itself.

**Correction.** Three parts of the reasoning/impact are wrong or overstated. (1) "This is the /credentials bug's exact shape" is not right. /credentials was a navigable page route that actually fired and erased two signed-in readers. These three are static asset URLs sitting behind lazy loaders that no exercised code path requests, and I confirmed both mechanisms positively rather than merely failing to disprove them — the finder only claimed "could not show". Same regex mechanism, materially different exposure. (2) The implied remedy (widen the walk to web/public) is not implementable where this test runs. 776 of the 789 files are gitignored build artifacts — web/.gitignore excludes /public/lab/, /public/pyodide/ and /public/monaco/, and `git ls-files web/public | wc -l` returns 13 — while .github/workflows/ci.yml's `lambdas` matrix job runs `npm ci && npm test` inside lambda/analytics with no web build, so a web/public walk would find zero files in CI and silently assert nothing. The gap is structural, not an oversight in the walk's root. (3) "The test also misses routes defined by anything other than page.tsx" is vacuous today: `find web/src/app -name route.ts -o -name route.tsx -o -name page.mdx -o -name page.js` returns nothing; all 19 routes are page.tsx. The root-route omission is real but trivially safe.

**Impact.** This is the `/credentials` bug's exact shape, and the guard written to prevent its return does not cover the path space where it now lives. Because the rule convicts the visitor rather than the request, one such fetch anywhere in an address's day erases that reader entirely — and the readers at risk are the ones who opened the playground or the in-browser lab, i.e. the most engaged. I could not show that these three URLs are requested on the normal path (the Monaco chunk is a lazily-loaded shell-language contribution and the editor is set to `python`; nothing under `/lab` references `build/schemas/` at runtime), so this is latent rather than currently firing — but the guard's stated job is to make it impossible, and it does not.

### The history the stack exists to preserve was never written: the table holds 8 days, and backfill.mjs writes no rows by design

`lambda/analytics/template.yaml:216-219` — `f3aeb637d` · low · partly true · correctness · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 06

**Claim.** The `BackfillCommand` output advertises `node scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs` as the way to "Populate history before this stack existed" and then says, in the same sentence, "(reads only; writes no rows)". Both halves are accurate and they contradict each other: backfill.mjs writes `daily.json` to the local cache directory (backfill.mjs:181) and never constructs a `PutItemCommand`. README.md:84-93 repeats the framing ("To populate history back to launch (2026-06-28…)") and then states "It is read-only and writes no DynamoDB rows". Nothing in the repo moves the backfill's output into `quantum-analytics-daily`.

**Correction.** Two parts of the reasoning are wrong. (1) "Nothing in the repo moves the backfill's output into quantum-analytics-daily" is true only of backfill.mjs. The repo DOES contain a per-day write path into the table: lambda/analytics/index.mjs:60 takes `event.day ?? previousDay(today)` for ANY date and line 95 PutItems it, and lambda/analytics/README.md's "Local dev loop" documents invoking it that way ("this writes to DynamoDB"). That is demonstrably how the table's odd 2026-07-28 row got there — its computedAt is 2026-08-20T17:19:28Z, the backfill session's own date. The gap is that nothing LOOPS that path over the 52 missing days, not that no path exists. (2) The impact overstates the loss: the commit's measured result does not exist "only" in daily.json, and the days are not near-unrecoverable. The same gitignored .analytics-cache/ also holds all 54 raw day CSVs (2026-06-28.csv onward, 1.6M+ each), and Amplify still serves the launch day's logs today, 60 days on — so the missing history is recoverable right now by a loop over the existing handler, and the finding is a completeness gap, not a data loss.

**Impact.** The stated premise of the whole stack — "Amplify's GenerateAccessLogs serves roughly one day per call and refuses wider windows, so history only exists if something collects it daily" — applies with equal force to the 53 days before the collector existed, and those days are not in the table. The commit's measured result (142,559 requests, 216 human visits, 11 Google sign-ins, launch to 2026-08-20) exists only in an untracked, gitignored `daily.json` on one laptop. Once Amplify's retention passes those days they are unrecoverable, which is the exact failure the `errors` alarm description warns about.

**Evidence.** `aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-analytics-daily` returns 8 items: 2026-07-28 (computed 2026-08-27, a manual re-run) and 2026-08-20 through 2026-08-26. Nothing between 2026-06-28 and 2026-08-19. `grep -n PutItem scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs` returns nothing; backfill.mjs:181 is `writeFileSync(join(cacheDir, "daily.json"), …)`. Local `.analytics-cache/daily.json` reads `from 2026-06-28 to 2026-08-20, rows 54, gaps 0, requests 142559, humans 216, google 11` — matching the commit message figures, and stored nowhere else.

**Split verdict.** reproduces: partly true · correct as written: refuted. Published at the more severe reading.

**Severity drift.** Finder claimed medium; verification published low.

**Verification — reproduces** (partly true, low, observed live). Every factual assertion in the claim reproduces; the impact framing does not.

Confirmed by read: lambda/analytics/template.yaml:216-219 is verbatim `BackfillCommand` / "Populate history before this stack existed (reads only; writes no rows)." / `node scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs`, sitting directly under an `AnalyticsTableName` output that says "Read the history with: aws dynamodb scan". `grep -n "PutItem\|writeFileSync" scripts/analytics/backfill.mjs` returns no PutItem and confirms backfill.mjs:181 is `writeFileSync(join(cacheDir, "daily.json"), ...)`; the only other writes are cached CSVs and ip-ranges.json. README.md's "## Backfill" section repeats the framing and then says "It is read-only and writes no DynamoDB rows". So the labeling gap is real: the CFN output that reads as the history-population command populates a laptop directory, not the stack's durable store.

Confirmed live (read-only): `aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-analytics-daily --region us-east-2 --projection-expression "#d" --expression-attribute-names '{"#d":"day"}'` returns Count 8 — ['2026-07-28', '2026-08-20' … '2026-08-26']. 2026-06-28 through 2026-08-19 are absent (52 days). Local `.analytics-cache/daily.json` reads from 2026-06-28 to 2026-08-20, rows 54, gaps 0, requests 142559, humans 216, google 11 — exactly the commit-message figures — and `.gitignore:96` is `.analytics-cache/`.

Where the finding overreaches, also checked live: `aws amplify generate-access-logs --app-id d1ao02to23x85y --domain-name altivum.ai --start-time 2026-06-28T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-06-28T01:00:00Z` returns a logUrl today, and curling it yields 927 real rows for that one hour. Launch-day source data is still retrievable 60 days later, so nothing is lost yet; combined with the handler's arbitrary-`day` PutItem path, the table can be filled by a loop over `{"day": "..."}` invocations. No learner data, money, or public-facing surface is involved — this is an internal observability completeness gap with a live remedy, which is why I rate it low rather than medium.

It calls amplify:GenerateAccessLogs and downloads the presigned result; it mutates nothing." README.md:93 — "It is read-only and writes no DynamoDB rows — it reports and caches locally." "Populate history" reads as "produce the history report"; the parenthetical "(reads only; writes no rows)" is the clarification, not a retraction. The script prints a report table to stdout and never claims a write, so no operator is misled.

2) "Nothing in the repo moves history into quantum-analytics-daily" is FALSE. lambda/analytics/index.mjs:60 is `const day = event.day ?? previousDay(today)` — the handler writes a row for ANY day passed. That is the deployment-verification invocation the commit message describes ("verified by invocation, not by tests passing"), i.e. live proof the historical-write path works in production, not evidence of its absence. The other seven rows carry computedAt of 13:30:39-41Z on consecutive days — the schedule running normally since deploy.

4) IMPACT OVERSTATED. `ls .analytics-cache/*.csv | wc -l` returns 53 raw CSVs spanning exactly 2026-06-28..2026-08-19 (the claimed gap), and daily.json reads `from 2026-06-28 to 2026-08-20, rows 54, gaps 0`. The underlying data therefore does not depend on Amplify retention; the classifier can be re-run offline. "Once Amplify's retention passes those days they are unrecoverable" is wrong as stated.

WHAT SURVIVES, and why it is low: the durable table does not yet hold the 53 pre-stack days, and the local cache is gitignored and lives on one machine. ### googleSignIns counts requests while humans counts addresses, so the self-contradiction check that caught the /credentials bug is permanently tripped

`lambda/analytics/classify.mjs:395-405` — `f539adbd1` · low · partly true · correctness · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 06

**Claim.** `summarizeDay` reports `googleSignIns: google.length` where `google = googleSignIns(mine)` filters *rows* (classify.mjs:311-315), while `humans: buckets.human` counts *unique addresses*. The two are in different units and are not comparable. classify.mjs:330-337 nevertheless states the invariant it is enforcing as "a day can report three Google sign-ins and fewer humans than signers, which is not a conservative estimate but a self-contradiction", and classify.test.mjs:366-377 pins that reasoning. Because a single person can produce more than one matching `/auth/callback` row, `googleSignIns > humans` is reachable with no bug present at all — and classify.test.mjs:379-384 deliberately makes it reachable a second way, by convicting a signed-in visitor who also probed a hostile path.

**Correction.** Three parts of the reasoning are wrong. (1) There is no "check". Nothing in the repo compares googleSignIns to humans — I grepped all 13 references (`grep -rn "googleSignIns" . --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git`) and no assertion, alarm, or CloudWatch metric relates the two; `cd lambda/analytics && node --test` passes 41/41. Nothing is "tripped", permanently or otherwise. The /credentials bug was caught by a human eyeballing a pair of numbers during the 2026-08-20 investigation, not by a detector that has now broken. (2) classify.test.mjs:366-377 does not "pin that reasoning" — its only assertion is `classifyVisitor(rows, buildRangeIndex([])) === "human"`, the precedence rule. The self-contradiction language lives in a comment on line 367, not in an assert. (3) The invariant the comment actually names — "fewer humans than SIGNERS", i.e. distinct people — is not broken by the primary case. One person signing in three times yields humans=1 and one signer; the precedence rule correctly counted them. What is unsound is only the comparability of the reported pair, because googleSignIns is an event count and counting sign-in *events* is a defensible definition (README: "Report the two as separate series, never summed"). No visitor is misclassified and neither number is wrong for its own definition. That is why I judge this low rather than medium: it is a labeling/observability defect on a counts-only reporting Lambda, not a correctness bug.

**Impact.** The /credentials bug was found only because a day reported 3 Google sign-ins and 0 humans and someone noticed the impossibility. That detector no longer works: the stored production row for 2026-07-28 already reads humans=2, googleSignIns=3, so the condition the design treats as proof of a defect is now the steady state and will be dismissed as normal. Any future rule that erases real readers the same way will pass unnoticed.

**Evidence.** `aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-analytics-daily`, item `day = 2026-07-28`: `humans: 2`, `googleSignIns: 3`, `buckets.human: 2`. classify.mjs:312 filters rows, not addresses: `rows.filter(r => r.path === CALLBACK_PATH && r.status === "200" && GOOGLE_REFERER.test(r.referer))`.

**Split verdict.** reproduces: partly true · correct as written: refuted. Published at the more severe reading.

**Severity drift.** Finder claimed medium; verification published low.

## Identity, auth and infrastructure security

Surviving: 0 high, 2 medium, 10 low.

### How it actually works

Identity here is a single Cognito user pool, `quantum-workspace` (`$USER_POOL_ID`), defined in `infra/workspace/cognito.yaml`. Email is the username (`UsernameAttributes: email`), auto-verified on native sign-up, and the pool has `DeletionProtection: ACTIVE` plus `DeletionPolicy: Retain`. One public SPA client (`quantum-workspace-web`, `GenerateSecret: false`) allows only `ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH` + refresh, sets `PreventUserExistenceErrors: ENABLED`, and pins 60-minute access/ID tokens with 30-day refresh. A `GoogleIdP` maps both `email` and `email_verified` — the latter deliberately, because `lambda/qpu/qpu-core.mjs:763` gates real-hardware spend on that claim and an unmapped IdP would strand every federated learner; `tests/test_workspace_cognito.py` fails CI if any IdP drops it. A `PostConfirmation` trigger (`quantum-signup-alert`, inline in the template) publishes to SNS and is written to never throw, because a failing trigger is a failing front door. Google and native sign-ins are NOT linked, so one human can hold two subs — a fact the whole Founding Ten design is built around.

On the browser side, `web/src/components/auth/amplify-auth-bridge.tsx` owns every `aws-amplify` import behind `next/dynamic({ssr:false})`. It reads identity from the ID token's claims only (never `fetchUserAttributes`, which needs a scope Google sessions cannot carry), moves Cognito tokens to per-tab `sessionStorage` (line 103), and namespaces local progress per `sub` via `setCurrentOwner`. `web/src/lib/auth-session.ts` exposes `hasUserPoolAdminScope()`, the token-derived test for "can this session call `cognito-idp` user APIs" — used by `delete-account.tsx:78` to refuse the whole deletion flow up front for federated sessions rather than destroying data it then cannot finish removing. `auth-wall.tsx` gates every route except `/`, `/pricing`, `/login`, `/auth/callback`, `/privacy`, `/changelog`, `/e2e-fixtures/*`, `/founding-ten/*`, and documents honestly that it is an access gate, not a confidentiality boundary (static export serializes lesson content into the RSC payload).

Three HTTP APIs sit behind Cognito JWT authorizers with `IdentitySource: $request.header.Authorization` and audience pinned to the client id: `lambda/sync` (`/progress` GET/PUT/DELETE), `lambda/review-email`'s `/prefs`, and `lambda/qpu`. All three take identity solely from `requestContext.authorizer.jwt.claims.sub` and never from a body. `lambda/sync/index.mjs` is deliberately dumb — versioned optimistic concurrency, a `qc:*`-namespace check, a 256 KB **byte-length** cap — and additionally persists the ID token's `email` claim (line 52) so the review-email sender can address a learner without a Cognito lookup. `lambda/review-email` owns a separate prefs table so sync's full-item PUT can never clobber consent; sending is opt-in (`remindersOn === true`), capped at one per 7 days, and hard-refuses while SES is in the sandbox — which it still is (`ProductionAccessEnabled: false`, verified live), so the entire send path is dormant. Unsubscribe is an unauthenticated Function URL verifying an HMAC-over-`sub` token with `timingSafeEqual`.

CI is two-track. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs on `pull_request` (fork tokens are read-only, no secrets) across python/web/lambdas/build-smoke. `drift.yml` is the only AWS-touching workflow: OIDC into `quantum-ci-drift-check`, whose trust policy pins both `aud` and `sub` to `repo:AltivumInc-Admin/quantum-computing:ref:refs/heads/main`. `infra/ci-standby` is a warm CodeBuild mirror, idle at $0 (webhook confirmed `null` today) until `failover.sh engage` arms it. `customHttp.yml` carries HSTS, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, `frame-ancestors 'self'` and disjoint Cache-Control blocks — but no `script-src`/`style-src`. The Founding Ten registry binds badges to an unsalted SHA-256 of the normalized email (`scripts/lib/email-hash.mjs`), never a sub, and `scripts/verify-founding-ten.mjs` fails the build if an issued badge no longer resolves to an enabled Cognito user — a check that only runs on the CodeBuild standby, because GitHub Actions has no AWS credentials.

### What is genuinely good here

- `infra/workspace/cognito.yaml:241` maps Google's `email_verified` onto the pool attribute, and `tests/test_workspace_cognito.py:79-91` fails CI if any IdP drops it — a guard that exists because `lambda/qpu/qpu-core.mjs:763` gates hardware spend on exactly that claim, so an unmapped IdP would strand every federated learner behind an unactionable error.
- `web/src/components/auth/delete-account.tsx:78-85` refuses the entire deletion flow when `hasUserPoolAdminScope()` is false. This is the fix for a real incident: without it, a Google session's progress and email preference were destroyed first and the account delete then failed every time. The check is derived from the token's own `scope` claim (`web/src/lib/auth-session.ts:34-36`), not from configuration, so it stays correct if the app client's scopes are widened later.
- `web/src/components/auth/amplify-auth-bridge.tsx:85` deliberately keeps the cosmetic badge lookup out of the auth verdict — `hashEmail(...).catch(() => null)` — so a `crypto.subtle` failure in an insecure context degrades to "no badge" instead of flipping a live session to unauthenticated and repointing local storage at the anonymous bucket.
- `web/__tests__/infra/wallet-ttl.test.ts:29-40` does not merely count `expiresAt` occurrences: for each one it walks backwards to the nearest row key and the nearest `TableName` and refuses anything that is not provably the `EVENT#` marker or the `DAY#` ledger row. That is the only mechanical defense against the table-wide TTL landmine CLAUDE.md records.
- `web/__tests__/infra/credit-writers.test.ts:29-58` is a named allowlist of every file permitted to move a wallet balance, each with a written reason — so a "small signup bonus" landing in a new file fails CI rather than reviewing clean.
- `scripts/design-sync/preflight.mjs:38-43` turns the two-projects-share-one-name hazard from prose into a mechanical refusal: `SYNC_TARGET` and `COMMISSIONED` are pinned constants and the config is rejected on mismatch, with `COMMISSIONED_MARKERS` as a second check on the remote tree.
- `scripts/verify-founding-ten.mjs:29-34,68-81` refuses to print addresses under `CI`/`CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID`/`GITHUB_ACTIONS`, and treats only genuine credential absence as a skip — every other failure (AccessDenied, throttling, a drifted pool id) reds the build, so the check cannot go permanently green and blind.
- `scripts/check-rate-parity.mjs:14-19,74-76` is value-blind by construction: values are compared in memory, `delete r.value` runs before anything prints, and the header explains why even a hash prefix is unacceptable for a low-entropy factor. This is rule 6 honored in a script whose output lands in a public Actions log.
- `infra/github-oidc-drift-role.yaml:46-50` requires BOTH `aud` and `sub` conditions and pins `sub` to a single ref, with the reasoning written inline — without `aud` any GitHub tenant could mint a token, without `sub` any repository could.
- `lambda/sync/index.mjs:80-86` caps the snapshot on `Buffer.byteLength(serialized, "utf8")` rather than string length, with the reason stated: curriculum content is full of 3-byte glyphs, so a UTF-16 count would admit ~780 KB past DynamoDB's item limit and turn a clean 413 into a permanently wedged sync.

### `.git/config`'s notebook filters now point at a repo-tracked script, so checking out a fork PR executes contributor code on a maintainer's machine

`Makefile:20-23` — `faed4bf25` · medium · confirmed · security · ran locally · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 04

**Claim.** PR #246 replaced `nbstripout --install` (which baked an absolute interpreter path plus `-m nbstripout` into `.git/config`) with `git config filter.nbstripout.clean "scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh"` and `git config diff.ipynb.textconv "scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh -t"`. `.gitattributes:1-2` assigns `filter=nbstripout` and `diff=ipynb` to every `*.ipynb`, and there are 45 tracked notebooks. The target is now a shell script under version control, so its contents change with the checked-out branch. The commit message itself states the underlying rule — "git refuses to let a repo configure its own filters, since cloning would then execute code" — and then opts in manually anyway, moving from a value a PR cannot influence to one it can.

**Correction.** Two parts of the reasoning are wrong. (1) The trigger list is overstated: `gh pr checkout` alone does NOT execute the script — `filter.nbstripout.smudge` is `cat`, so checkout never invokes it, and I confirmed a clean-state `git checkout <pr-branch>` leaves the payload unfired. `git diff <base>` fires reliably via textconv, and `git add`/`git commit` fire via clean; `git status` fires only when a notebook's stat data is stale against the index (I had to `touch` the notebook to make it fire), and a fresh checkout refreshes that stat data. So "then `git diff` or `git status`" is correct for diff, conditional for status. (2) "This is a PUBLIC repo that accepts fork PRs" overstates present exposure: the repo has 0 forks, 1 star, 1 contributor, and 0 cross-repository PRs out of 225 — all 225 authored by the sole owner. The attacker population is currently empty, so this is a latent regression, not a live exposure.

**Impact.** This is a PUBLIC repo that accepts fork PRs (`ci.yml:22` is `on: pull_request`). A contributor opens a PR that edits `scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh`. A maintainer who has run `make setup` does the normal thing — `gh pr checkout <n>` then `git diff` or `git status` — and git invokes the checked-out version of that script as the clean filter or textconv on the first notebook it touches, running arbitrary code as the maintainer, in the checkout that holds their AWS credentials and Stripe keys. Before #246 the same PR was inert, because `.git/config` named a python binary and the module, not a repo file. I confirmed the configuration is live on this machine: `git config --get filter.nbstripout.clean` returns `scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh` and `filter.nbstripout.required` is `true`.

**Evidence.** `Makefile:20` `@git config filter.nbstripout.clean "scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh"`; `Makefile:23` `@git config diff.ipynb.textconv "scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh -t"`; `.gitattributes:1-2` `*.ipynb filter=nbstripout` / `*.ipynb diff=ipynb`; `scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh:42` `exec "$py" -m nbstripout "$@"` — the script is a plain `set -euo pipefail` bash file with no integrity check. Verified locally: `git config --get filter.nbstripout.clean` → `scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh`, `filter.nbstripout.required` → `true`.

**Split verdict.** reproduces: confirmed · correct as written: partly true. Published at the more severe reading.

**Verification — reproduces** (confirmed, medium, ran locally). Every cited fact is exact, and I reproduced arbitrary code execution as the maintainer in an isolated clone. The real repo was not modified (verified: `git status --short` and `git rev-parse HEAD` at /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum are byte-identical to the starting snapshot, HEAD still 1f38013 on main).

CITED FACTS, ALL VERIFIED
- `sed -n '18,24p' Makefile` -> line 20 is `@git config filter.nbstripout.clean "scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh"` and line 23 is `@git config diff.ipynb.textconv "scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh -t"`. Exact.
- `cat .gitattributes` -> lines 1-2 are `*.ipynb filter=nbstripout` / `*.ipynb diff=ipynb`. `git ls-files '*.ipynb' | wc -l` -> 45.
- `git config --local --get-regexp 'filter\.nbstripout|diff\.ipynb'` -> the config is LIVE on this machine: clean=`scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh`, textconv=`scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh -t`, required=`true`, smudge=`cat`. Nothing in `--global`.
- `git ls-files -s scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh` -> mode `100755`, tracked, so a fork PR ships it executable. `sed -n '42p'` -> `exec "$py" -m nbstripout "$@"`. No signature, hash pin, or integrity check anywhere (`grep -n 'nbstripout-filter|sha|hash|integrity' tests/test_notebook_hygiene.py` -> the new test in #246 checks notebook cleanliness only, never the wrapper's contents).
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` -> `on: pull_request`. Public repo.

THE "NEW EXPOSURE" HALF IS ALSO TRUE
`git show 590050f^:Makefile` -> pre-#246 setup ran `@nbstripout --install --attributes .gitattributes`, which bakes an absolute interpreter path plus `-m nbstripout` into `.git/config` — a value no PR can influence. `git config --get core.hooksPath` is unset, `ls .git/hooks` has only `.sample` files, and `git ls-files` shows no tracked hooks, `.envrc`, or pre-commit config, so #246 introduced the only repo-controlled exec-on-git-operation path that exists.

REPRODUCTION (scratchpad clone at .../scratchpad/repro/clone, wired with the same four `git config` values as the real repo)
I created branch `hostile-fork-pr-2` carrying a realistic contributor PR: a one-line notebook edit plus a rewritten `scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh` whose body is `echo "PWNED by $(id -un) ..." >> .../PWNED.txt; exec cat`. Then the maintainer's normal flow:
  git -C "$C" checkout hostile-fork-pr-2      # == `gh pr checkout <n>`; marker 0 — checkout itself is silent
  git -C "$C" status --short                  # marker 1  <-- clean filter ran the contributor's script
  git -C "$C" diff main -- 00-prereqs/notebooks/01-python-numpy-warmup.ipynb   # marker 3 <-- textconv ran it too
Payload log: `PWNED by cperez cwd=<repo root> argv=[]` (clean, twice) and `... argv=[-t /var/folders/.../git-blob-0pHE1k/01-python-numpy-warmup.ipynb]` (textconv). Executed as the real user, cwd = repo root, with no prompt and no output shown to the operator.

SEVERITY — I agree with medium, and note one aggravator and one limiter.
Aggravator: the checkout is silent but `git status` is not, and every git-aware editor/prompt runs `git status` continuously — so the payload fires seconds after `gh pr checkout`, BEFORE the human has read the diff that contains it. The finding's "on the first notebook it touches" is accurate.
Limiter: it requires the maintainer to check the PR out locally (reviewing on github.com is inert) and to have run `make setup`. Not high, because it needs that user action and nothing is in flight; not low, because the blast radius is the checkout holding AWS and Stripe credentials, and git refuses repo-configured filters for precisely this reason — a rule #246's own commit message quotes and then opts out of.

**Verification — correct as written** (partly true, low, ran locally). The mechanism is real and I reproduced it rather than reasoning about it. I built a throwaway repo in the scratchpad mirroring the exact wiring (`.gitattributes` = `*.ipynb filter=nbstripout` / `diff=ipynb`; `git config filter.nbstripout.clean "scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh"`, `smudge cat`, `required true`, `diff.ipynb.textconv "scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh -t"`), committed a "contributor PR" branch that rewrote `scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh` to write a marker file, then ran each maintainer command in isolation with the marker deleted between runs:

  git checkout contrib-pr           -> clean  (smudge is `cat`; nothing runs)
  touch lesson.ipynb; git status    -> PWNED
  git add lesson.ipynb              -> PWNED
  git diff main -- lesson.ipynb     -> PWNED   ("arbitrary code ran as cperez at Thu Aug 27 ...")

So the checked-out branch's version of the script does execute as the maintainer. Git runs filter/textconv commands through the shell with cwd at the worktree root, which is exactly what makes the repo-relative path work — and also what makes it branch-controlled.

The regression claim is accurate. `git show 590050f^:Makefile` confirms the pre-#246 target ran `nbstripout --install --attributes .gitattributes`, which bakes an absolute interpreter path plus `-m nbstripout` into `.git/config` — a value no PR can influence. `Makefile:20-23` now names a tracked file (`git ls-files -s` -> mode `100755`, so a contributor branch carries its own exec bit). Live config on this machine matches the finding: `git config --get filter.nbstripout.clean` -> `scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh`, `.required` -> `true`, textconv -> `... -t`. 45 tracked notebooks.

I looked hard for the refutation and did not find one. There is no integrity check, hash pin, or allowlist anywhere — `git grep nbstripout-filter` returns only the Makefile lines and the script's own header comments. No `core.hooksPath`, no pre-commit, no husky. `tests/test_notebook_hygiene.py` is a notebook-output guard reading the git index; it does not validate the filter script. Notably, both that test's docstring and the #246 commit message state the underlying rule verbatim ("git refuses to let a repo configure its own filters ... cloning would execute code") and then opt in manually, so this is a known-principle-applied-inconsistently case, not an undocumented one — but nothing records it as an accepted trade-off.

Severity: low, down from the finder's medium. Impact-if-triggered is genuinely bad (arbitrary execution in a checkout holding AWS and Stripe credentials) and the fix is trivial, but the preconditions do not exist: no forks, no outside contributor has ever opened a PR. The incremental risk is also narrower than it first looks — this repo's normal review flow already executes contributor code (`make test` executes all 45 notebooks, `make setup` does `pip install -e .`), so what #246 actually added is that commands a reviewer reasonably believes are read-only (`git diff`, `git add`) now execute contributor code too. That is a real erosion of a boundary git deliberately maintains, and it should be re-rated medium the day this project accepts its first outside PR.

(2) "This is a PUBLIC repo that accepts fork PRs" overstates present exposure: the repo has 0 forks, 1 star, 1 contributor, and 0 cross-repository PRs out of 225 — all 225 authored by the sole owner. ### The CI drift role's account-wide `lambda:ListFunctions` grant exposes every Lambda environment variable in the production account, including a live HMAC secret

`infra/github-oidc-drift-role.yaml:64-68` — `f1ee43fd4` · medium · partly true · security · observed live · re-raised from `f50e54cb6` · fix plan 04

**Claim.** The template grants `lambda:ListFunctions` on `Resource: "*"` and justifies it in an inline comment as "read-only and returns metadata only (no code, no environment secrets)". That premise is false, and I verified it against the live API rather than the docs. `ListFunctions` returns full `FunctionConfiguration` objects including `Environment.Variables`; the AWS reference states only that `State`, `StateReasonCode`, `StateReason`, `LastUpdateStatus*` and `RuntimeVersionConfig` are omitted. Nothing in the repo calls `ListFunctions`: `scripts/check-lambda-drift.mjs:76,92` uses `get-function` and `get-function-configuration` by explicit name, and `scripts/check-rate-parity.mjs:36-51` uses `get-function-configuration`. Both are already covered by the prefix-scoped grant on lines 59-63.

**Correction.** The two named "not theoretical" impacts are both wrong, and they are the finding's entire punch. UNSUB_SECRET and RATE_CARD live on `quantum-*` functions, so both are ALREADY fully readable through the prefix-scoped grant on lines 59-63 that the finding itself endorses as legitimate and necessary. `aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name quantum-review-email-unsubscribe --region us-east-2 --query 'keys(Environment.Variables)'` returns `["UNSUB_SECRET","PREFS_TABLE","SITE_URL"]`, and `scripts/check-rate-parity.mjs:36-51` reads `Environment.Variables.RATE_CARD` off `quantum-tutor`/`quantum-qpu-submit` by exactly that route, deliberately. Deleting lines 64-68 does not reduce exposure of either secret by one bit. The actual marginal exposure from lines 64-68 is the env vars of the NON-quantum functions: 188 of 269 in us-east-2 carry env vars outside the prefix, plus 21 more in us-east-1 (`aws lambda list-functions --region <r> --query 'length(Functions[?Environment!=null && !starts_with(FunctionName, `quantum-`)])'`) — other Altivum workloads sharing the production account. Second, "any workflow that lands on refs/heads/main in this PUBLIC repo" overstates reachability: the trust policy pins `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` to `repo:AltivumInc-Admin/quantum-computing:ref:refs/heads/main`, and a fork PR carries a `pull_request` sub, so a member of the public cannot assume this role by opening a PR. Assumption requires main-branch write plus a workflow granting `id-token: write` — and `grep -ln "id-token" .github/workflows/*` shows drift.yml is the only one. The repo being public is not what makes it reachable.

### Unsubscribe mutates consent on an unauthenticated GET, so a mail-security link scanner silently disables an opted-in learner's reminders

`lambda/review-email/review-email-core.mjs:325-343` — `fb7182bdb` · low · partly true · correctness · observed live · fix plan 04

**Claim.** `createUnsubscribeCore` reads the token from `event.queryStringParameters.t` and, on a valid HMAC, immediately issues an `UpdateItemCommand` setting `remindersOn = false` and `optOut = true`. There is no method check and no confirmation step: `template.yaml:146-147` exposes it as a Function URL with `AuthType: NONE`, so a plain GET is sufficient. The email embeds that URL as an `<a href>` in both the HTML and text parts (`renderEmail`, lines 127 and 135). Corporate mail security (Microsoft Defender Safe Links, Proofpoint URL Defense), Gmail's image/link prefetch and antivirus scanners all issue GETs against links in delivered mail; each one is indistinguishable from a real click and each one is a permanent opt-out. RFC 8058 requires POST for one-click unsubscribe for exactly this reason, and neither `List-Unsubscribe` nor `List-Unsubscribe-Post` headers are set anywhere in `SendEmailCommand`.

**Correction.** Four things in the reasoning are wrong or overstated, though the defect itself stands.

(1) **Gmail does not fetch in-body links.** Gmail proxies and prefetches IMAGES through googleusercontent; it does not issue GETs against anchor hrefs in a message body. The accurate examples are Microsoft Defender Safe Links detonation and Proofpoint URL Defense, which do fetch URLs. Dropping Gmail from the list removes the single largest consumer mailbox provider from the claimed exposure, which materially shrinks the population the finding says is at risk.

(2) **RFC 8058 does not apply to this link.** RFC 8058 governs the `List-Unsubscribe` / `List-Unsubscribe-Post` HEADER mechanism and requires POST for URLs advertised there. It imposes nothing on an ordinary in-body unsubscribe anchor. The rationale the finder cites is real and is stated in the RFC, but "RFC 8058 requires POST for one-click unsubscribe" is not a rule this code is in violation of, because the code advertises no one-click header at all.

(3) **"Permanent opt-out" overstates it.** The write is a reversible preference toggle. `web/src/components/reminder-prefs.tsx` is a working re-enable surface, and the confirmation page links to `/workspace`. The learner is not permanently anything; they are silently off until they notice.

(4) **This is the third report of the same item.** `docs/codebase-audit-2026-08-16.md:482-487` carries it as finding #5, verified there against the same lines and adjudicated **Partly true / low** with substantially the same reasoning I reached independently. `docs/codebase-audit-2026-08-18.json` carries it again at `/prior/findings/44`. The finding is presented as new; it is a known, twice-adjudicated item.

**Correction.** Three parts of the reasoning are wrong or overstated. (1) "Gmail's image/link prefetch" does not apply: Gmail proxies and prefetches IMAGE URLs, not anchor hrefs — it does not issue GETs against links in delivered mail. That removes the largest consumer-mailbox population from the exposure set and leaves only corporate URL-detonation products (Defender Safe Links, Proofpoint URL Defense) and AV scanners, which for a consumer-facing learning product is a much smaller slice than the sentence implies. (2) RFC 8058 governs the `List-Unsubscribe` / `List-Unsubscribe-Post` HEADER mechanism; it imposes no requirement on an in-body `<a href>`. Citing it as "requires POST for exactly this reason" borrows a mandate that does not reach this anchor — the underlying hazard is real, the standard's authority over it is not. (3) "silently opted back out, with no notification and no way to distinguish it" overstates the user-visible impact: `web/src/components/reminder-prefs.tsx` fetches server state on mount and renders the literal string "Reminders are off.", and `createPrefsCore`'s PUT-true branch (line 403) is `SET remindersOn = :v ... REMOVE optOut`, so a learner sees the wrong state in the workspace and can fully self-recover in one click. It is unlogged, not undiscoverable.

**Impact.** A learner who deliberately opted in (the default is off, `remindersOn` must be exactly `true`) is silently opted back out by their own mail provider, with no notification and no way to distinguish it from a real click — the operation is idempotent and logs nothing that separates the two. The fix is a confirmation page on GET and the mutation on POST. Dormant today: I verified `aws sesv2 get-account` returns `ProductionAccessEnabled: false`, and `review-email-core.mjs:214-219` refuses the entire run in the sandbox, so no email has ever been delivered and no scanner has ever seen the link. The Function URL itself is live and publicly reachable (`AuthType: NONE`, confirmed), but rejects any token that fails the HMAC.

**Evidence.** `review-email-core.mjs:326-343` — token read from query string, `UpdateItemCommand` with `SET remindersOn = :off, optOut = :out` executed unconditionally on a valid token, no method inspection. `lambda/review-email/template.yaml:146-147` `FunctionUrlConfig: AuthType: NONE`. `review-email-core.mjs:272-286` `SendEmailCommand` sets only `Subject`/`Html`/`Text` — no `List-Unsubscribe` header. Live: `aws lambda get-function-url-config --function-name quantum-review-email-unsubscribe` → `{"auth": "NONE", "url": "https://$LAMBDA_URL/"}`; `aws sesv2 get-account` → `ProductionAccessEnabled: false`.

**Verification — reproduces** (partly true, low, observed live). **Reproduced the mutation.** I wrote a scratchpad harness stubbing the DynamoDB client and drove `createUnsubscribeCore` with a Function-URL v2 event shaped like a scanner request (`node /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/repro.mjs`, run from `lambda/review-email`). A bare GET carrying a valid token returned `200` and issued exactly one `UpdateItemCommand`: `SET remindersOn = :off, optOut = :out, updatedAt = :t` with `:off {BOOL:false}`, `:out {BOOL:true}`. A **HEAD** request with the same token mutated identically — `HEAD status: 200 writes: 1`. There is no method inspection on any path. The same harness confirmed via `renderEmail` that the URL ships as an `<a href>` in the HTML part and as a bare `Unsubscribe: <url>` line in the text part.

**The endpoint is live and open.** `aws lambda get-function-url-config --function-name quantum-review-email-unsubscribe --region us-east-2` → `"AuthType": "NONE"`, `https://$LAMBDA_URL/`, created 2026-07-08. Matches `template.yaml:145-147`. I did not send a request to it (that would mutate state).

**Dormancy confirmed.** `aws sesv2 get-account --region us-east-2` → `ProductionAccessEnabled: false`, `EnforcementStatus: HEALTHY`, quota 200/day. `review-email-core.mjs:214-219` checks `ProductionAccessEnabled !== true` and returns `{skippedSandbox: true}` before scanning anything, so no email has been delivered and no scanner has ever seen a token. The token is HMAC-SHA256 over the `sub` (`unsubToken`, line 82-85), so the URL is unguessable — only a delivered email can leak one. That closes the exposure completely for now.

**The header claim checks out.** `grep -rniE "list-unsubscribe|one-click|8058" . --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git` returns only prose (README, i18n copy, the prior audit) — no header is set anywhere. The `SendEmailCommand` at lines 272-286 passes only `Content.Simple.Subject/Body`.

**What genuinely strengthens the finding, and the finder missed it:** the sibling endpoint in the same file does this correctly. `createPrefsCore` (lines 375-421) reads `event.requestContext?.http?.method`, serves GET read-only, gates mutation behind PUT/DELETE, and returns `405` for anything else — and `review-email-core.test.mjs:426-428` asserts that 405. So mutate-on-GET is not this codebase's house style; the unsubscribe handler is the lone divergence from a discipline the file otherwise keeps and tests.

**Why low, not higher:** the blast radius is one reversible boolean on a retention email that has never been sent, recoverable from `/workspace` in two clicks. The right fix is the one the finder names — confirmation page on GET, mutation on POST — plus `List-Unsubscribe` + `List-Unsubscribe-Post` headers when SES leaves the sandbox, which is the moment this stops being theoretical.

The accurate examples are Microsoft Defender Safe Links detonation and Proofpoint URL Defense, which do fetch URLs. Dropping Gmail from the list removes the single largest consumer mailbox provider from the claimed exposure, which materially shrinks the population the finding says is at risk.

(2) **RFC 8058 does not apply to this link.** RFC 8058 governs the `List-Unsubscribe` / `List-Unsubscribe-Post` HEADER mechanism and requires POST for URLs advertised there. The finding is presented as new; it is a known, twice-adjudicated item.

**Verification — correct as written** (partly true, low, observed live). The mechanical claim is exactly right and every citation verifies line-for-line. `createUnsubscribeCore` (review-email-core.mjs:325-343) reads `event?.queryStringParameters?.t`, and on a valid HMAC issues `UpdateItemCommand` with `SET remindersOn = :off, optOut = :out, updatedAt = :t` — no `event.requestContext.http.method` read anywhere in the function, and no confirmation step. Contrast `createPrefsCore` (line 377), which DOES branch on method — so the omission is real, not a framework convention I missed. `template.yaml:146-147` is `FunctionUrlConfig: AuthType: NONE` verbatim, and the template has no CORS block on that function (and Function-URL CORS `AllowMethods` would not restrict a non-browser GET anyway). `renderEmail` embeds `unsubUrl` at line 127 (text) and 135 (html). `SendEmailCommand` (272-286) sets only Subject/Html/Text — `grep -n "List-Unsubscribe" lambda/review-email/*.mjs` returns nothing. `unsubscribe.mjs` wires the core straight to a real DynamoDBClient with no wrapper. `review-email-core.test.mjs:326` exercises only `{ queryStringParameters: { t: ... } }` — no method is ever passed, so no test covers this.

I searched for a recorded decision and found none that considers scanner GETs. README.md and `en.ts:943` both call it "one-click unsubscribe," and the README's drafted SES production-access use-case description repeats it — that is intent to have a one-click link, not a considered acceptance of prefetch.

Live checks (read-only, us-east-2):
- `aws lambda get-function-url-config --function-name quantum-review-email-unsubscribe --region us-east-2` → `"AuthType": "NONE"`, `https://$LAMBDA_URL/`, created 2026-07-08. The finder's URL matches.
- `aws sesv2 get-account --region us-east-2 --query ProductionAccessEnabled` → `false`. Sandbox guard at 214-219 refuses the whole run.
- `aws events list-rules --region us-east-2 --query 'Rules[?contains(Name,`review-email`)]'` → `quantum-review-email-SenderFunctionDaily-hNpzhoP0FzmY`, **State: DISABLED**. The finder missed this second dormancy layer; the sender is not even invoked, so its own dormancy claim is understated in its favor.

Severity: low is the right call and is not inflated. Three independent layers stop any email existing (disabled schedule, SES sandbox, no verified recipient identities), the worst outcome is one missed weekly reminder on a free surface, and it is fully self-recoverable from a control that already displays the wrong state. Nothing here touches money, credentials, or the monetization rules. The fix the finder names (confirmation page on GET, mutation on POST) is correct and cheap, and adding `List-Unsubscribe` + `List-Unsubscribe-Post` is worth doing at the same time for Gmail/Yahoo bulk-sender compliance — but that is a separate deliverability item, not this defect.

### `delete-account.tsx` hardcodes English error strings that already exist verbatim as translated i18n keys, and the Google-refusal message has no key at all

`web/src/components/auth/delete-account.tsx:80-82` — `fae7ca83c` · low · partly true · consistency · ran locally · fix plan 12

**Claim.** Every other string in the component goes through `t("deleteAccount.*")`, but all five error paths build English literals inline. Four of them duplicate existing keys word for word: line 108 equals `deleteAccount.partialPrefs`, line 109 equals `prefsFailed`, line 124 equals `partialAccount`, line 125 equals `accountFailed`, and the `" Try again."` suffix equals `tryAgain`. All five keys are defined in `en.ts:431-437` AND translated in `es.ts:429-435` — and referenced nowhere: `grep -rn "partialPrefs\|prefsFailed\|partialAccount\|accountFailed" web/src` returns only the two locale files. The Google-session refusal at lines 79-84 ("Accounts created with Google can't be deleted from here yet…") has no key in either locale.

**Correction.** Four peripheral claims are wrong, none of which touch the core defect:

1. TEST COUNT: the finder says "27 tests pass — I ran it." The suite has 12. `cd web && npx jest __tests__/components/auth/delete-account.test.tsx` -> "Tests: 12 passed, 12 total". The assertion about WHAT it asserts (English regexes only, lines 160/176/190-191) is correct.

2. "ALL FIVE ERROR PATHS": there are four `setError(...)` message sites (lines 79, 93, 106, 122), two of which carry a syncConfigured/prefsConfigured ternary, producing six distinct messages. Neither count is five.

3. THE FINDING UNDERSTATES THE GAP: it says only the Google refusal "has no key at all." Two messages are keyless, not one. The sync-delete failure at :94 ("Couldn't delete your synced progress from the server. Nothing was deleted - your account is untouched. Try again.") has no key in either locale, and neither does the :110 suffix " Your account was NOT deleted. Try again to finish." The `deleteAccount` block holds exactly 17 keys and none match those two. So of six messages, four map to existing keys and two are untranslatable without new keys.

4. DIMENSION MISLABEL: filed under "Identity, auth and infrastructure security." There is no security consequence — no auth bypass, no data exposure, no incorrect state. It is an i18n/UX consistency defect (the finder's own category field, "consistency", is the right one).

Path nit: the privacy contact is at `web/src/components/privacy/privacy-page-content.tsx:6`, not `privacy-page-content.tsx:6` at top level; line 6 and the value are as claimed.

**Correction.** Three parts of the write-up are wrong or incomplete. (1) The executed-evidence figure is false: `cd web && npx jest __tests__/components/auth/delete-account.test.tsx` reports "Tests: 12 passed, 12 total", not 27. ### The tutor README still instructs attaching `policy.json`, a Bedrock-only policy that cannot start the post-Bedrock handler

`lambda/tutor/policy.json:9` — `f108c1790` · low · confirmed · docs-drift · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · re-raised from `f54ce715f` · fix plan 10

**Claim.** `policy.json` grants `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream` on an inference profile and three foundation models, plus logs. The tutor moved off Bedrock on 2026-08-17: `lambda/tutor/index.mjs` now reads an Anthropic key with `GetSecretValueCommand({SecretId: process.env.SECRET_ID})`, and `lambda/tutor/template.yaml:163-165` is the only place granting `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`. `README.md:100-109` still walks an operator through `aws iam put-role-policy --policy-document file://lambda/tutor/policy.json` followed by `--environment "Variables={SECRET_ID=quantum-tutor}"`, producing a role with a dead Bedrock grant and no permission to read the secret the handler needs. The prior audit also flagged the embedded production account id on this line; that half does not stand — the same id is deliberately published at `scripts/founding-credit/cohort-2026-08.json:9` as `expectedAccountId`, so scrubbing it here un-publishes nothing.

**Correction.** The impact's "The failure is loud and immediate" is wrong on "loud." It is immediate and total, but silent: `index.mjs:580-583` commits `statusCode: 200` before streaming, so the `catch` at `:421-433` emits only a `console.error(JSON.stringify({tutorError: true, ...}))` and an in-band `TUTOR_ERROR_SENTINEL` + "The tutor hit an error" — the HTTP status stays 200 and the Lambda `Errors` metric never moves (the code comment at :426-428 says exactly this). The `tutorError` metric filter and its alarm are stack-managed in `template.yaml`, so the raw-CLI path the finding is about creates neither: an operator who takes that path gets a generic apology, a 200, and no alarm. That makes the drift slightly harder to diagnose than described, not less real; severity stays low for the other reason the finder gives (an explicitly-secondary, never-executed path). Also minor: the AccessDenied lands on the Secrets Manager read that precedes the model call, not on the model call itself.

**Impact.** The documented raw-CLI deploy path builds a role that AccessDenies on the first model call. The failure is loud and immediate, and SAM is labelled "recommended" at README.md:34, so this is drift on an explicitly secondary path rather than a live break — but the file is presented as a live IAM document and grants a permission the function no longer uses, which is the wrong default for a policy someone may copy.

### The Founding Ten registry ships a named person beside an unsalted SHA-256 of their email, in a public repo and in the public JS bundle

`web/src/data/founding-ten.json:5-7` — `f1a08c7fb` · low · partly true · privacy · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · re-raised from `f428e799a` · fix plan 05

**Claim.** The registry pairs `"holder": "$FOUNDING_HOLDER_NAME"` with `"emailHash": "$FOUNDING_EMAIL_HASH…"`, an unsalted SHA-256 over `email.trim().toLowerCase()` (`scripts/lib/email-hash.mjs:17-20`). `web/src/lib/founding-ten.ts:18` imports the JSON with a static `import registry from "@/data/founding-ten.json"`, and `allBadges()` is called from `cohortSlots()` and `badgeForEmailHash()` in client components (`web/src/components/founding-ten/my-badges.tsx:12`), so the file is bundled into the static export and served to every visitor — the `/founding-ten/*` routes are in `PUBLIC_PREFIXES` (`auth-wall.tsx:28`) precisely so third parties can verify a badge without an account.

**Correction.** The remedy is wrong, and wrong in a way that would leave the reader believing the hole was closed. The finding proposes "a per-registry random salt committed beside the hashes would keep every property the design needs while removing the oracle." A committed salt is a public salt: the attacker reads it out of the same JSON, and testing a candidate address still costs exactly one SHA-256. Zero oracle capability is removed. A salt only defeats precomputed rainbow tables, which are not the threat here (the finding's own threat model is "anyone holding a candidate address for a named individual").

Worse, the architecture forces any salt to be public regardless of intent: `web/src/components/auth/amplify-auth-bridge.tsx:85` computes `await hashEmail(emailClaim)` in the browser from the ID-token email claim, and `web/src/lib/founding-ten.ts:47` implements it on Web Crypto precisely so it runs client-side. In a static export with client-side badge matching, a salt the browser can apply is a salt every visitor downloads. So the proposed fix is ineffective twice over.

Closing the oracle actually requires giving up one of the two things being combined: either the digest stops being client-reproducible (an HMAC under a key only a server holds — which breaks `badgeForEmailHash` in a static export), or the public artifact stops binding the name to the digest (e.g. the registry ships names and opaque per-badge random ids, with the email->id mapping held server-side or uncommitted).

Everything else in the finding — location, mechanism, bundling, public reachability, severity — is accurate as written.

**Impact.** Full name plus unsalted digest is a confirmation oracle: anyone holding a candidate address for a named individual can hash it and get a yes/no, at zero cost, forever, from a public artifact. The code's own comment concedes this ("The hash is not a privacy guarantee (emails are enumerable, so a guess can be tested against this file)") and justifies it as "the holder's name is already public on their proof page by consent" — which covers publishing the name, not publishing the name bound to a testable digest of a private address. Low, because the cohort is one person today and the design's motivation (email-keyed identity survives account recreation and native-vs-Google duplication) is sound; a per-registry random salt committed beside the hashes would keep every property the design needs while removing the oracle.

**Evidence.** `web/src/data/founding-ten.json:5-7` `"holder": "$FOUNDING_HOLDER_NAME", "issuedAt": "2026-07-29", "emailHash": "$FOUNDING_EMAIL_HASH"`. `scripts/lib/email-hash.mjs:19-20` `createHash("sha256").update(normalizeEmail(email)).digest("hex")` — no salt. `web/src/lib/founding-ten.ts:14-16` acknowledges the enumerability. `web/src/components/auth/auth-wall.tsx:28` `const PUBLIC_PREFIXES = ["/e2e-fixtures", "/founding-ten"];`

**Split verdict.** reproduces: partly true · correct as written: refuted. Published at the more severe reading.

**Verification — reproduces** (partly true, low, observed live). The exposure reproduces exactly as described, on the live production site, unauthenticated.

WHAT I RAN

1. Local source, all cited lines confirmed verbatim:
`cat /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/src/data/founding-ten.json` — lines 5-7 are `"holder": "$FOUNDING_HOLDER_NAME"`, `"issuedAt": "2026-07-29"`, `"emailHash": "$FOUNDING_EMAIL_HASH"`.
`grep -n "" /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/scripts/lib/email-hash.mjs | sed -n '15,21p'` — lines 19-20 are `createHash("sha256").update(normalizeEmail(email)).digest("hex")`. No salt.
`grep -rn "salt" scripts/ web/src/` over the badge path returns nothing.
`sed -n '18p' web/src/lib/founding-ten.ts` is the static `import registry from "@/data/founding-ten.json"`; `auth-wall.tsx:28` is `const PUBLIC_PREFIXES = ["/e2e-fixtures", "/founding-ten"];`.

2. Local static export:
`grep -rl "$FOUNDING_EMAIL_HASH..." /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/out` → `_next/static/chunks/02kiszu.nv5py.js`. The chunk contains `holder:"$FOUNDING_HOLDER_NAME",issuedAt:"2026-07-29",emailHash:"$FOUNDING_EMAIL_HASH..."` — name and digest literally adjacent.

3. Live deployment (quantumlearner.dev 301-redirects to quantum.altivum.ai):
`curl -sL https://quantumlearner.dev/founding-ten` → 200, contains "$FOUNDING_HOLDER_NAME".
Iterating the 8 chunks referenced by that page with `curl -s "https://quantum.altivum.ai$c" | grep -q "$FOUNDING_EMAIL_HASH..."` → HASH FOUND IN `/_next/static/chunks/02kiszu.nv5py.js`.
`curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://quantum.altivum.ai/_next/static/chunks/02kiszu.nv5py.js` → `status:200 bytes:32626`, no cookies, no auth.

NOT A FIXTURE. `scripts/verify-founding-ten.mjs` fails the build unless the hash still matches an enabled Cognito user in pool `$USER_POOL_ID`, and its `--who` flag refuses to run in CI because "printing an address to a build log would put it in exactly the widely-readable place this whole design exists to keep it out of." So it is a real person's real address, and the repo's own code treats that address as sensitive. The same digest is also committed at `scripts/founding-credit/cohort-2026-08.json:14`, and git history makes both permanent.

PRACTICAL BOUND. I ran an offline dictionary against the published digest (`node /tmp/oracle.mjs`, 1,392 name-derived candidates: 30 local-part forms x 16 domains incl. gmail/yahoo/outlook/icloud/proton/quantumlearner.dev/altivum.io) — no match. Blind recovery from the name alone is not trivial; the leak is confirmation-only, given a candidate, which is what the finder claimed. Low severity stands: one holder, name already public by consent, and what the oracle confirms is the address, not the membership.

WHY NOT FULLY CONFIRMED — see correction.

> Correction. The remedy is wrong, and wrong in a way that would leave the reader believing the hole was closed. The finding proposes "a per-registry random salt committed beside the hashes would keep every property the design needs while removing the oracle." A committed salt is a public salt: the attacker reads it out of the same JSON, and testing a candidate address still costs exactly one SHA-256. Zero oracle capability is removed. A salt only defeats precomputed rainbow tables, which are not the threat here (the finding's own threat model is "anyone holding a candidate address for a named individual").

Worse, the architecture forces any salt to be public regardless of intent: `web/src/components/auth/amplify-auth-bridge.tsx:85` computes `await hashEmail(emailClaim)` in the browser from the ID-token email claim, and `web/src/lib/founding-ten.ts:47` implements it on Web Crypto precisely so it runs client-side. In a static export with client-side badge matching, a salt the browser can apply is a salt every visitor downloads. So the proposed fix is ineffective twice over.

Closing the oracle actually requires giving up one of the two things being combined: either the digest stops being client-reproducible (an HMAC under a key only a server holds — which breaks `badgeForEmailHash` in a static export), or the public artifact stops binding the name to the digest (e.g. the registry ships names and opaque per-badge random ids, with the email->id mapping held server-side or uncommitted).

Everything else in the finding — location, mechanism, bundling, public reachability, severity — is accurate as written.

**Verification — correct as written** (refuted, low, ran locally). Every mechanical fact the finder cites reproduces, but the finding does not stand as a defect: it is a documented, explicitly deliberated, accepted tradeoff, and the remedy it proposes is inert.

WHAT REPRODUCES (I ran these against the checked-in static export at /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/out):
- `grep -rl "$FOUNDING_EMAIL_HASH" web/out` -> exactly one hit, `web/out/_next/static/chunks/02kiszu.nv5py.js`.
- `grep -o '.\{80\}$FOUNDING_EMAIL_HASH...\{20\}' web/out/_next/static/chunks/02kiszu.nv5py.js` -> `{charter:[{serial:1,holder:"$FOUNDING_HOLDER_NAME",issuedAt:"2026-07-29",emailHash:"$FOUNDING_EMAIL_HASH..."}],patron:[]}`. Name and digest ship adjacent in a public JS chunk.
- `grep -rl "$FOUNDING_HOLDER_NAME" web/out` -> also `founding-ten.html`, `founding-ten/charter-01.html`.
- `/Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/src/components/auth/auth-wall.tsx:28` is `PUBLIC_PREFIXES = ["/e2e-fixtures", "/founding-ten"]` as quoted, and `/Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/scripts/lib/email-hash.mjs:20` is bare `createHash("sha256").update(normalizeEmail(email))` with no salt.

WHY IT IS REFUTED:

1. The finder's central rhetorical move is directly contradicted by the spec it did not read. It argues the code comment "covers publishing the name, not publishing the name bound to a testable digest." But `/Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-founding-ten-badges-design.md:54-60` carries a section headed "Accepted weakness, stated plainly" that states the finder's exact attack AND the exact marginal disclosure it claims is unaddressed: "emails are enumerable, so anyone can hash a guess and test it against the registry. Since the holder is already named publicly on the proof page, the marginal disclosure is 'this named person uses this address.' Accepted knowingly, in exchange for a binding that does not silently detach." The name-bound-to-digest case is precisely what was weighed and accepted, not an oversight. `scripts/verify-founding-ten.mjs:23-33` goes further and refuses to print addresses in CI, so the privacy boundary the design actually claims (no plaintext address anywhere widely readable) is enforced, not assumed.

2. The proposed fix does not work. The finder says "a per-registry random salt committed beside the hashes would keep every property the design needs while removing the oracle." A committed salt is public. Against the stated threat — someone holding a candidate address for a named individual — SHA-256(salt||candidate) costs exactly as much as SHA-256(candidate). A public salt defeats precomputed rainbow tables across many targets; it removes nothing here, with one target and a known salt. Nor could the salt be secret: `web/src/components/auth/amplify-auth-bridge.tsx:85` calls `hashEmail(emailClaim)` in the browser via `crypto.subtle` and matches it against the statically-imported registry, in an `output: "export"` build with no server. Any input to that hash must ship to every visitor. Removing the oracle would require a server-side lookup, which contradicts the design goal the finder itself quotes (a third party verifies a badge with no account).

3. What actually leaks is bounded and consented. `holder` is rendered publicly by design (`web/src/components/founding-ten/badge-proof.tsx:29`, roster), and the spec records "Requires the holder's consent" plus "A public name is permanent" as a risk. The gain to an attacker is confirming an address they already possess against a name already published — not learning either.

SEVERITY: the finder said low; I would go lower still, to informational. This is not a defect the reader should spend time on: it is a recorded decision with a working guard around the part that matters, and the only proposed mitigation is a no-op.

### `lambda/sync/node_modules` is the only vendored dependency tree in the repo — 2,560 tracked files that every sibling Lambda gitignores

`.gitignore:75` — `fc2af8f78` · low · confirmed · hygiene · ran locally · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 14

**Claim.** `.gitignore:75` ignores `lambda/sync/.aws-sam/` but not `lambda/sync/node_modules/`, while lines 47, 79 and 84 ignore the tutor, review-email and qpu trees and `lambda/stripe/.gitignore` and `lambda/analytics/.gitignore` each carry their own `node_modules/` entry. `git ls-files lambda/sync/node_modules | wc -l` returns 2,560 (14 MB); the same command for every other Lambda returns 0. Git history shows these files landed in the original sync PR (`8ea76b8`, #110, 2026-07-05) and every Lambda added since has been ignored — this is an omission, not a decision. The vendored versions do currently match `package-lock.json` exactly (I compared all 29 entries; zero missing, zero mismatched), but nothing asserts that: CI runs `npm ci` (`ci.yml:180-182`), which deletes and reinstalls the tree, so the committed bytes are never the bytes under test, and `scripts/check-lambda-drift.mjs:61-67` reads only top-level `.mjs`/`.js` from the source directory, so the drift gate cannot see them either.

**Correction.** Three parts of the reasoning are wrong. (1) "This is an omission, not a decision" is materially false as of today. The identical finding was raised by the 2026-08-16 audit, verified, and filed as GitHub issue #219 on 2026-08-17 (labels `audit-2026-08`, `area:infra`, state OPEN) — and re-reported at `docs/codebase-audit-2026-08-18.md:1634` plus its metrics table at line 45. So the present state is a knowingly-tracked, deliberately-deferred item with a written remediation, not an unnoticed omission — the opposite of what the finding tells the reader. (2) "Two-thirds of the repo's tracked files" is imprecise: 2560/3474 = 73.7%. (3) "`npm ci` leaves the working tree dirty across 2,560 files" is overstated to the point of being misleading — npm installs from integrity-pinned, content-addressed tarballs, so `npm ci` from this lockfile reproduces the package bytes exactly; `git status --porcelain lambda/sync` returns clean right now on a machine that has the tree. The realistic dirty surface is at most the single tracked `node_modules/.package-lock.json`, not 2,560 files.

**Impact.** Two-thirds of the repo's tracked files are one Lambda's dependencies, which is a review blind spot: a diff spanning 2,560 vendored files is exactly where a reviewer stops reading, and no test, lint or drift check would object to a changed byte inside it. It also means `npm ci` leaves the working tree dirty across 2,560 files whenever npm's install differs at all from what was committed, with nothing to warn.
