### A test pins the ABSENCE of a full CSP, so hardening the policy turns CI red

`web/__tests__/infra/custom-http.test.ts:179-183` — `f11694c76` · low · partly true · rule-violation · ran locally · SPLIT VERDICT · re-raised from `f63d74755` · fix plan 04

**Claim.** The suite asserts `expect(csp).not.toContain("script-src")`, `not.toContain("style-src")` and `not.toContain("default-src")` on the `/**` block's `Content-Security-Policy`. The shipped policy is `frame-ancestors 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'` (`customHttp.yml:43`), and its comment describes a script-src/style-src policy as "staged for later". A test that locks the absence of a control makes the future work fail the gate: whoever adds `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'` must delete the test in the same PR, and deleting a security test to ship a change is the shape that gets waved through. This is the same failure mode the repo already learned from in the pricing copy guards, where locking a promise's PRESENCE is recorded in CLAUDE.md as exactly how that promise outlived its withdrawal.

**Correction.** Three parts of the reasoning are wrong.

(1) The pricing-guard analogy is inverted in consequence. The sponsorship guards locked a FALSE customer-facing promise into shipped copy — a live rule-13 violation the test kept alive. This test locks the absence of an unshipped hardening; nothing false reaches a user meanwhile, and the shipped header (`object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`, `frame-ancestors 'self'`) is itself XSS/clickjacking hardening.

(2) "The guard is pointed the wrong way" singles out one assertion in a file whose entire design is to pin the header contract verbatim — the `it.each` at :74-105 pins every `Cache-Control` string, and :168-177 pins that no cache block carries a security key. `git log -S"stages no full CSP yet" -- web/__tests__/infra/custom-http.test.ts` and `git log -S"frame-ancestors 'self'; object-src 'none'" -- customHttp.yml` both return exactly one commit, 1612ceb (#156) — the assertion shipped in the SAME commit as the header it guards, in the same idiom as the rest of the file. It is a contemporaneous note on a deliberate deferral, not a lock retro-fitted over a known gap, and `ls .github/` shows workflows only (no CODEOWNERS), so there is nothing to "wave through" — the CSP change and the test edit land in one visible diff.

(3) The implied fix, `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'`, would break shipped behavior, so the red test is a correct alarm rather than a tax. `grep -rl "new Function(" web/public/lab/build/*.js` hits jlab_core.46b51ee.js and six other shipped chunks — JupyterLite needs `'unsafe-eval'`, not `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`. And `web/src/lib/pyodide-runtime.ts:55` keeps `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/pyodide/v.../full/` as the worker's boot failover, reached via `importScripts` (web/public/pyodide.worker.js:63,80), which a `'self'`-only script-src blocks — the `/**` pattern covers the worker's own response too.

What survives is a low-value code-health note: a negative assertion on a security control is weaker justified than the file's positive ones and would read better as a positive assertion of the intended policy. There is no runtime effect and no security regression.

**Correction.** Not applicable — refuted. For the record, the one sub-claim that survives is purely mechanical: adding `script-src` would turn this suite red. That is the tripwire working as designed, not a defect.

**Impact.** The static export has no server, so `customHttp.yml` is the only response-header surface. Today the site runs with no script-src, style-src or default-src — meaning any injected script executes and any exfiltration endpoint is reachable. The absence is a deliberate, documented staging decision (Pyodide needs `wasm-unsafe-eval` and `worker-src blob:`, Next emits inline scripts), so it is not itself the defect; the defect is that the guard is pointed the wrong way and now taxes the fix. I ran the suite: 27 tests pass, including this one.

**Evidence.** `custom-http.test.ts:179-183`: `it("stages no full CSP yet (script-src/style-src would break Pyodide + Next inline scripts)", () => { const csp = byPattern.get("/**")!.headers["Content-Security-Policy"]; expect(csp).not.toContain("script-src"); expect(csp).not.toContain("style-src"); expect(csp).not.toContain("default-src"); });`. `customHttp.yml:42-43` ships `"frame-ancestors 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'"`. `npx jest __tests__/infra/custom-http.test.ts` → 27 passed.

**Split verdict.** reproduces: partly true · correct as written: refuted. Published at the more severe reading.

**Verification — reproduces** (partly true, low, ran locally). The mechanical claim reproduces exactly; the framing around it does not.

REPRODUCED.   `cd web && npx jest --rootDir <scratch>/web --config <scratch>/web/jest.config.ts`
Result: `Tests: 1 failed, 14 passed` — the only failure is `custom-http.test.ts:181` "Expected substring: not \"script-src\"". Notably the positive baseline test at :152-166 still passes (it uses `toContain`), so exactly one assertion, the negative one, blocks the hardening. So yes: adding a real CSP turns CI red until lines 179-183 are edited or deleted.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (read /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/__tests__/infra/custom-http.test.ts and /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/customHttp.yml in full): the three negative assertions are at lines 179-183, and customHttp.yml:43 ships `frame-ancestors 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'`.

### Account deletion leaves the QPU ledger and wallet rows behind, and both the UI list and the privacy page describe the deletion as complete

`web/src/components/auth/delete-account.tsx:87-129` — `faa4641d6` · low · partly true · privacy · observed live · re-raised from `f6abb88d4` · fix plan 05

**Claim.** `handleDelete` performs exactly three server steps: `deleteProgress()` (sync), `deleteReminderPrefs()`, then `deleteUser()`. Nothing anywhere deletes the learner's `WALLET#<sub>` row on `quantum-stripe-wallet` or their rows on `quantum-qpu-ledger` / `quantum-qpu-tasks`. `grep -rn "DeleteItemCommand\|dynamodb:DeleteItem" lambda/qpu/ lambda/stripe/` returns nothing outside `node_modules` — neither handler has the permission, let alone the code path. The UI's list (lines 175-180) names progress, prefs, account and local copy only. The privacy page is worse than silent: `storeHardware` explicitly discloses that a hardware run record (device, shots, cost, circuit hash) is stored, and `retentionDelete` then promises the control "permanently removes your synced progress, your email preference, your account itself, and this device's local copy" — a list that conspicuously omits the record it just disclosed.

**Correction.** Two parts of the framing are wrong.

(1) The impact's "mostly dormant" is understated. The finder ties the surviving rows to hardware runs and the wallet, both of which are off — but `POST /qpu/credential` (`lambda/qpu/qpu-core.mjs:283-307`) writes a permanent `CRED#<sub>` ledger row for ANY signed-in learner who prices the sample run correctly. It requires no cap, no wallet, no hardware run, and it is not gated on `emailVerified` (only `submit` is). That path is live: `aws amplify get-app --app-id d1ao02to23x85y --region us-east-2 --query 'app.environmentVariables'` shows `NEXT_PUBLIC_QPU_URL` set (and no `NEXT_PUBLIC_BILLING_URL`), so the credentials wall renders for every signed-in learner. The residue therefore grows with signups that touch the credentials wall, not with hardware use — it is an accumulating live path, not a frozen 7 rows.

(2) The finder cites the weaker of the two UI claims. Lines 176-179 merely enumerate what is removed and never assert completeness. The flat false statement is `deleteAccount.blurb`, rendered at `delete-account.tsx:154` on the collapsed trigger: "Permanently removes your account and all data." (`web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:428`). That is the sentence the finding should have led with.

Countervailing, and why I keep this at low: what survives is a Cognito `sub` UUID plus device/shots/cost/circuit-hash. Once `deleteUser()` removes the Cognito record, the operator has no way to resolve that sub back to a person, so the surviving rows self-anonymize at deletion time. The durable defect is the copy inaccuracy, not a lasting identifiable-data exposure.

**Correction.** Three parts of the reasoning are wrong. (1) The finder pins the live residue on hardware-run records, but those are unreachable for every learner who exists today: `LIFETIME_CAP_MICROS = 0` (lambda/qpu/qpu-core.mjs:47) plus the load-bearing `effectiveCap > 0` guard means no new learner can submit a run at all — only the one grandfathered row could. The row a signed-in learner CAN create right now and leave behind is `CRED#<sub>`: `POST /qpu/credential` (qpu-core.mjs:283-307, routed at :769) does a bare PutItem with no cap gate and no email-verified gate. A live `aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-qpu-ledger --projection-expression pk` returns exactly `USER#…` and `CRED#…` — so half of the finder's own "2 ledger rows" is the row it never identified. That row is not disclosed anywhere in the privacy page's "what we store" list either, which is a slightly better version of the finder's claim than the one it made. (2) The privacy impact is overstated. `deleteUser()` destroys the Cognito sub→email mapping, and the sync snapshot (which carries the stored email claim) and the prefs row are both deleted first, so a surviving USER#/CRED#/task row is keyed only by an orphaned opaque sub and carries no identifier — effectively de-identified. The one row that would NOT be is `WALLET#<sub>`, which carries `stripeCustomerId` (lambda/stripe/index.mjs:1010) and is re-identifiable through Stripe — and that is precisely the table holding 0 items with the storefront closed. (3) "neither handler has the permission, let alone the code path" understates the stripe side: `lambda/stripe/template.test.mjs:108` affirmatively asserts the grant must be absent — `assert.doesNotMatch(b, /dynamodb:DeleteItem/, "the handler never deletes; do not grant it")` — a deliberate least-privilege decision. ### The privacy page says no analytics exist anywhere on the site while a deployed daily job classifies visitor IP addresses and retains the derived counts forever

`web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:934-935` — `f88e19069` · low · partly true · privacy · observed live · fix plan 05

**Claim.** Under the heading "What we don't collect", the privacy page renders `noAnalytics`: "No analytics or tracking scripts — none exist anywhere on this site." Its only statement about logs is `retentionLogs`: "Operational service logs (used for debugging and abuse prevention) are retained in AWS CloudWatch for 30 days and then deleted automatically." Since 2026-08-20 the `quantum-analytics` Lambda has run daily against Amplify's CloudFront access logs, grouping every request by `c-ip`, running each address through `classifyVisitor` (hostile-path, declared-bot, AWS datacenter-range, asset-loading, page-rate and per-day-volume signals), and extracting Google sign-ins from `/auth/callback` referers. The purpose is measurement, which is neither debugging nor abuse prevention, and it is not disclosed. The derived rows are deliberately permanent — `template.yaml:64-68` states "DELIBERATELY NO TimeToLiveSpecification … meant to be permanent" — against a page that tells the reader logs die in 30 days. The Spanish copy carries the identical claim at `es.ts:863`.

**Correction.** The retention half of the claim is wrong. The permanent rows contain no IP address, user agent, path, or any other identifier — only aggregate counts. A live scan of `quantum-analytics-daily` returns exactly `day, requests, uniqueIps, humans, humanPageViews, googleSignIns, malformed, buckets{8 counts}, botFilterComplete, computedAt`, matching the allowlist pinned in `lambda/analytics/index.test.mjs:81-87` (widening it fails the build). IPs are grouped and classified in memory and discarded; the raw access logs are fetched through a presigned `GenerateAccessLogs` URL, parsed, and never stored by this system. So the title's "classifies visitor IP addresses and retains the derived counts forever" is only half true — nothing IP-derived at row level survives, and the page's 30-day CloudWatch sentence is not contradicted, because what persists forever is an aggregate count row, not a log. What remains is a pure copy-accuracy defect on one bullet, not a data-handling defect, which is why I rate it low rather than medium.

**Correction.** Three parts of the finding are wrong or inflated. (1) The retention contradiction does not exist. `retentionLogs` is a claim about CloudWatch service logs, and `aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda/quantum-analytics --region us-east-2` returns `retentionInDays: 30` — exactly what the page says. The permanent rows live in DynamoDB and are not logs, so "a page that tells the reader logs die in 30 days" is not falsified by them. (2) "classifies visitor IP addresses and retains the derived counts forever" reads as retention of per-visitor derived data, and that is not what happens: `aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-analytics-daily --region us-east-2 --max-items 3` returns rows of exactly `{day, requests, uniqueIps, humans, humanPageViews, googleSignIns, malformed, buckets{8 counts}, botFilterComplete, computedAt}` — no address, no user agent, no path, no per-visitor row. IP classification is transient, in-memory, over logs that already existed. `lambda/analytics/index.test.mjs:69-88` ("STORES NO IDENTIFIERS") pins that with a 10-key attribute allowlist, so widening it fails the build. (3) "Nothing ties the page to reality" overstates: the decision is deliberately reasoned in three places (`index.mjs` header, `template.yaml` Description, `README.md:11-18`) and guarded by that test. What is genuinely missing is a guard on the PAGE COPY — `grep -rl noAnalytics web/__tests__ web/src` hits only the two locale files and the component, no test — which is the sharper version of the finding. Category and severity are also inflated: this is not an identity/auth/infrastructure security defect and not medium; no personal data is retained, nothing is added to the browser, nothing is shared, and there is no data subject to remediate.

**Impact.** A live, legal-facing page in both locales makes a representation about data processing that the deployed system contradicts. The Lambda's own header argues the claim survives because "nothing is added to the browser" — true of the word "scripts", but the bullet sits under "What we don't collect" and a reader takes it as a statement about collection, not about script tags. The stack is literally named `quantum-analytics`. Nothing ties the page to reality: `LAST_UPDATED` is a hand-maintained constant still reading "2026-07-12", while the page's own `storeTutor` bullet was rewritten on 2026-08-17 (commit dd7abb7) to name Anthropic instead of Bedrock — so the page has already silently drifted once under a stale date stamp. This is exactly the copy-honesty failure mode rule 13 exists for, on the one page where it carries legal weight.

Live: `aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name quantum-analytics` → `LastModified 2026-08-20T17:17:57`, and `quantum-analytics-daily` holds 8 items.

**Severity drift.** Finder claimed medium; verification published low.

WHAT STANDS

A daily server-side pipeline whose stack is literally named `quantum-analytics`, whose stated purpose in its own README is answering "how many users do we have?", runs against real traffic while a live legal page states under the heading "What we don't collect" that no analytics exist anywhere on the site. The Lambda's defence ("nothing is added to the browser: no script, no cookie, no beacon") defends the words "tracking scripts" and does not defend the word "analytics" sitting under a collection heading. Measurement is also not one of the two purposes the page names for logs ("debugging and abuse prevention"), and Amplify/CloudFront access logs are never mentioned on the page at all — its only log sentence is about CloudWatch.

The actual data practice is the least invasive form of server-log analytics: no browser artifact, no third party, no per-visitor record, immediate aggregation, and a build-enforced attribute allowlist. Nothing a reader could be harmed by is happening — one bullet's wording is now overbroad. The fix is a sentence, and the strongest part of the finding's impact framing (permanent retention of IP-derived visitor data contradicting a 30-day promise) does not survive the live scan.

The finder is right that a reader under "What we don't collect" takes "No analytics" as a statement about measurement, not about script tags, and the stack is named `quantum-analytics`. Worth one added clause: aggregate daily counts, derived from existing access logs, no identifiers stored.

2. LAST_UPDATED is stale and unguarded — this part of the finding verified exactly. `git log -G'Bedrock' -- web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts` shows dd7abb7 rewrote `storeTutor` from "AWS Bedrock" to "AWS ... forwards them to Anthropic" and also rewrote `storeHardware`; `git log -L5,6:web/src/components/privacy/privacy-page-content.tsx` shows `LAST_UPDATED = "2026-07-12"` introduced in f146702 and never touched since. So the policy has already changed substantively twice under a frozen date stamp.

Why low, not medium: the actual practice is more privacy-preserving than the copy's imprecision suggests — no cookie, no beacon, no client-side script, no third party, and verifiably zero identifiers retained. The exposure is a legal-facing page carrying one overbroad sentence and a stale date, in both locales. Real, cheap to fix, no operational remediation.

Files: /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:934, /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/src/i18n/locales/es.ts:863, /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/src/components/privacy/privacy-page-content.tsx:5, /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/lambda/analytics/index.mjs, /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/lambda/analytics/index.test.mjs:69

> Correction. Three parts of the finding are wrong or inflated. (1) The retention contradiction does not exist. `retentionLogs` is a claim about CloudWatch service logs, and `aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda/quantum-analytics --region us-east-2` returns `retentionInDays: 30` — exactly what the page says. The permanent rows live in DynamoDB and are not logs, so "a page that tells the reader logs die in 30 days" is not falsified by them. (2) "classifies visitor IP addresses and retains the derived counts forever" reads as retention of per-visitor derived data, and that is not what happens: `aws dynamodb scan --table-name quantum-analytics-daily --region us-east-2 --max-items 3` returns rows of exactly `{day, requests, uniqueIps, humans, humanPageViews, googleSignIns, malformed, buckets{8 counts}, botFilterComplete, computedAt}` — no address, no user agent, no path, no per-visitor row. IP classification is transient, in-memory, over logs that already existed. `lambda/analytics/index.test.mjs:69-88` ("STORES NO IDENTIFIERS") pins that with a 10-key attribute allowlist, so widening it fails the build. (3) "Nothing ties the page to reality" overstates: the decision is deliberately reasoned in three places (`index.mjs` header, `template.yaml` Description, `README.md:11-18`) and guarded by that test. What is genuinely missing is a guard on the PAGE COPY — `grep -rl noAnalytics web/__tests__ web/src` hits only the two locale files and the component, no test — which is the sharper version of the finding. Category and severity are also inflated: this is not an identity/auth/infrastructure security defect and not medium; no personal data is retained, nothing is added to the browser, nothing is shared, and there is no data subject to remediate.

### The Cognito pool never requires verification before an email change, so `lambda/sync` persists an attacker-chosen unverified address as the learner's identity

`lambda/sync/index.mjs:48-52` — `f113d42b6` · low · partly true · security · observed live · re-raised from `f150cdd31` · fix plan 04

**Claim.** `infra/workspace/cognito.yaml` declares `email` as `Mutable: true` (line 217) and sets no `UserAttributeUpdateSettings` block anywhere. AWS documents the default explicitly: "When `AttributesRequireVerificationBeforeUpdate` is false, your user pool doesn't require that your users verify attribute changes before Amazon Cognito updates them. In a user pool where `AttributesRequireVerificationBeforeUpdate` is false, API operations that change attribute values can immediately update a user's `email` or `phone_number` attribute." A native (SRP) session carries `aws.cognito.signin.user.admin`, so it can call `UpdateUserAttributes` and have the next ID token carry the new, unverified address. `lambda/sync/index.mjs:52` takes that claim on a bare `typeof claims.email === "string"` test — no `email_verified` check — and writes it into the progress table at line 98. Only `lambda/qpu/qpu-core.mjs:763` checks `email_verified` anywhere in the codebase.

**Correction.** The Founding Ten half of the impact is wrong. Badges and the credit gift key on the Cognito `email` attribute, not on the row `lambda/sync` writes: `scripts/verify-founding-ten.mjs:85-99` hashes addresses from `cognito-idp list-users`, and `web/src/components/auth/amplify-auth-bridge.tsx:57-85` hashes the ID-token claim. The progress table's `email` is never read by that path, so this defect does not touch badges or the gift; and because email is a `UsernameAttributes` alias, pointing your account at another enabled holder's verified address is refused by Cognito alias uniqueness, so the badge/gift takeover the sentence implies is not reachable this way at all. Second, the mail half is dormant behind two switches, not one — the finder cited only the SES sandbox and missed that the sender's daily EventBridge rule is DISABLED, so the sender never fires even if SES were approved.

**Correction.** Two parts of the impact narrative are wrong. (1) "Two things key on it" — the Founding Ten half does not. Nothing in the badge or credit-gift path reads the progress table's `email`: `web/src/components/auth/amplify-auth-bridge.tsx:85` hashes the LIVE ID-token claim in the browser and `my-badges.tsx:12` renders from that, and `scripts/founding-credit/issue.mjs` is a hand-run operator script over the git-committed `cohort-2026-08.json` roster. The hijack that paragraph gestures at is also impossible: the pool uses `UsernameAttributes: [email]` (verified live), so an address already registered cannot be re-assigned — `UpdateUserAttributes` throws `AliasExistsException`, and AWS's alias-vs-username table states outright that username attributes cannot assign the same email to more than one user — while `scripts/verify-founding-ten.mjs` fails the build unless every issued badge matches an *enabled Cognito user*, i.e. every badge address is already taken. (2) "an unsubscribe token that is a valid HMAC over the victim's own `sub`" — the sub is the ATTACKER's; the mailed stranger has no account and no sub in this system. Separately, the dormancy is stronger than the finder showed: besides SES sandbox, the daily schedule itself is off — `aws events list-rules --region us-east-2` returns `quantum-review-email-SenderFunctionDaily-hNpzhoP0FzmY` in state `DISABLED`. Severity is low, not medium: the only live effect is an unverified string on the actor's own row, with no consumer today.

**Impact.** An authenticated learner can point their stored identity at an address they do not control. Two things key on it. `lambda/review-email/review-email-core.mjs:257,275` reads `it.email.S` straight from that table and passes it to SES as `ToAddresses` — turning the platform into a relay that mails a stranger from an SES-verified domain, with an unsubscribe token that is a valid HMAC over the victim's own `sub`. And the Founding Ten registry binds badges and the one approved credit gift to the SHA-256 of the email (`scripts/lib/email-hash.mjs:19`), so email is the project's durable identity, not the sub. The mail half is DORMANT — I verified `aws sesv2 get-account` returns `ProductionAccessEnabled: false`, and `review-email-core.mjs:214-219` hard-refuses the whole run in that state. The persistence half is live: `quantum-workspace-sync` is deployed and writing today. The fix is one template block (`UserAttributeUpdateSettings: {AttributesRequireVerificationBeforeUpdate: [email]}`) plus an `email_verified` guard at index.mjs:52.

**Evidence.** `lambda/sync/index.mjs:52` `const email = typeof claims.email === "string" ? claims.email : undefined;` and line 98 `...(email ? { email: { S: email } } : {})`. `infra/workspace/cognito.yaml:213-217` Schema declares `Mutable: true` for email; `grep -rn "UserAttributeUpdateSettings\|AttributesRequireVerificationBeforeUpdate" infra/ web/` returns nothing. AWS `API_UserAttributeUpdateSettingsType` documents the false/default behavior verbatim as quoted. Live: `aws sesv2 get-account --region us-east-2` → `{"prod": false, "enforce": "HEALTHY"}`.

**Severity drift.** Finder claimed medium; verification published low.

**Verification — reproduces** (partly true, low, observed live). The mechanism reproduces; the impact reasoning is partly wrong.

WHAT HOLDS (live + executed):
1. Pool config. `aws cognito-idp describe-user-pool --user-pool-id $USER_POOL_ID --region us-east-2` (pool id from `aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name quantum-workspace-auth`) returns `UserAttributeUpdateSettings: {"AttributesRequireVerificationBeforeUpdate": []}`, email `Mutable: true`, `UsernameAttributes: [email]`. `aws cognito-idp describe-user-pool-client --client-id 2sg8nejrf2j8p28j6khjil99ir` returns `ExplicitAuthFlows: [ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH, ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH]` and `WriteAttributes: null` (default — email writable). The AWS quote in the finding is verbatim (SDK reference for `AttributesRequireVerificationBeforeUpdate`), so an SRP session's `UpdateUserAttributes` changes the address immediately.
2. It is an ID token, so both claims are present. `lambda/sync/template.yaml:86-93` sets `audience: !Ref UserPoolClientId`, and `web/src/lib/sync-client.ts:126` sends `tokens?.idToken?.toString()` — `email_verified` is sitting unused right beside `email`.
3. The persistence half is live and unguarded. I pulled the deployed artifact — `aws lambda get-function --function-name quantum-workspace-sync --region us-east-2 --query Code.Location`, curl + unzip — and `diff` against `/Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/lambda/sync/index.mjs` reports IDENTICAL. Local repro through the real exported core (`node` script calling `createHandlerCore({ddb: stub})` with claims `{sub:"attacker-sub", email:"victim@example.com", email_verified:"false"}`) returns 200 and writes `Item.email = {"S":"victim@example.com"}` under the attacker's `userId`. The comment at `lambda/sync/index.mjs:48` calling it "The verified email claim" is simply false. `lambda/qpu/qpu-core.mjs:763` is indeed the only `email_verified` consumer, and no GitHub issue covers this (`gh issue list --state all --limit 200 --json number,title`, 22 issues).

WHAT DOES NOT HOLD: see correction. Also note this is a third recurrence — docs/codebase-audit-2026-08-16.md #8 and docs/codebase-audit-2026-08-18.md #8 both raised it and both landed "Partly true"; nothing has changed since.

SEVERITY: low, not medium. Every consumer is gated. The mail sender is off twice over: `aws sesv2 get-account --region us-east-2` → `ProductionAccessEnabled: false`, `ReviewDetails.Status: DENIED` (and `review-email-core.mjs:212-219` hard-returns `skippedSandbox`), and `aws events list-rules --region us-east-2` shows `quantum-review-email-SenderFunctionDaily-hNpzhoP0FzmY` in state `DISABLED` — a second switch the finder did not check, so the sender does not even run. The money path (QPU) already checks `email_verified`. What is real today is one unverified third-party address stored on a progress row in a 14-user pool (`EstimatedNumberOfUsers: 14`), plus a lying comment, in a trap that arms the day SES production access is granted. The proposed fix (template block + `email_verified` guard at index.mjs:52) is correct and cheap.

### `failover.sh engage` arms a CodeBuild webhook with no contributor filter on a public repo, handing any fork PR the standby's AWS role

`infra/ci-standby/failover.sh:83-89` — `fa92808af` · low · partly true · security · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · re-raised from `f66ea059e` · fix plan 04

**Claim.** `engage()` calls `aws codebuild create-webhook` with filter groups on `PULL_REQUEST_CREATED, PULL_REQUEST_UPDATED, PULL_REQUEST_REOPENED` and `PUSH` to main, and no `ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID` filter group. On a public repository that means every fork PR, from anyone, triggers a build. The buildspec is inline in `infra/ci-standby/template.yaml:156-240` and runs the PR's own `npm ci`, `npm test`, `pip install -e .` and `make test` — all of which execute code from the pull request. That code inherits `quantum-ci-standby-codebuild` via the container credentials endpoint.

**Correction.** The mechanism and impact are wrong. "Every fork PR, from anyone, triggers a build" and "handing any fork PR the standby's AWS role" do not hold: CodeBuild's `CreateWebhook` applies a `pullRequestBuildPolicy` default of `requiresCommentApproval: ALL_PULL_REQUESTS` with `approverRoles: [GITHUB_ADMIN, GITHUB_MAINTAIN, GITHUB_WRITE]` when the field is omitted, so an untrusted fork PR is marked "Failed — Pull request approval required for starting a build" and executes nothing until a repo admin/maintainer/writer posts `/codebuild_run(<sha>)`. What survives is much smaller and defence-in-depth only: `engage()` omits the `ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID` filter AWS names as a best practice for public-repo webhooks, so the safety of the whole procedure rests on an unstated AWS service default that nothing in the repo records or pins. The "self-approves" framing is also overstated — `app_id: -1` lets any source post that context, but a fork author has no `statuses: write` on the base repo and cannot merge; a maintainer still has to click merge. Finally, `infra/ci-standby/template.yaml:148-155` deliberately uses an inline buildspec, which is one of the four controls AWS's own best-practices page lists for exactly this scenario — the finding credits none of them.

**Impact.** While engaged, an unreviewed fork PR gets: `cognito-idp:ListUsers` on the live `quantum-workspace` pool (template.yaml:103-106) — the full learner roster with email addresses; `codeconnections:GetConnectionToken` and `UseConnection` on the GitHub App connection (lines 87-95); and read/write on the CI cache bucket (lines 71-75), which the next legitimate build restores from. It also self-approves: `engage()` re-points main's required checks at the single `CI (CodeBuild standby)` context with `app_id: -1` (lines 91-96), so the merge gate is satisfied by whatever that build reports. Dormant today — I verified read-only that `aws codebuild batch-get-projects --names quantum-ci-standby` returns `webhook: null`, i.e. disengaged and idle — but this is the one procedure that runs during an outage, under time pressure, and it arms it in a single command.

**Evidence.** `failover.sh:86-89` filter groups: `[[{"type": "EVENT", "pattern": "PULL_REQUEST_CREATED, PULL_REQUEST_UPDATED, PULL_REQUEST_REOPENED"}], [{"type": "EVENT", "pattern": "PUSH"}, {"type": "HEAD_REF", "pattern": "^refs/heads/main$"}]]` — no `ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID` group. `template.yaml:96-106` `PolicyName: founding-ten-verify` grants `cognito-idp:ListUsers` on `userpool/$USER_POOL_ID`. `template.yaml:87-95` grants `codeconnections:GetConnectionToken` / `UseConnection`. Live state: `webhook: null`.

**Split verdict.** reproduces: partly true · correct as written: refuted. Published at the more severe reading.

**Severity drift.** Finder claimed medium; verification published low.

**Verification — reproduces** (partly true, low, observed live). Source facts check out. `infra/ci-standby/failover.sh:83-89` does call `create-webhook` with only EVENT/HEAD_REF filter groups; `grep -rn "ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID" . --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git` returns hits only inside `docs/codebase-audit-2026-08-18.json` (a prior audit), nothing in `infra/`. `template.yaml:96-106` grants `cognito-idp:ListUsers`, `:87-95` the codeconnections token perms, `:71-75` the cache bucket, and lines 91-96 of failover.sh do set `app_id: -1`.

Live, read-only: `gh repo view AltivumInc-Admin/quantum-computing --json visibility` = PUBLIC (forkCount 0). `aws codebuild batch-get-projects --names quantum-ci-standby --region us-east-2` returns `webhook: null`, `created 2026-07-16`, source GITHUB/CODECONNECTIONS. `aws iam get-role-policy --role-name quantum-ci-standby-codebuild --policy-name founding-ten-verify` confirms the ListUsers grant is deployed, and `aws cognito-idp describe-user-pool --user-pool-id $USER_POOL_ID --region us-east-2` returns Name `quantum-workspace`, 14 users — so the blast radius the finder names is real permissions, not hypothetical. `gh api repos/.../branches/main/protection` shows `required_pull_request_reviews: NONE`, `enforce_admins: true`, 8 Actions contexts pinned to app 15368 (i.e. currently stood down).

What breaks the exploit chain: `aws codebuild create-webhook help` (CLI 2.35.4) exposes `--pull-request-build-policy`, and the live doc page https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/pull-request-build-policy.html (fetched via the AWS docs MCP) states verbatim "Pull request build policy is enabled by default for all newly created CodeBuild projects", `ALL_PULL_REQUESTS` is "the default value" for `requiresCommentApproval`, and the GitHub `approverRoles` default is `["GITHUB_ADMIN","GITHUB_MAINTAIN","GITHUB_WRITE"]`. Untrusted contributors get build status "Failed / Pull request approval required for starting a build" until a trusted contributor comments `/codebuild_run(<sha>)`. `engage()` never passes `DISABLED`, so the default stands.

Limit of what I could prove: confirming the default materializes on THIS project would require calling `create-webhook`, a mutation, which is out of scope — and no other CodeBuild project in the account (`altivum-hq-ci-standby`, `bedrock-agentcore-vetroi_resume_agent-builder`, `ai-noc-build`) carries a live webhook to read the materialized policy from. So this rests on AWS's current documentation, not on an observed webhook object. That residual uncertainty, plus the genuine gap (AWS's https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/webhooks.html "Best practices" page names `ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID` filters and "scope down the permissions for your build IAM role" — the standby implements neither), is why this is PARTLY_TRUE and not REFUTED. Worth fixing as one line in `engage()`, but as belt-and-braces: add `ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID` as a filter *inside* the PR group (filters within a group are AND-ed; a separate group would be OR-ed and change nothing), and/or pass `--pull-request-build-policy requiresCommentApproval=FORK_PULL_REQUESTS` explicitly so the protection is pinned in the repo rather than inherited silently.

> Correction. The mechanism and impact are wrong. "Every fork PR, from anyone, triggers a build" and "handing any fork PR the standby's AWS role" do not hold: CodeBuild's `CreateWebhook` applies a `pullRequestBuildPolicy` default of `requiresCommentApproval: ALL_PULL_REQUESTS` with `approverRoles: [GITHUB_ADMIN, GITHUB_MAINTAIN, GITHUB_WRITE]` when the field is omitted, so an untrusted fork PR is marked "Failed — Pull request approval required for starting a build" and executes nothing until a repo admin/maintainer/writer posts `/codebuild_run(<sha>)`. What survives is much smaller and defence-in-depth only: `engage()` omits the `ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID` filter AWS names as a best practice for public-repo webhooks, so the safety of the whole procedure rests on an unstated AWS service default that nothing in the repo records or pins. The "self-approves" framing is also overstated — `app_id: -1` lets any source post that context, but a fork author has no `statuses: write` on the base repo and cannot merge; a maintainer still has to click merge. **Verification — correct as written** (refuted, low, observed live). The exploit chain does not work. `engage()` (infra/ci-standby/failover.sh:83-89) calls `create-webhook` without `--pull-request-build-policy`, and AWS's default for that field is NOT permissive. AWS's "Pull request comment approval" page (docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/pull-request-build-policy.html, read via aws___read_documentation) states three things verbatim: "Pull request build policy is enabled by default for all newly created CodeBuild projects"; for `requiresCommentApproval`, "ALL_PULL_REQUESTS - All pull requests require comment approval before builds execute ... This is the default value"; and `approverRoles` "Default: ["GITHUB_ADMIN", "GITHUB_MAINTAIN", "GITHUB_WRITE"]". So an untrusted fork PR gets build status "Failed" with "Pull request approval required for starting a build", and a repo Admin/Maintain/Write user must post `/codebuild_run(<SHA>)` before one line of PR code runs. The finding's stated impact — "an unreviewed fork PR gets cognito-idp:ListUsers ... GetConnectionToken ... cache read/write" — is therefore false as written.

Timing verified, because the default only applies to projects created after the feature landed. `aws codebuild batch-get-projects --names quantum-ci-standby --region us-east-2` (read-only) returns created `2026-07-16T06:40:48.255000-05:00`, lastModified 2026-07-29, `webhook: null`, role `arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:role/quantum-ci-standby-codebuild`. `grep -n -B12 pullRequestBuildPolicy /opt/homebrew/Cellar/awscli/2.35.4/CHANGELOG.rst` puts the API addition at AWS CLI **2.28.8** ("AWS CodeBuild now supports PullRequestBuildPolicy in webhook object") — 205 releases before the installed 2.35.4 (counted with grep over the version headers; the file holds 918 releases back to 2.0.0/Feb-2020, ~2.7 releases/week), i.e. roughly a year before this project was created. AWS's security blog on CodeBuild webhooks (31 Jul 2025, bulletin AWS-2025-016) predates it and does not mention the feature, consistent with an Aug-2025 launch.

The "it also self-approves" half is separately wrong. `app_id: -1` (failover.sh:94-96) only unpins the required context from a GitHub App, and the code comment on lines 92-93 gives the reason ("CodeBuild reports a commit *status*, not an Actions check run, so the context must not be app-pinned"). Posting a commit status on the base repo requires write access; merging requires write access. A fork PR author has neither, so nothing about `-1` is reachable from the claimed threat.

What is accurate and survives, at low severity: there is genuinely no ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID filter (`grep -rn ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID` over the repo hits only the prior audit docs), and the deployed role is broader than AWS's "scope down the permissions for your build IAM role" guidance — `aws iam get-role-policy --role-name quantum-ci-standby-codebuild --policy-name founding-ten-verify` returns live `cognito-idp:ListUsers` on `arn:aws:$SERVICE:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:userpool/$USER_POOL_ID`, and `aws iam list-role-policies` confirms `github-connection` (GetConnectionToken/UseConnection) alongside it. That surface is reachable by an already-trusted contributor or a malicious transitive npm/pip dependency once engaged — not by an anonymous fork PR. Worth a hardening note that the safety rests entirely on an unstated service default nothing in infra/ci-standby/ records or asserts, plus the mechanical detail the finder got backwards: an ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID filter must be added *inside* each existing filter group (filters within a group are AND-ed); a separate group would be OR-ed and change nothing.

## The web portal

Surviving: 0 high, 4 medium, 9 low.

### How it actually works

`web/` is a Next.js 16 App Router app built with `output: "export"` — 19 routes, ~126 components, no server at runtime. `src/app/layout.tsx` wires the whole tree: `next/font/google` loads Sora/Geist/Geist Mono as `--font-sora`/`--font-geist`/`--font-geist-mono`, then `ThemeProvider` (next-themes, class strategy) → `LocaleProvider` → `AuthProvider` → `AuthWall` → `Nav`/`FogField`/`AskTutor`/`Footer`. A blocking inline script pre-paints `<html lang>` so a returning Spanish reader is not announced as English before hydration.

Theming is two token blocks in `src/app/globals.css`: `:root` (daylight — warm silver `--surface-base: #e9e9e7`, gold `--accent: #a38560`) and `.dark` (after-dark — abyss `#071710`, lifted gold `#c2a379`). Everything downstream reads `var(--ink)`, `var(--mut)`, `var(--surface-1)`, `--bd`, `--focus`. `layout.tsx:62-67` emits `viewport.themeColor` as two literal hexes, and `__tests__/app/theme-color.test.ts` re-derives both from the CSS so they cannot drift. Section colour is a hue *angle* (`sections.ts:29 sectionHue = [192,290,75,160,15,230]`) fed to `.hue-text`/`.hue-soft-bg`/`.hue-border` utilities.

Auth is a client-side wall, not a boundary: `auth-wall.tsx` holds a `PUBLIC_PATHS` set (`/`, `/pricing`, `/login`, `/auth/callback`, `/privacy`, `/changelog`) plus `/e2e-fixtures` and `/founding-ten` prefixes; everything else redirects unauthenticated visitors to `/login?mode=signup&next=…`. Its own doc admits the full RSC payload for walled routes is recoverable from the static export.

Learner state is localStorage, namespaced per owner. `progress-owner.ts:124 ownedLocalKeys()` scans `localStorage` and filters to the signed-in account's bucket; `review-store.ts` layers card state, `dueCardIds()`/`dueCount()` on top; `activity-log`, `progress-store`, `skill-measure` sit beside it. Three `useSyncExternalStore` consumers hang off one `"qc-progress"` event: `review-nav-badge.tsx:16`, `review-dashboard.tsx:110 snapshot()`, and `hooks/use-workspace.ts:24 snapshot()` — each `getSnapshot` re-scans storage and JSON-parses every card.

The new changelog (#238) is `lib/changelog.ts` (`CHANGELOG` + a `SILENT` ledger of deliberately unannounced PRs) with `changelog-es.ts` as an id-keyed twin, rendered by `changelog/changelog-page-content.tsx` into month groups via `groupByMonth`/`monthLabel` (Intl at UTC). Its CI half is `scripts/changelog/rules.mjs` — a literal `LEARNER_VISIBLE` path list and a pure `verdict()` — driven from `ci.yml:150` by `git diff --name-only HEAD^1 HEAD` on a `fetch-depth: 2` checkout.

The after-dark pass (#243/#244) rebuilt `welcome/hero.tsx` as a 1440×780 SVG dial: `dialPt` rounds to hundredths to avoid Node/browser ULP hydration mismatches, minor ticks on a 1.5° grid with majors at each station's exact angle, and station `<g role="button" tabIndex={0}>` controls rendered *after* the `<h1>` in DOM order. The dial, needle and readout are `md:` only. `logo.tsx` is the `|Q⟩` mark, size-adaptive stroke weights.

The 220-suite Jest corpus (2,602 tests, green at HEAD, `testEnvironment: "node"` with per-file jsdom docblocks) is mostly behavioural: `token-contrast.test.ts` computes real oklch→OKLab→sRGB WCAG ratios out of `globals.css`; `contrast-guard`/`caption-contrast` sweep every source file; `changelog.test.ts` asserts en/es parity in both directions. Its 118 `jest.mock` calls are almost entirely boundary stubs (`next/link`, `next/navigation`, `aws-amplify/auth`), not the units under test.

### What is genuinely good here

- web/__tests__/token-contrast.test.ts:58-373 — a genuinely computed WCAG guard, not a class-string grep: it strips comments from globals.css, parses the :root and .dark token blocks, resolves var() indirection, converts oklch→OKLab→linear sRGB with Ottosson's matrices, and asserts real ratios for every pairing the token comments promise, in both themes, across every entry in sectionHue.
- web/__tests__/app/theme-color.test.ts:39-44 — binds the one palette literal that ships straight to browser chrome (layout.tsx:62-67 viewport.themeColor) back to --surface-base by re-reading BOTH files from disk. Byte-for-byte equality, so a palette retune that misses the hexes reddens.
- web/__tests__/lib/changelog.test.ts:86-110 — bidirectional en/es parity for changelog entries, explicitly written because the repo's other i18n guard (i18n.test.ts:119-122) computes en ⊆ es only and would let an orphaned Spanish key for a renamed id sit forever with CI green. It also rejects an untranslated paste (es.body !== en.body).
- scripts/changelog/check.mjs:23-32 — the guard's own doc states what a green check does NOT prove ("It proves the author CONSIDERED announcing the change. That is all… do not mistake this check for editorial review"), and check.mjs:41-48 refuses to report a pass on an empty stdin rather than silently succeeding on a shallow clone.
- web/src/lib/qpu-handoff.ts:33-53 — readValid() validates every field of the sessionStorage payload (schema version, non-empty QASM, a UTF-8 byte cap via utf8ByteLength, a finite numeric ts) before the submit panel trusts it, and consumeHandoff clears even a corrupt value so garbage cannot linger across visits.
- web/src/lib/review-store.ts:143-157 — getAllCardIds() iterates ownedLocalKeys() rather than all of localStorage, with the comment naming the exact defect it fixes ("scanning all of localStorage is what showed one learner's due cards to the next account on a shared browser").
- web/src/components/welcome/hero.tsx:45-53 — dialPt() rounds coordinates to hundredths specifically because Math.sin/cos are not required to be correctly rounded and Node's server render really does differ from the browser by an ulp, which React flagged as a hydration mismatch on every tick.
- web/src/app/globals.css:916-925 — the prefers-reduced-motion: reduce block sets animation-iteration-count: 1 !important alongside the usual 0.01ms duration, so an infinite animation that missed a per-element motion-reduce override freezes on its end state instead of sampling a random frame forever. It also covers the hero's inline `animation:` and `transition:` styles, which a class-scoped override could not reach.
- web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts + es.ts — verified by running flattenKeys in both directions: zero English keys missing from Spanish, zero orphaned Spanish keys, and only 17 byte-identical leaves, all of which are proper nouns or loanwords ("Playground", "Hardware", "Runbook", "OpenQASM 3.0", "GitHub"). Dictionary parity is genuinely complete.

### Status live regions are still mounted at the same moment their content appears, so the announcement may never fire

`web/src/components/quantum/review-card.tsx:211-213` — `f8a103fbc` · medium · confirmed · accessibility · ran locally · re-raised from `f0f7d9816` · fix plan 12

**Claim.** Unchanged at HEAD — review-card.tsx was not touched by any of the nine commits since 4aec7f8. The `role="status"` paragraph at :212-213 is created by `{outcome && (…)}`, so the live region enters the accessibility tree already populated; a polite region must be present and empty before its content changes for the mutation to be announced reliably. The same shape persists at quiz.tsx:294 (`{outcome && …}`), review-dashboard.tsx:189 (`{sessionComplete && …}`) and qpu-submit-panel.tsx:869 and :888 (`{state === "wrong" && …}`, `{state === "throttled" && …}`). The codebase knows the correct pattern and applies it elsewhere: challenge.tsx:256-258 and debug-circuit-widget.tsx:216-219 carry comments saying "mounting a fresh region per verdict is not reliably announced" and keep an always-mounted `<div role="status">`, live-status.tsx:7 says "the node stays mounted so aria-live fires on text change", and playground/saved-panel.tsx:124-132 keeps a `min-h-4` region mounted with an empty string.

**Impact.** The one piece of feedback a self-graded review card gives — whether the grade advanced the schedule and when the card is next due — can be silent for a screen-reader user, on the surface whose whole purpose is that feedback. Same for the quiz outcome and the /review session-complete banner.

**Evidence.** review-card.tsx:211 `{outcome && (` / :213 `role="status"`. `git diff 4aec7f8..HEAD -- web/src/components/quantum/review-card.tsx` is empty; the diff for review-dashboard.tsx (10 lines) and review-nav-badge.tsx (2 lines) is class-name-only from the #243 token pass. Counter-examples: playground/saved-panel.tsx:124-132, live-status.tsx:16, debug-circuit-widget.tsx:219.

**Verification — reproduces** (confirmed, medium, ran locally). Reproduced in a real render, not just read.

I wrote a throwaway jsdom probe (created, run, then deleted — `git status --porcelain` afterwards shows only the pre-existing untracked entries, no repo change) at web/__tests__/zz_probe_live_region.test.tsx and ran `cd /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web && npx jest __tests__/zz_probe_live_region.test.tsx`. It counted `[role="status"],[aria-live]` nodes in the ReviewCard subtree at three moments:

  BEFORE reveal — live regions: 0
  AFTER reveal, BEFORE grade — live regions: 0
  AFTER grade — live regions: 1 | text: "Next review tomorrow."

So the polite region and its text enter the accessibility tree in the same React commit. There is no earlier, empty region for a screen reader to have been observing — which is exactly the shape the finding describes, and exactly the shape this codebase elsewhere documents as unreliable.

Every cited location checks out, at absolute paths:
- /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/src/components/quantum/review-card.tsx:211-213 — `{outcome && (<p role="status" …>)}`.
- .../quantum/quiz.tsx:294 — identical `{outcome && (<p role="status" …>)}`.
- .../review-dashboard.tsx:189-191 — note the path is web/src/components/review-dashboard.tsx, NOT under quantum/; `{sessionComplete && (<div role="status" …>)}`.
- .../quantum/qpu-submit-panel.tsx:869 and :888 — `{state === "wrong" && (<p role="status" …>)}` and `{state === "throttled" && …}`.

Counter-examples confirmed too: challenge.tsx:255-258 and debug-circuit-widget.tsx:215-219 both carry the comment "mounting a fresh region per verdict is not reliably announced" over an always-mounted `<div role="status">`; live-status.tsx:6-7 says "the node stays mounted so aria-live fires on text change"; playground/saved-panel.tsx:124-132 keeps a `min-h-4` region mounted rendering `{status}` (empty string when idle). So the project has an explicit, written internal standard that these five sites do not follow.

Git claims verified: `git diff 4aec7f8..HEAD -- web/src/components/quantum/review-card.tsx | wc -l` returns 0. The only change to quiz.tsx in that range is `font-bold` → `font-medium` on the index chip (#243 token pass), which does not touch the region.

Nothing upstream rescues it: `grep -rn 'aria-live' web/src/app` returns no matches, so there is no page-level polite region these announcements could bubble into.

The impact statement is if anything understated for review-card. Reading web/src/components/quantum/review-card.tsx:135-146, `onGrade` also calls `setRevealed(false)`, which unmounts the rating buttons — including the one the user just activated, dropping focus to `<body>` — and `streak` is suppressed while `outcome.kind === "graded"` (line 146), so the header chip does not change either. The freshly-mounted status paragraph genuinely is the only feedback the interaction produces.

Two calibration notes rather than corrections. First, this is a reliability defect, not guaranteed silence: some browser/screen-reader pairs do announce a newly inserted populated `role="status"`, which is why "may never fire" is the right hedge and I did not upgrade the severity. Second, qpu-submit-panel.tsx sits on the hardware path that is deliberately switched off, so two of the five instances are dormant; review-card, quiz and the /review session-complete banner are all on live, free, shipped surfaces, which is what keeps this at medium (WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages, AA) rather than low.

The region therefore genuinely enters the a11y tree already populated — there is no path where it is mounted empty first. `grep -n 'aria-live|role="status"' review-card.tsx` finds exactly one hit (:213), and `grep -rn 'aria-live' src/app/layout.tsx src/components/*.tsx` shows no global announcer or ancestor live region that could catch the mutation. `git diff 4aec7f8..HEAD --stat -- web/src/components/quantum/review-card.tsx` returns empty output — unchanged at HEAD (1f38013).

The house standard is real and self-documented, which is what makes this a defect rather than an opinion: challenge.tsx:255-258 and debug-circuit-widget.tsx:216-219 both carry comments reading "mounting a fresh region per verdict is not reliably announced" over an always-mounted `<div role="status">` wrapping conditional children; live-status.tsx:7 says "the node stays mounted so aria-live fires on text change"; saved-panel.tsx:124-132 and copy-button.tsx:154 keep mounted regions with empty strings. No test covers it — `grep -n 'status|announce|aria-live' __tests__/components/quantum/review-card.test.tsx` returns nothing.

SEVERITY — I downgrade medium to low. The finder's impact ("can be silent ... on the surface whose whole purpose is that feedback") overstates it in three ways: (1) the outcome text stays in the DOM and is reachable by ordinary screen-reader navigation, so the announcement is lost, not the information; (2) the failure is AT/browser-dependent, not universal — the finder's own "may never fire" hedge is the honest framing, and several Chrome/NVDA combinations do announce an inserted role=status; (3) one of the four cited sites (qpu-submit-panel) is on the deliberately dormant hardware path. Real WCAG 2.1 SC 4.1.3 robustness gap on live free surfaces, and a genuine inconsistency with a rule this codebase wrote down itself — but polish, not breakage.

A Spanish learner's session is substantially English on purpose; four more English panels on /workspace is a consistency gap inside an unresolved scope decision, with no functional, financial, data-integrity or security consequence. The one argument for medium is real and worth keeping: `discardAnonBucket` (src/lib/progress-owner.ts:176-184) does a hard `localStorage.removeItem` on every anon key with no undo, so "Not mine" is genuinely irreversible and is presented only in English. That makes claim-anon-progress.tsx the right thing to fix first, but it does not lift the cluster above low.

### The new hero ships visible body text at 3.3:1 in hardcoded arbitrary colours that none of the three contrast guards can see

`web/src/components/welcome/hero.tsx:309` — `faf5d38ec` · medium · confirmed · accessibility · ran locally · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 12

**Claim.** The micro-badge row ("Free · In-browser · No install") sets `text-[rgba(224,235,229,0.4)]` at `text-[10px]` over the `bg-abyss` (#03110d) island — 3.32:1 composited, against a 4.5:1 AA floor for normal-size text. The HUD telemetry line built at hero.tsx:163 uses `text-[rgba(224,235,229,0.45)]` at the same 10px — 3.90:1. Both are best-case figures computed over pure abyss; the actual ground is abyss plus a fog image at opacity .55, which lightens it and lowers the ratio further. These are Tailwind arbitrary values and raw `fill="#C2A379"` literals, not tokens, so token-contrast.test.ts (which parses only the `:root`/`.dark` blocks of globals.css) is structurally blind to them, and contrast-guard.test.ts / caption-contrast.test.ts match class-name shapes (`bg-accent`, `text-gray-400`) that these do not have.

**Correction.** Two parts of the reasoning are wrong, both about the fog and the HUD — the core defect stands.

(1) THE FOG CLAIM IS BACKWARDS. The finder says "the actual ground is abyss plus a fog image at opacity .55, which lightens it and lowers the ratio further." Measured, the fog image's mean RGB in the badge region is [6.1, 9.7, 12.0] — its GREEN channel (which carries 0.7152 of luminance) is far below abyss's 17, so the fog DARKENS that region rather than lightening it, and the 0.82 spine scrim at hero.tsx:174 pulls it back toward abyss regardless. The real composited ground is [3.3, 16.3, 12.9], giving 3.32:1 — indistinguishable from the pure-abyss figure. The numbers are right; the "and it's actually worse in practice" embellishment is unsupported. The finder never mentions the scrim layer at all.

(2) THE HUD ROW IS AUTHOR-MARKED DECORATIVE. The impact line says "two rows of informational text," but the :164 HUD is applied at hero.tsx:246 with aria-hidden="true" and is `hidden … sm:flex` (desktop only), rendering only `hudLive` telemetry beside an animated signal dot. It still fails 1.4.3 for sighted low-vision users, but it has a defensible WCAG "pure decoration" argument that the micro-badge row does not. Treating the two rows as equivalent overstates the HUD half. (The finder was careful to scope the no-aria-hidden claim to the badges only — that part is accurate.)

Minor: the HUD is at :164, not :163; the const declaration opens on 163.

**Impact.** The site's highest-traffic public page ships two rows of informational text below AA. The micro-badges are the product's three headline claims and carry no aria-hidden, so they are read by both eyes and AT. The after-dark pass's commit message claims "WCAG floors recomputed and passing in both themes" — true of the token layer, not of the hero that pass introduced.

**Evidence.** hero.tsx:309 `… text-[10px] font-medium uppercase tracking-[0.18em] text-[rgba(224,235,229,0.4)]` wrapping `{microBadges.map(...)}` at :314. hero.tsx:163 `const hud = "… text-[10px] … text-[rgba(224,235,229,0.45)] sm:flex"`. Ground is `bg-abyss` (globals.css:35 `--color-abyss: #03110d`) at hero.tsx:174. Composited ratios computed with the WCAG relative-luminance formula: 0.40 alpha → 3.32:1, 0.45 → 3.90:1, 0.62 (subtitle) → 6.46:1, 0.60 (right HUD) → 6.11:1.

**Split verdict.** reproduces: confirmed · correct as written: partly true. Published at the more severe reading.

**Verification — reproduces** (confirmed, medium, ran locally). Every checkable assertion reproduces. (1) Source verified verbatim: hero.tsx:309 carries `text-[10px] font-medium uppercase tracking-[0.18em] text-[rgba(224,235,229,0.4)]` wrapping `{microBadges.map(...)}` at :314; hero.tsx:163 defines `hud` with `text-[10px] ... text-[rgba(224,235,229,0.45)] sm:flex`; globals.css:35 is `--color-abyss: #03110d` (the bg-abyss div is line 175, finder cited 174 — trivial off-by-one).

(2) I recomputed the ratios independently rather than trusting the finder, via a node script using the WCAG linear-sRGB relative-luminance formula with proper alpha compositing (`node scratchpad/c.mjs`). Output: alpha 0.40 -> 3.32:1, 0.45 -> 3.90:1, 0.62 -> 6.46:1, 0.60 -> 6.11:1 — all four match the finder to the decimal. At text-[10px] these are normal-size text (large-text relief begins at 18.66px bold / 24px), so the 4.5:1 AA floor is the right one.

(3) The fog claim holds. Sweeping fog luminance 40-200 through the real stack (abyss -> fog opacity .55 -> scrim rgba(3,17,13,0.82/0.55)), alpha .40 lands 2.83-3.35:1 and alpha .45 lands 3.17-3.91:1. The scrim reclaims most of the fog's lift, so "lowers it further" is directionally right but modest — never rises meaningfully above the pure-abyss best case.

(4) The guard-blindness claim is proven empirically, not merely argued: `npx jest __tests__/token-contrast.test.ts __tests__/contrast-guard.test.ts __tests__/caption-contrast.test.ts` -> 3 suites, 83 tests, ALL PASSING while the defect ships. Their sources say why: token-contrast regexes only the `:root`/`.dark` blocks of globals.css (its `themeBlock()` reads nothing else); contrast-guard matches `bg|from|via|to-accent` + `text-white`/`fill-white`; caption-contrast matches `text-gray-(400|500)` and explicitly excludes opacity-modified tokens. An arbitrary `text-[rgba(...)]` in TSX matches none.

(5) It genuinely ships: `grep -o 'text-\[rgba(224,235,229,0\.4)\]' out/index.html` hits in the built static export, as do the strings `In-browser` and `No install`. Badges are t("home.badgeFree"/"badgeInBrowser"/"badgeNoInstall") — the three headline claims — on a row with no aria-hidden.

SCOPE REFINEMENT (contradicts nothing the finder wrote; their aria-hidden sentence was correctly scoped to the micro-badges only): the 3.90:1 HUD is used at exactly one site, hero.tsx:246, and it IS `aria-hidden="true"`, as is the 6.11:1 counts row at :256. Both are `hidden ... sm:flex`, so mobile never renders them. The HUD is thus a sighted-only 1.4.3 failure — aria-hidden does not exempt it, since "Simulator live · in-browser" conveys information and is not pure decoration. Only the micro-badge row fails for both eyes and AT. Severity medium concurs with the finder: real, shipping, user-visible AA failure on the highest-traffic public page and on the product's three headline claims, but legibility rather than functional or security impact, and one of the two rows is desktop-only and AT-exempt.

**Verification — correct as written** (partly true, medium, ran locally). I tried to refute this and could not — the core defect is real, and one part of it is STRONGER than claimed.

VERIFIED BY READING. Both class strings are verbatim as quoted. hero.tsx:309 is `… text-[10px] font-medium uppercase tracking-[0.18em] text-[rgba(224,235,229,0.4)]` wrapping `{microBadges.map(...)}` at :314. The badges are real translated content, not chrome: home-page-content.tsx:176 passes `[t("home.badgeFree"), t("home.badgeInBrowser"), t("home.badgeNoInstall")]`, defined in both locales (en.ts:166 `badgeFree: "Free"`, es.ts:167 `badgeFree: "Gratis"`), and the row carries no aria-hidden.

VERIFIED BY EXECUTION — `python3` heredoc run from web/, compositing alpha over ground and computing WCAG relative luminance, plus PIL sampling of public/welcome/hero-fog.webp (2688x1536) over the badge region:
  - Reproduced all four of the finder's ratios EXACTLY: 0.40 -> 3.32:1, 0.45 -> 3.90:1, 0.62 -> 6.46:1, 0.60 -> 6.11:1. The arithmetic is sound.
  - THE STRONGEST RESULT, which the finder missed: I brute-forced the entire sRGB cube and `rgba(224,235,229,0.40)` tops out at 3.35:1 against ANY background that exists (best case bg [21,21,21]); 0.45 tops out at 3.92:1. There is no ground, no scrim, no layering, no viewport that rescues these. The failure is unconditional, not contingent on the abyss island — which makes the finder's whole fog argument unnecessary as well as backwards.

GUARD BLINDNESS CONFIRMED, and I hunted for a fourth guard and found none (no axe, no Playwright a11y pass). contrast-guard.test.ts matches only `bg|from|via|to-accent` + `text-white`, and `fill-accent` + `fill-white`. caption-contrast.test.ts matches only `text-gray-(400|500)` shapes. token-contrast.test.ts regex-parses the `:root`/`.dark` blocks of globals.css and never sees a component file. An arbitrary `text-[rgba(...)]` value in a .tsx passes all three.

THE PROJECT'S OWN STANCE CONVICTS THIS. caption-contrast.test.ts carries the comment: "bg-abyss islands are deliberately NOT exempted: gray-500 computes only 4.0:1 on #03110D, so a bare muted gray on an abyss line should be flagged and re-tokenized." The hero ships 3.32:1 on that exact abyss ground — below the 4.0:1 the project explicitly refuses to exempt. This is not a finder inventing a standard the codebase does not hold itself to.

The author was demonstrably contrast-aware — the h1 dim span at :288 carries "It clears the 3:1 large-text floor over the spine scrim," which is the CORRECT floor for that large text. The 10px rows are normal-size text where 4.5:1 applies, and simply got missed.

SEVERITY: medium is right, not inflated. This is the live public homepage, not one of the dormant paths (storefront/metering) the brief warns about — but it is a contrast shortfall on three short badge words that remain legible to most users, not a functional block, so it is not high.

### The after-dark changelog entry announces a steerable dial that does not exist below 768px

`web/src/lib/changelog.ts:58` — `f019d482e` · low · confirmed · docs-drift · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · fix plan 13

**Claim.** Entry 2026-08-24-after-dark-redesign tells learners "The welcome page's curriculum is now a dial — choose any section number and the needle moves to it with a short description, so you can weigh a module before you open it" (:58, and the Spanish twin at changelog-es.ts:21). In hero.tsx the entire interactive dial is `md:` gated: the needle group is `className="hidden md:block"` (:222), the stations SVG that carries the `role="button"` controls is `className="absolute inset-0 z-20 hidden h-full w-full md:block"` (:407), and the blurb card is `hidden … md:block` (:340). Below 768px a visitor sees a static bezel and the plain curriculum grid — no station to choose, no needle, no description card. The file's own doc comment (changelog.ts:14-16) sets the standard being missed: "Never announce a surface the deployed system does not expose. The repo is public and this page is indexed, so an entry here is a rule 13 claim with SEO reach."

**Correction.** The framing is wrong on two counts. (1) This is not a "surface the deployed system does not expose" / rule-13 case. ### ChangeEntry.section is declared, documented and test-validated, but never rendered

`web/src/lib/changelog.ts:46` — `f1b0a77ef` · low · confirmed · dead-code · ran locally · fix plan 13

**Claim.** `section?: SectionSlug` is declared at changelog.ts:46 with a doc comment ("Optional curriculum section, reusing the glossary's slug union"), is set on one live entry (`section: "04-quantum-ml"` at :74), and is guarded by a test that asserts every value resolves through getSectionBySlug (__tests__/lib/changelog.test.ts:53-57). `grep -rn '\.section' web/src/components/changelog/ web/src/app/changelog/` returns nothing — ChangelogPageContent reads id, kind, title, body and href only. Meanwhile the field that IS rendered, `href`, is validated only for shape: changelog.test.ts:47-51 asserts it starts with "/", and nothing checks that the route exists.

**Correction.** Only a citation slip, not a reasoning error: the tagged entry's `section: "04-quantum-ml"` is at changelog.ts:76, not :74 (:74 is that entry's `href`). The primary location (:46), the section test (changelog.test.ts:53-57) and the href test (:47-51) are all cited exactly.

**Impact.** Zero user-visible effect today. The cost is a false signal: a green test suite implies the section tag is doing something, so a future author will keep tagging entries that render nothing, and the validation effort is aimed at the dead field while the live one (href, which under output:"export" 404s on a typo'd route) has none. Either render the section tag or delete the field, and move the existence check onto href.

**Evidence.** changelog.ts:45-46 field declaration; changelog.ts:74 `section: "04-quantum-ml"`; __tests__/lib/changelog.test.ts:53-57 validates it; `grep -rn '\.section' web/src/components/changelog/ web/src/app/changelog/` → no matches. changelog-page-content.tsx:74-101 destructures `{ title, body }` and reads `entry.id`, `entry.kind`, `entry.href`.

**Verification — reproduces** (confirmed, low, ran locally). I tried to refute this three ways and could not. It reproduces.

1) The field and its guard exist as cited. `sed -n '45,46p' web/src/lib/changelog.ts` shows `section?: SectionSlug` under the quoted doc comment; `grep -n "section" web/src/lib/changelog.ts` shows exactly one live use, at :76 (the finder wrote :74, which is that entry's `href` — the only inaccuracy I found). `sed -n '47,57p' web/__tests__/lib/changelog.test.ts` confirms the href test asserts only `startsWith("/")` and the section test asserts `getSectionBySlug` resolves.

2) The finder grepped only two directories, so I widened it. `grep -rn "lib/changelog" --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx" --include="*.mjs" web/src web/__tests__ web/e2e scripts` finds the module has exactly two importers: changelog-page-content.tsx and the tests. `grep -rn "\.section\b|section:" ... web/src web/__tests__ scripts` returns only glossary/route hits, none on a ChangeEntry. The component destructures `{ title, body }` and reads `entry.id`, `entry.kind`, `entry.href` — no spread that could pass `section` through.

3) Executed proof it renders nothing. I copied a render probe to `web/__tests__/zz-probe-section.test.tsx` (untracked, deleted immediately; `git status --porcelain web/` is clean), rendering ChangelogPageContent with a synthetic entry carrying `section: "05-quantum-chemistry"`. `npx jest __tests__/zz-probe-section.test.tsx` printed `SLUG in HTML: false`, `'Chemistry' in HTML: false`, and full text content of "PROBE TITLE / New / PROBE BODY" only. Nothing of the section reaches the DOM. `npx jest __tests__/lib/changelog.test.ts` → 33 passed, so the suite is green over the dead field.

One thing that makes it slightly worse than written: the guarding test cannot fail. `SectionSlug` (glossary.ts:3-10) is a 7-literal union, so TypeScript already constrains the value at compile time, and glossary.test.ts:50-55 already asserts all 7 union members resolve through `getSectionBySlug` against the manifest. The changelog's section test is therefore a tautology layered on an unrendered field.

The href half of the impact also holds: `next.config` line 4 is `output: "export"`, and no route-existence check exists anywhere (no link crawler in e2e/). Both live hrefs happen to be valid today — `/` exists and `/learn/04-quantum-ml` resolves via the generated manifest through `src/app/learn/[section]` — so there is no live breakage, only an unguarded surface.

### The nav badge still runs a full localStorage scan plus a JSON.parse per card inside getSnapshot, on every page

`web/src/components/review-nav-badge.tsx:16` — `f3ab89465` · low · confirmed · performance · ran locally · SPLIT VERDICT · re-raised from `f65b9f6f4` · fix plan 13

**Claim.** Still true, and the pattern is wider than the prior audit recorded. `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, () => dueCount(), () => 0)` at :16 makes every React invocation of getSnapshot — which happens during render and again in the store-consistency check, not once per event — walk `dueCount()` → `dueCardIds()` → `getAllCardIds()` (a full `localStorage.length` loop in progress-owner.ts:129-137) and then `getCardState(id)` (a getItem + JSON.parse) for every stored card. The badge is in the layout, so this is every page of the site. Two more consumers do the same or more: review-dashboard.tsx:110 `snapshot()` runs the scan twice per call (dueCardIds() and getAllCardIds()), and hooks/use-workspace.ts:24 `snapshot()` runs getAllCardStates() (scan + parse per card) plus completedCount(), getAllMeasurements(), activeDays() and dueCount() (another full scan + parse per card).

**Correction.** Three parts of the framing are wrong. (1) The novelty claim — "the pattern is wider than the prior audit recorded" — is false. Both extra consumers are already on the record: docs/codebase-audit-2026-08-16.md:417 names `use-workspace.ts:24-39` and its extra scans verbatim, and the 2026-08-18 adjudication (docs/codebase-audit-2026-08-18.md:1270-1280) already corrected the count to four scans and named review-dashboard. This is the THIRD submission of the same finding; it was adjudicated Partly true / low twice, and docs/feature-optimization.md:929 has tracked it OPEN since 2026-06-17. Nothing here is new. (2) "The cost is proportional to how much a learner has done, so the site gets slower for exactly the people who use it most" overstates the growth curve: N is capped by the curriculum, not by usage — a learner who completes everything reaches ~102 cards and stops. (3) The evidence cites `review-store.ts:74-77` for the per-card JSON.parse; that is `getCardContent`, which `dueCount` never calls. The parse on the badge path is `parseCardState` at review-schedule.ts:178-186. Conversely the finding UNDERSTATES one thing: nav.tsx mounts `<ReviewNavBadge />` twice (:89 lg-rail, :107 small-screen pill), so every render pass runs the scan two components deep, not one.

**Impact.** Repeated synchronous storage work on the render path of every route. Bounded in practice — the curriculum ships 28 qcard blocks plus six graded-Rep kinds, so a heavy learner holds tens of keys, not thousands — which is why this stays low. The shape is the concern: the cost is proportional to how much a learner has done, so the site gets slower for exactly the people who use it most, and nothing memoizes between the badge, the dashboard and the workspace model.

**Evidence.** review-nav-badge.tsx:16 `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, () => dueCount(), () => 0)`; review-store.ts:179-181 dueCount → :169-175 dueCardIds → :146-156 getAllCardIds → progress-owner.ts:124-142 ownedLocalKeys (full `for (let i = 0; i < localStorage.length; i++)`); review-store.ts:98-101 getCardState (getItem) and :74-77 (JSON.parse). Also review-dashboard.tsx:110 and hooks/use-workspace.ts:24-40.

**Split verdict.** reproduces: confirmed · correct as written: partly true. Published at the more severe reading.

**Verification — reproduces** (confirmed, low, ran locally). Every cited line is verbatim accurate, and the mechanism reproduces. If anything the finder UNDERSTATES it.

Reads (all confirmed): review-nav-badge.tsx:16 is exactly `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, () => dueCount(), () => 0)`; review-store.ts dueCount→dueCardIds→getAllCardIds→progress-owner.ts `ownedLocalKeys` (`for (let i = 0; i < localStorage.length; i++)`), then `getCardState(id)` = getItem + `parseCardState`→JSON.parse per card id; review-dashboard.tsx:110 is `return \`${dueCardIds().join(",")}|${getAllCardIds().length}\`` (two scans/call); use-workspace.ts:24-40 does getAllCardStates + completedCount + getAllMeasurements + activeDays + dueCount. Nothing memoizes across the three. `<Nav />` is at src/app/layout.tsx:106, so it is every route.

1) getSnapshot call count, real React 19 + jsdom, exact hook shape (script at scratchpad/count.ts, run with `cd web && TS_NODE_COMPILER_OPTIONS='{"module":"commonjs",...}' node_modules/.bin/ts-node --transpile-only .../count.ts`): mount = 3 calls per badge instance, unrelated re-render = 3 per instance, one qc-progress event = 1 per instance. The "render plus the store-consistency check, not once per event" claim is right.

2) The real module against a real jsdom localStorage (scratchpad/bench.ts, same ts-node invocation, importing web/src/lib/review-store.ts unmodified): 34 cards / 98 keys → 0.083 ms per dueCount(); 340 cards / 780 keys → 1.25 ms; 1000 cards → 6.7 ms.

3) Real Chromium (playwright headless_shell-1234, `node scratchpad/browser-bench.mjs`, faithful replication of the same loop against Chrome's own localStorage): 98 keys → 0.030 ms; 260 keys → 0.088 ms; 660 keys → 0.236 ms; 2200 keys → 0.771 ms. Linear, not quadratic.

Two places the finding is conservative rather than wrong. (a) nav.tsx mounts `<ReviewNavBadge />` TWICE — line 89 (lg action rail) and line 107 (small-screen pill row) — both unconditionally, hidden by CSS only. So it is 2 hook instances × 3 getSnapshot calls = 6 full scans per page render, ~0.18 ms typical / ~0.53 ms for a completionist in real Chrome. (b) the card inventory is ~3x what the impact paragraph implies: English guides carry 28 qcard + 18 qexpect + 16 qpredict + 15 qchallenge + 11 qcostestimate + 8 qdebug + 6 qblochtarget = 102 card-minting fences, plus 5 quiz blocks that mint one card per question (quiz.tsx `quizCardId`), and each graded card also writes a sibling `qc:card-content:` key the scan walks — so ~250-300 keys, i.e. hundreds not "tens". Both errors push the true cost up, not down.

Even so the conclusion stands as written: sub-millisecond per render at any realistic key count, linear in a browser, so low is the correct severity. The value is the shape (cost scales with how much the learner has done; three unmemoized consumers), not the current number.

**Verification — correct as written** (partly true, low, ran locally). Call chain verified by reading, exactly as quoted: /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/web/src/components/review-nav-badge.tsx:16 passes an inline `() => dueCount()` to useSyncExternalStore; review-store.ts:179-181 dueCount -> :170-176 dueCardIds -> :146-157 getAllCardIds -> progress-owner.ts:124-142 ownedLocalKeys, which is a literal `for (let i = 0; i < localStorage.length; i++)` walk, then a getItem (getCardStateRaw, :98-104) plus JSON.parse (review-schedule.ts:178-186) per card id. I read review-store.ts and progress-owner.ts in full — there is no cache, no memo, no dirty flag anywhere in that layer, so the scan really does re-run per invocation. Nav is in the persistent root layout (app/layout.tsx:106), and review-dashboard.tsx:109-111 does run two scans per snapshot (`dueCardIds()` then `getAllCardIds()`), and use-workspace.ts:24-40 runs the four the finding lists. So the mechanics are correct and this is not a pattern-match error.

What does not survive is the magnitude framing. I measured the exact loop shape against a Blink-like storage area (Map + ordered key array, O(1) key(i)) at the curriculum ceiling: `node /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-cperez-dev-altivum-inc-quantum/b7fc46e5-3806-4423-bbf8-8ccaa78ee81d/scratchpad/bench.mjs` -> `keys=802 cards=102 due=51  dueCount() = 0.0392 ms/call`. Two badge instances x ~3 getSnapshot invocations per render pass is ~0.24 ms — three orders of magnitude under the 200 ms INP budget. The ceiling itself is fixed by content, not by usage: `for k in qchallenge qpredict qblochtarget qcostestimate qdebug qexpect qcard; do grep -rho "^\`\`\`$k" 0*/GUIDE.md | wc -l; done` totals 15+16+6+11+8+18+28 = **102** card-bearing fences across the whole curriculum, so "the site gets slower for the people who use it most" tops out at 102 parsed records.

Also worth noting for the reader: ownedLocalKeys parses nothing — it is `localStorage.key(i)` plus a `startsWith` compare — so the ~700 non-card `qc:` keys cost a string compare each, not a parse. And the number-valued snapshot at review-nav-badge.tsx:9-10 is a documented deliberate guard (a stable value-equal snapshot for React's identity check), so there is no re-render loop hiding here.

Net: a real, un-memoized synchronous scan on a layout-level render path, already known and already tracked as open cleanup work in this repo. It is a memoization nit, not a defect in correctness, and low is generous.
