  cd web/jupyterlite-build/static/pyodide && python3 -c "import re;s=open('pyodide.asm.js',errors='replace').read();[print(s[m.start()-800:m.end()+400]) for m in re.finditer('sha256',s)]"
`PackageManager.downloadPackage` does, verbatim from the minified source:
  o=Y(n,this.installBaseUrl), i="sha256-"+Xt(l.sha256)   // l = lockfile_packages[pkg]
  ... return await Q(o,i)
and the browser branch of the binary fetch is:
  function kn(t,e){let r=new URL(t,location);return{response:fetch(r,e?{integrity:e}:{})}}
i.e. a genuine `fetch(url, {integrity: "sha256-<base64>"})`. `Xt` is `base16ToBase64`. It is on by default and hard to turn off accidentally: `loadPackage(e,r={checkIntegrity:!0})`, and `async downloadAndInstall(e,r,n,o,i=!0)` re-defaults the flag, so even a caller (like the JupyterLite kernel) that passes an options object omitting `checkIntegrity` still gets `i=true`.

I then confirmed the staged artifacts are actually integrity-consistent, i.e. the SRI would pass and the control is live rather than theoretical. Command:
  cd web/jupyterlite-build/static/pyodide && python3 -c "import json,hashlib,pathlib;d=json.load(open('pyodide-lock.json'));staged={p.name for p in pathlib.Path('.').iterdir() if p.name.endswith('.whl')};print(sum(hashlib.sha256(pathlib.Path(v['file_name']).read_bytes()).hexdigest()==v['sha256'] for v in d['packages'].values() if v['file_name'] in staged), len(staged))"
Result: 27 staged wheels, 27 hash-match the staged lock, 0 mismatches. Sample SRI the browser sends for numpy: sha256-LKRrcGYcrqj5+AidIklceiTBIPxYgeaJNKw6BNP8igI=.

Two supporting points. (1) `prune_lock.py` only DELETES lock keys (`del packages[key]`); it never rewrites an entry, so every surviving package keeps its upstream `sha256` and the staging step does not weaken the check. (2) The cross-origin binding is the interesting part: the hash comes from GitHub (the core tarball) and the bytes come from jsdelivr, so compromising jsdelivr alone gets nothing into a browser — the fetch is rejected and `downloadAndInstall` records it in the failure map and logs "Failed to load", which is fail-closed and loud.

WHAT SURVIVES, AND IT IS REAL. The core tarball is the unverified trust anchor: `curl -fsSL --retry 3 https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide/releases/download/${version}/pyodide-core-${version}.tar.bz2` with no pinned digest, cached at `.cache/pyodide-core-${version}.tar.bz2` and reused on `[[ -s "$tarball" ]]` alone, persisted by both `amplify.yml:27` and the `jupyterlite-v3-...` actions/cache key. That tarball carries `pyodide.asm.wasm` (8.6 MB), `python_stdlib.zip` (2.4 MB), `pyodide.asm.js` and the lock itself — none SRI'd anywhere, and the lock being inside it means a bad tarball would supply self-consistent hashes for tampered wheels too. The `requirements.txt:3-4` floating/hashless pins are also accurately reported.

WHY THE TRADE-OFF IS NOT AN OVERSIGHT. web/src/lib/pyodide-runtime.ts:47-53 states it precisely and in advance: "this guards only pyodide.js; the wasm/stdlib it then fetches carry no SRI (Pyodide verifies downloaded package wheels against the lockfile's hashes, but not the core runtime blobs). Acceptable because same-origin is primary, so this weaker-integrity path is exercised only when same-origin is unreachable." That comment is about the runtime fallback rather than the build-time fetch, so it does not fully cover the finding — but it shows the exact distinction the finder's headline erases was already reasoned through and written down.

SEVERITY. Low is right and I would not raise it. The residual risk is a compromised GitHub release asset or a poisoned build cache, both of which require an adversary who has already breached a TLS-authenticated upstream or the CI/Amplify cache; the version-keyed cache does not self-heal for a valid-but-malicious tarball (it only self-heals a CORRUPT one, via the `tar -xjf ... || rm -f "$tarball"` path), which is the sharpest remaining edge. The honest framing is "the core tarball wants a pinned sha256," not "the browser runtime is unverified."

> Correction. The impact sentence "the wasm, the stdlib, and every wheel the in-browser lab loads are accepted on TLS alone" is wrong for the wheels — which are the large majority of the fetches the finding cites (27 of them for the lab, 3 for the lesson runtime). Every wheel `fetch_closure_wheels` pulls from jsdelivr is a Pyodide-lock package, and Pyodide applies real Subresource Integrity to each one at load time in the browser, keyed on a hash from a DIFFERENT origin (the GitHub-released core tarball's `pyodide-lock.json`). A tampered jsdelivr wheel therefore fails closed in the learner's browser instead of executing. "It is the one input to the build that nothing in the repo verifies" also overstates: the repo does hold a hash pin for a Pyodide artifact (`PYODIDE_CDN_SRI`, sha384, in `web/src/lib/pyodide-runtime.ts`), and that file records this exact supply-chain analysis as a deliberate decision. What survives is narrower than the title: the pyodide-core TARBALL from GitHub — `pyodide.asm.wasm`, `python_stdlib.zip`, `pyodide.asm.js`, and `pyodide-lock.json` itself — is the unverified root of trust, and the floating `jupyter-server>=2.14` / `build>=1.2` pins are real.

### The CodeBuild standby webhook has no actor filter, so on this public repo a fork PR would run arbitrary code with AWS credentials and post the status that is the merge gate

`infra/ci-standby/failover.sh:83-91` — `fa7a050d0` · low · partly true · security · observed live · SPLIT VERDICT · re-raised from `f9805323f` · fix plan 04

**Claim.** `engage()` creates the webhook with two filter groups keyed only on `EVENT` (`PULL_REQUEST_CREATED, PULL_REQUEST_UPDATED, PULL_REQUEST_REOPENED`) and `HEAD_REF`. There is no `ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID` filter group, which is CodeBuild's mechanism for restricting who can trigger a build. The repository is public. The build runs the inline buildspec against the PR head, which includes `npm ci` and `pip install -e .` — arbitrary code from the fork's lockfiles and setup — inside a project whose role also carries the `founding-ten-verify` policy (it runs `node scripts/verify-founding-ten.mjs`, which enumerates the production Cognito user pool). `BuildStatusConfig` with `ReportBuildStatus: true` means the build also posts the commit status that `engage()` has just made main's sole required check.

**Correction.** The factual code observation stands (no ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID filter, public repo, live role holding cognito-idp:ListUsers), but the impact — "an outside contributor's PR runs untrusted code ... and controls the merge gate's outcome" — is wrong. CodeBuild's pull-request build policy defaults to requiresCommentApproval=ALL_PULL_REQUESTS with approverRoles [GITHUB_ADMIN, GITHUB_MAINTAIN, GITHUB_WRITE] for projects created after the feature shipped (this one: 2026-07-16), so an untrusted fork PR never executes and posts a FAILED status rather than a green gate. What survives is a defense-in-depth gap — the repo states no fork control anywhere and relies on an unstated service default — which is low, not medium.

**Correction.** The impact is wrong. A fork PR would NOT auto-run: `create-webhook` omits `--pull-request-build-policy`, so CodeBuild applies its service default `requiresCommentApproval: ALL_PULL_REQUESTS` with `approverRoles: [GITHUB_ADMIN, GITHUB_MAINTAIN, GITHUB_WRITE]`. An untrusted contributor's webhook build is refused with "Pull request approval required for starting a build" until a maintainer comments `/codebuild_run(<sha>)`. ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID is therefore not "CodeBuild's mechanism for restricting who can trigger a build" — it is one of two, and not the one AWS now recommends. "Controls the merge gate's outcome" is also overstated: main has no required reviews and merging still needs write access, so a fork author could at most make their own PR display green, never merge. What survives is thinner and different: the protection is an undeclared AWS service default that nothing in this repo pins or asserts, and `engage()`'s own `start-build --source-version "pr/$pr" --report-build-status-override` loop bypasses that policy entirely — a path the finder did not identify.

**Impact.** While the standby is engaged, an outside contributor's PR runs untrusted code with production AWS credentials and controls the merge gate's outcome. Currently dormant: `aws codebuild batch-get-projects` shows `webhook: null`, i.e. the standby is disengaged and idle, so nothing is exposed until someone runs `failover.sh engage` — which is exactly the moment nobody is going to be reviewing the webhook's filter groups.

**Evidence.** `infra/ci-standby/failover.sh:86-89`: `--filter-groups '[[{"type": "EVENT", "pattern": "PULL_REQUEST_CREATED, ..."}], [{"type": "EVENT", "pattern": "PUSH"}, {"type": "HEAD_REF", "pattern": "^refs/heads/main$"}]]'` — no ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID group. `aws codebuild batch-get-projects --names quantum-ci-standby` → `webhook: null` (currently disengaged).

**Split verdict.** reproduces: refuted · correct as written: partly true. Published at the more severe reading.

**Severity drift.** Finder claimed medium; verification published low.

**Verification — reproduces** (refuted, low, observed live). The code reading is accurate but the exploit chain does not hold: CodeBuild's own default blocks it.

WHAT IS TRUE (verified). `sed -n '78,100p' /Users/cperez/dev/altivum-inc/quantum/infra/ci-standby/failover.sh` shows `engage()` at lines 81-92 calling `aws codebuild create-webhook` with exactly the two quoted filter groups and no `ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID` filter. `grep -rn "ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID|pull-request-build-policy|PullRequestBuildPolicy|requiresCommentApproval"` over the repo returns hits only inside docs/codebase-audit-*.json — nothing in infra/. The repo is public: `curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/AltivumInc-Admin/quantum-computing | head -c 600` → `"private": false`. The standby is disengaged: `aws codebuild batch-get-projects --names quantum-ci-standby --region us-east-2` → `"webhook": null`, `"reportBuildStatus": true`, `"buildStatusConfig": {"context": "CI (CodeBuild standby)"}`. The role is live: `aws iam get-role-policy --role-name quantum-ci-standby-codebuild --policy-name founding-ten-verify` → `cognito-idp:ListUsers` on `userpool/$USER_POOL_ID`.

WHY IT IS REFUTED. `create-webhook` omitting `--pull-request-build-policy` does not mean "no policy". Per https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/pull-request-build-policy.html, read in full: "**Default behavior**: Pull request build policy is enabled by default for all newly created CodeBuild projects", and for `requiresCommentApproval`, "ALL_PULL_REQUESTS — All pull requests require comment approval before builds execute (unless contributor is one of the approver roles). **This is the default value**", with `approverRoles` defaulting to `["GITHUB_ADMIN","GITHUB_MAINTAIN","GITHUB_WRITE"]`. So an outside contributor's fork PR does not execute: CodeBuild marks the status **Failed — "Pull request approval required for starting a build"**, and a repo admin/maintainer/writer must post `/codebuild_run(<sha>)` first. That also inverts the second half of the impact — the fork build posts a FAILED "CI (CodeBuild standby)" status, so it cannot turn the gate green, let alone "control the merge gate's outcome" (and an outside contributor cannot merge regardless).

The default applies here: `aws codebuild batch-get-projects --names quantum-ci-standby --region us-east-2 --query 'projects[0].created'` → `2026-07-16T06:40:48-05:00`, six months after AWS bulletin 2026-002-AWS (2026-01-15) already cites the feature as an existing mitigation. `aws codebuild create-webhook help` confirms the installed CLI (aws-cli/2.35.4) exposes `--pull-request-build-policy`, i.e. the field is optional on the request, not absent from the API.

Two caveats I am reporting honestly. (1) This is settled from AWS documentation plus the project's creation date, not from a live webhook — confirming it live would require running `create-webhook`, which is a mutation and would engage the standby, so I did not. (2) What genuinely remains is a hardening gap, not the described defect: nothing in failover.sh, template.yaml or README.md mentions forks, actor filters or the PR build policy, so the safety rests entirely on an unstated AWS service default that a future `--pull-request-build-policy DISABLED` or a doc-default change would silently remove. AWS's "Best practices for using webhooks" names ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID filters for public repos, and the stack implements only one of the four listed controls (the deliberately inline buildspec). Worth a hardening ticket at low severity on a path where `webhook: null` today.

Aside, since the finder's blast-radius framing was also off in the other direction: "production AWS credentials" overstates a role scoped to logs, one cache bucket, one connection ARN and `ListUsers` on one pool — but it understates the sharpest item, `codeconnections:GetConnectionToken` on the live connection (`aws iam get-role-policy --policy-name github-connection`), which build code could reach via the container credentials endpoint. That matters only once a maintainer has approved a build, which is exactly the control the finding assumed was absent.

> Correction. The factual code observation stands (no ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID filter, public repo, live role holding cognito-idp:ListUsers), but the impact — "an outside contributor's PR runs untrusted code ... and controls the merge gate's outcome" — is wrong. CodeBuild's pull-request build policy defaults to requiresCommentApproval=ALL_PULL_REQUESTS with approverRoles [GITHUB_ADMIN, GITHUB_MAINTAIN, GITHUB_WRITE] for projects created after the feature shipped (this one: 2026-07-16), so an untrusted fork PR never executes and posts a FAILED status rather than a green gate. What survives is a defense-in-depth gap — the repo states no fork control anywhere and relies on an unstated service default — which is low, not medium.

**Verification — correct as written** (partly true, low, observed live). WHAT IS ACCURATE (read): `infra/ci-standby/failover.sh:83-91` does create the webhook with only EVENT and HEAD_REF filters — no `ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID`/`GITHUB_ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID` group. The inline buildspec in `infra/ci-standby/template.yaml` genuinely executes attacker-controlled code (`npm ci` x7, `pip install -e ".[dev,full]"`, `make test` importing repo conftest), and `ServiceRole` really does carry `founding-ten-verify` (`cognito-idp:ListUsers` on `$USER_POOL_ID`) plus `codeconnections:GetConnectionToken` on the connection ARN. `grep -rn -i "ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID|pullRequestBuildPolicy|fork" infra/ .github/ CLAUDE.md` returns nothing — the repo records no decision here either way.

WHY THE IMPACT FAILS (AWS docs, read via aws___read_documentation on https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/pull-request-build-policy.html): "Pull request build policy is enabled by default for all newly created CodeBuild projects"; `requiresCommentApproval` — "ALL_PULL_REQUESTS ... This is the default value"; `approverRoles` default `["GITHUB_ADMIN","GITHUB_MAINTAIN","GITHUB_WRITE"]`. `API_CreateWebhook.html` confirms `pullRequestBuildPolicy` is `Required: No`, so omitting it takes the service default rather than disabling it. The timing works out: `history.html` dates "Pull request comment approval" to August 7, 2025, and `aws codebuild batch-get-projects --names quantum-ci-standby --region us-east-2 --query 'projects[0].created'` returns 2026-07-16 — the project is ~11 months newer than the feature, so it is unambiguously covered by the default. `aws codebuild create-webhook help` on aws-cli/2.35.4 shows `--pull-request-build-policy` present, i.e. the API shape is live in the caller here too.

LIVE STATE (observed): `aws codebuild batch-get-projects --names quantum-ci-standby --region us-east-2` → `webhook: null`, role `quantum-ci-standby-codebuild`, `reportBuildStatus: true`, auth CODECONNECTIONS — dormant, as the finder said. `gh repo view AltivumInc-Admin/quantum-computing --json visibility,forkCount` → PUBLIC, **forkCount 0**. `gh api repos/.../branches/main/protection` → 8 required contexts all pinned to app_id 15368 (GitHub Actions), `enforce_admins: true`, `required_pull_request_reviews: null` — the gate is on Actions, and there is no reviews requirement for a green status to substitute for. No other project in the account (`altivum-hq-ci-standby`, `bedrock-agentcore-vetroi_resume_agent-builder`, `ai-noc-build` in us-east-1) has a live webhook, so I could not observe the default's materialized value in-account; creating one would be a mutation on live prod and out of scope. That is the one soft spot in my ruling — the default is documented, not observed.

THE REAL RESIDUAL, which the finding misses: `engage()` does not stop at the webhook. It then loops `aws codebuild start-build --source-version "pr/$pr" --report-build-status-override` over every open PR. A manually started build is not subject to `pullRequestBuildPolicy` at all, so if an untrusted fork PR is open at the moment an operator engages, the script builds that fork head with the full role and posts the gating status — no comment approval, no filter group. An ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID filter on the webhook would not have closed that either.

SEVERITY: low, not medium. Dormant (webhook null), zero forks, and when engaged the webhook path is gated by AWS's default comment approval. The defensible ask is narrow and cheap: pass an explicit `--pull-request-build-policy` (pin `FORK_PULL_REQUESTS` or `ALL_PULL_REQUESTS`) so the safety is stated rather than inherited, and skip or confirm fork-owned heads in the `start-build` loop.

> Correction. The impact is wrong. A fork PR would NOT auto-run: `create-webhook` omits `--pull-request-build-policy`, so CodeBuild applies its service default `requiresCommentApproval: ALL_PULL_REQUESTS` with `approverRoles: [GITHUB_ADMIN, GITHUB_MAINTAIN, GITHUB_WRITE]`. An untrusted contributor's webhook build is refused with "Pull request approval required for starting a build" until a maintainer comments `/codebuild_run(<sha>)`. ACTOR_ACCOUNT_ID is therefore not "CodeBuild's mechanism for restricting who can trigger a build" — it is one of two, and not the one AWS now recommends. "Controls the merge gate's outcome" is also overstated: main has no required reviews and merging still needs write access, so a fork author could at most make their own PR display green, never merge. What survives is thinner and different: the protection is an undeclared AWS service default that nothing in this repo pins or asserts, and `engage()`'s own `start-build --source-version "pr/$pr" --report-build-status-override` loop bypasses that policy entirely — a path the finder did not identify.

## The fix plan

Ordered. One finding appearing in six files is one item of work, not six.

### 01 — The withdrawn hardware promise, on every surface that still ships it

Effort: medium. Covers 5 findings.

**Why.** All three high-severity findings are the same defect in different files: the sponsored-QPU promise withdrawn on 2026-07-28 still renders on the landing page (both locales), the README's opening tagline, and the 02-hardware lesson (both locales) — and the repo's own sandbox script generates it into Stripe product descriptions. A new learner's lifetime QPU allowance is 0 and there is no funded path to a hardware run at all, so every one of these is a present-tense claim the deployed system refuses. The 2026-08-17 sweep ended this promise on the pricing family and stopped there; nothing extends the copy-honesty guard past the pricing page, which is why the curriculum and homepage copies survived. Fix the copy first, then widen the guard to the surfaces that carried it, or the next sweep will miss a different corner the same way. The homepage's 'Included free for every learner' tutor line rides along: it is the same shape of unqualified permanence claim on the same file, and it is equally unguarded.

**First commit.** Delete the sponsored-budget paragraph at 02-hardware/GUIDE.md:18-20 ('a free Workspace account comes with a sponsored budget on IQM Garnet ... you pay nothing') and its verbatim Spanish twin in 02-hardware/GUIDE.es.md, and cut the clause 'sponsored, so a learner never pays' from README.md:7. Those three edits clear all three high-severity findings and touch no code.

- `f6c986ea5` web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:156 — The public landing page advertises real quantum hardware in the present tense, in both locales, while the QPU Lambda refuses every learner's submit
- `f98cc585b` README.md:7 — README.md's opening tagline still promises sponsored, never-pay QPU runs — the promise withdrawn on 2026-07-28
- `f3451313b` 02-hardware/GUIDE.md:18-20 — The hardware lesson promises every free account a sponsored QPU budget on IQM Garnet, in both locales, and it is live in the shipped static export
- `f27c4ea26` web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:193-194 — The homepage promises in both locales that the AI tutor is "Included free for every learner", a permanence claim the settled monetization model contradicts and no copy-honesty guard covers
- `fc3f365fd` scripts/stripe/provision-sandbox.mjs:120-131 — Sandbox provisioning generates Stripe product descriptions that advertise hardware runs the deployed system cannot perform, and the catalog guard does not check for it

### 02 — "At cost, no markup" — retire the promise, and turn the three tests that pin it

Effort: medium. Covers 10 findings.

**Why.** Rule 9 retired the at-cost framing; the phrase still ships on the pricing page's share-card metadata (the most-copied sentence the project publishes), on five QPU strings, and in PRODUCT.md. Three tests assert the phrase is PRESENT, one with a comment saying it 'must survive the switch' — verbatim the mechanism CLAUDE.md records for how the sponsorship copy outlived its withdrawal. So the tests must be inverted before the copy can be touched; that ordering is the whole reason this is one unit of work. Two adjacent defects belong in the same pass because they are in the same files and the same sweep: the QPU panel's money copy is hardcoded English (so neither locale-parity nor the rendered-text guards can see it), and cost-estimator.tsx writes the QPU markup out as a percentage — a live rule-6 disclosure that walks straight through the guard widened in August specifically to stop the multiplier form. Finally, the credit counts hardcoded into i18n bullets duplicate the TIERS-derived line on the same card, which is rule 13 violated literally.

### 03 — The copy-honesty guards' own rationales have rotted

Effort: small. Covers 5 findings.

**Why.** The pricing page's guard is the project's reference implementation of honest copy, and its stated reasons are now demonstrably false about the code they cite — one asserts ask-tutor.tsx is 473 lines and renders no cost value, when the file is 560 lines and renders exactly that at :466-473. The pricing.ts TUTOR_RATES docblock, which is the recorded justification for withholding per-tier model chips from the published sheet, describes a Bedrock tutor that takes no model parameter; the roster has taken one since it landed. The bans themselves are still correct — nothing is metered, so the copy would still be false — but the guard's own doctrine says a ban whose rationale has expired should be re-examined, and a reviewer who checks these will find them wrong and lose confidence in the file. This is small, isolated, and worth doing right after the copy sweep so the guard is trustworthy when the cutover work starts leaning on it.

### 04 — Live security: a fork PR that runs on the maintainer's machine, and a CI role that reads every Lambda's environment

Effort: medium. Covers 9 findings.

**Why.** Two of these are live today and both are cheap. #246 moved the notebook filters to a repo-tracked script, so `.git/config` on any machine that ran `make setup` now names a file a fork PR can edit — and `gh pr checkout` followed by `git diff` executes it, in the checkout holding AWS credentials and Stripe keys. Before that commit the same PR was inert. Separately, the drift role's account-wide `lambda:ListFunctions` returns every function's plaintext environment in account $PROD_ACCOUNT — roughly 200 functions, including a live HMAC unsubscribe key today and the rule-6 rate factor the moment metering ships — under a comment that explicitly tells the reader it returns 'no environment secrets'. Grouped with them are three armed-but-idle exposures with the same character (the standby failover webhook has no contributor filter and self-approves the merge gate; email changes need no verification before `lambda/sync` persists an attacker-chosen address; unsubscribe mutates consent on an unauthenticated GET) and two missing controls (no CSP, with a test pinning its absence so hardening turns CI red; no integrity check on the Pyodide runtime shipped to every learner).

**First commit.** Change Makefile:20-23 so `make git-filters` points `filter.nbstripout.clean` and `diff.ipynb.textconv` at an absolute path outside the worktree rather than the repo-tracked `scripts/git/nbstripout-filter.sh`, keeping #246's move-survival property without letting a checked-out fork PR supply the executable.

### 05 — The privacy page no longer describes the system it governs

Effort: medium. Covers 7 findings.

**Why.** Four findings from three dimensions land on two sentences: the policy says 'No analytics or tracking scripts — none exist anywhere on this site' and that operational logs are deleted after 30 days, while a deployed daily job named quantum-analytics reads those logs, classifies every visitor address, and keeps a permanent derived record. The implementation is genuinely privacy-preserving; the disclosure is what lags, so this is a copy change, not an architecture change. Two nearby claims fail the same way and belong in the same pass: account deletion is described as complete in two places while sub-keyed QPU ledger and wallet rows survive it (7 rows today), and the page has already drifted silently once under a LAST_UPDATED constant that is hand-maintained and still reads 2026-07-12. The ops half is the same theme with a different fix: backfill.mjs left 69 MB of raw visitor logs — addresses, user agents, OAuth query strings — on local disk with gitignore as the only control, which is the exact artifact the runtime refuses to create; and the Founding Ten registry publishes a named person beside an unsalted digest of their email, which a committed per-registry salt would fix without losing any property the design needs.

**First commit.** Rewrite `noAnalytics` (web/src/i18n/locales/en.ts:934-935) and `retentionLogs` (:947-948) plus their es.ts counterparts to disclose the daily server-side access-log aggregation and the permanent aggregate derivative, and bump LAST_UPDATED in the same commit.

### 06 — The analytics counter: alarms that notify nobody, and a headline number that is not what it says

Effort: medium. Covers 8 findings.

**Why.** The stack shipped nine commits ago and its safety net is inert — the quantum-analytics SNS topic has zero subscriptions, so all four alarms including did-not-run (described in the template as guarding 'the one failure this stack must never produce') fire into nothing. That is a one-command fix and it is worse than a pending subscription, because redeploying will not recreate it. Behind it sits a measurement problem: `loadedAppAssets` discards every visitor whose browser already holds the immutable chunks, so 'humans' counts cold-cache first loads and is coupled to deploy cadence — which means the commit's own trend conclusion rests on a filter that cannot support it. Three more classifier defects push in different directions (a /shell hostile-path rule matching site-served URLs, only AWS prefixes loaded so Google Cloud and Azure agents pass, a units mismatch that permanently trips the self-contradiction check that caught the /credentials bug), and three collection defects mean a systematically broken run looks exactly like a quiet day. Do them together: the classifier changes are one file and one test suite.

**First commit.** Subscribe hq@quantumlearner.dev to the quantum-analytics SNS topic and confirm it from the inbox, then verify with `aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic` that the ARN is not PendingConfirmation. Until that lands, every other fix in this cluster is unobservable.

### 07 — Wallet ledger bugs to fix before the storefront opens

Effort: medium. Covers 4 findings.

**Why.** Four correctness defects in lambda/stripe/index.mjs, all dormant only because no money has moved, all of which become live the day rule 15 is lifted. The sharpest is the clawback: refund and dispute are capped separately against the same purchase, so a refunded-then-disputed $19 charge drains the balance AND books 1,900 credits of debt, leaving the learner at zero credits with both spend gates refusing them. Alongside it: the per-subscription grant is stamped at signup and never re-derived, so repricing CATALOG in lockstep with TIERS leaves existing subscribers on the old grant permanently with nothing able to see it; nothing prevents a second concurrent subscription, and cancelling either writes tier:'free' over a customer who is still paying; and the clawback's zero-floor is computed outside the transaction, so concurrent clawbacks drive the balance negative, which the client reads as 'metering unconfigured'. These are cheap now and expensive after the first real charge — rule 14's ordering says buying must work before metering turns on, and these are what 'work' means.

**First commit.** At lambda/stripe/index.mjs:589, cap `refundedCredits + disputedCredits` jointly against the purchase's original credit amount rather than capping each independently, so a refunded-then-disputed charge cannot reclaim twice what was bought.

- `f119ba729` lambda/stripe/index.mjs:752 — The per-subscription credit grant is stamped once at signup and never re-derived, so repricing CATALOG in lockstep with TIERS leaves existing subscribers on the old grant forever, undetected
- `f7be45dd5` lambda/stripe/index.mjs:589 — Refund and dispute clawbacks are capped separately against the same purchase, so a refunded-then-disputed charge reclaims up to twice what was bought
- `fa67d24a6` lambda/stripe/index.mjs:968 — Nothing prevents a second concurrent subscription, and cancelling either one resets the still-paying subscriber to the free tier
- `f3c1bf7e2` lambda/stripe/index.mjs:622-638 — The clawback's zero-floor on the balance is computed from a read outside the transaction and written with no condition, so a concurrent clawback drives the wallet negative

### 09 — Metering cutover: the preconditions the rate-card mechanism exposed and did not close

Effort: large. Covers 11 findings.

**Why.** The RATE_CARD mechanism shipped, metering stayed off, and the gap between them is this cluster. CLAUDE.md already names the blocker: the confirm step quotes a client re-derivation from raw cost, and rule 6 means the client can never hold the factor, so under any deployed factor the screen understates the debit — in rule 7's bad direction, on the screen whose only job is stating what is about to be spent, immediately before an irreversible click. Around it: a half-metered deploy still reports MATCH because the parity script checks only RATE_CARD and not WalletTableName; Haiku is free on every tier including Pro, which is an unbounded rule-5 hole the mechanism does not close and which breaks rule 12's cost bound for a subscriber who only asks Haiku; a thinking-only fable-5 generation debits the most expensive rate for zero answer text; the reconciler has no per-row isolation, so one throttled Braket call halts every refund thereafter; and the kernel's own comments state a $2.50 lifetime cap that the constant beneath them sets to 0, which is the sizing rationale for accepting a scriptable bypass. This is the largest unit here and it gates the storefront.

### 14 — Curriculum accuracy, CI parity, and repo hygiene

Effort: medium. Covers 8 findings.

**Why.** The curriculum teaches TN1 as a live, priced, dispatchable Braket simulator; it is retired in every region, it is the canonical answer to a device-selection exercise, and it appears in both GUIDEs and three notebooks — a learner following the module's own guidance submits to a machine AWS no longer runs. Nothing can catch it: the pricing-prose guard validates dollar amounts against PRICING and would bless $0.275/min forever, and nothing compares DEVICES ARNs to search-devices. The same class was caught once before by hand (IonQ Aria). The CI half is parity drift: the CodeBuild standby's inline buildspec omits the founding-credit money tests, the entire analytics suite, the changelog guard and the KaTeX assertion, so engaging it during an outage lowers the merge bar at exactly the moment nobody is watching; CI runs every Lambda on Node 20 while all ten deployed functions are nodejs22.x; the changelog guard's learner-visible path list omits lib/ and qcsim/, the code learners actually execute; and the unsolved-notebook gate asserts only that a check did not say 'correct', never that it said 'not attempted'. Hygiene: lambda/sync vendors 2,560 node_modules files, 72% of the repo's tracked files, that nothing verifies, CI deletes before testing, and the deploy overwrites — pure review surface in a public repo.

**First commit.** Remove or mark-retired the `tn1` entry at lib/hardware/devices.py:85-90 and update tests/solutions/02-hardware/01-device-discovery.py, whose canonical answer selects it, so the exercise stops teaching a retired device as the right choice.

## Unsettled

Questions this audit could not settle. Said out loud rather than dropped.

- **Is the /shell hostile-path rule erasing real readers right now, or only latently able to?** — The rule matches three URLs the site actually serves, and because it convicts the visitor rather than the request, one such fetch erases that reader's whole day — and the readers at risk are the ones who opened the playground or the lab. I could not show those URLs are requested on the normal path (the Monaco chunk is a lazily-loaded shell-language contribution and the editor is set to python; nothing under /lab references build/schemas at runtime). Settling it needs a grep of the raw Amplify logs for those three paths against the days already stored. (see `fa3dabafa`)
- **What fraction of the addresses classified `no-assets` are returning humans with a warm cache?** — The whole 'humans' series, the commit's July-vs-August trend, and the claim that 96-99% of unique addresses are automated all rest on treating no-assets as automated. Nothing in the data distinguishes a returning reader from a scraper on that signal alone, so the headline number cannot be validated in either direction without a second signal — and until it is, the README's 'floor by construction' understates the floor by an unknown amount. (see `f2436d472`)
- **Which Stripe account is the actually-provisioned sandbox?** — CLAUDE.md names $STRIPE_SANDBOX in one sentence and $STRIPE_SANDBOX_OLD in another; provision-sandbox.mjs and the Makefile document a third-hand id that --expect-account would refuse. The guard fails safe, so nothing is at risk — but it means the sandbox catalog and webhook endpoint were stood up by some route other than the documented one, and I could not determine which account e2e-sandbox.mjs has been running against. This is the repo whose own doctrine is that a written-down account id is never evidence. (see `f5dfdb4d3`)
- **Does Anthropic's introductory sonnet-5 rate expire on 2026-08-31, and has anyone re-checked it?** — RATES is either correct or overcharging depending on a date four days out from HEAD. The audit could read the constant and the comment calling the overcharge 'the safe direction'; it could not confirm the provider's current published rate or the window's end. This is the file that decides what a learner is charged in the product whose differentiator is honesty about money. (see `faa1b8f26`)
- **At cutover, does the published hardware sheet get derived from the factored formula, or does the factor get chosen so every debit stays under the sheet?** — CLAUDE.md records that the published per-task and per-shot credit figures do not stand in one common ratio to the provider's two list rates, so no single scalar reproduces the sheet exactly and integer-credit debits can exceed a fractional advertised figure. This is a founder pricing decision, not an audit finding, and it blocks the cutover either way — including whether TUTOR_RATES' typicalCreditsPerQuestion, which matches raw-cost charges today, goes stale. (see `f658df1cb`)
- **What is actually in the environment of the ~200 non-quantum Lambdas in account $PROD_ACCOUNT?** — I read the grant and confirmed ListFunctions returns configuration including Environment, and I named two concrete exposures (a live HMAC unsubscribe key, and RATE_CARD once metering ships). I did not enumerate the other Altivum products' functions, so the blast radius of the last five months of that grant is unmeasured. Deleting the grant costs nothing and does not require the answer, but rotating anything does. (see `f1ee43fd4`)
- **Was the 69 MB raw-log cache ever copied anywhere besides the one test fixture the commit message records?** — The commit message itself records that a real person's Google sign-in row — address, timestamp, and OAuth query — was copied out of this cache into a fixture and nearly published. That is one known egress. The cache is 53 days of every visitor's address and request history, sitting on a laptop against a published policy promising 30-day deletion, and the only mitigation added was a gitignore line. Whether other copies exist is a question for the machine's owner, not the repo. (see `f66baf8a0`)
- **Which other deployed CloudFormation resources have drifted, beyond the tutor WAF?** — `make drift` and the daily job answer 'is what is running what is in git?' for Lambda code only. The tutor WAF is two PRs behind under a green signal, and the analytics SNS topic has lost its subscription with nothing to notice — two confirmed drifts found by hand in seventeen templates. The audit could not sweep the rest, so the true drift count across non-Lambda resources is unknown and, by construction, unreported. (see `ff956fc7b`)
- **Does any live subscription exist on $STRIPE_LIVE today?** — The wallet table holds 0 items, which is what makes the grant-staleness, double-clawback, and tier-reset bugs dormant. But an empty wallet proves nothing about the Stripe side, and if a subscription exists there without a wallet row, the frozen-grant bug is already live rather than latent. A single account-verified subscriptions.list against the confirmed account id would settle it. (see `f119ba729`)

- `fe61f70c2` **grover_oracle and grover_diffusion silently become the identity for 4 or more qubits, so Grover's algorithm returns a uniform distribution with no error** — FIXED in 0108042 (#242). `03-algorithms/scripts/oracles.py:43-79` now carries `_apply_multi_controlled_z`, which builds C^(n-1)Z exactly at any n as a phase polynomial (one CNOT parity ladder + Rz per non-empty subset), and both `grover_oracle` (:105) and `grover_diffusion` (:136) call it. I verified independently rather than trusting the commit message: I reconstructed the full unitary column by column via `lib.utils.statevector.statevector` for n=2..6 and compared to the ideal. Oracle max deviation (after dividing out the documented global phase): 0.0, 0.0, 3.6e-16, 1.0e-15, 8.9e-16. Diffusion vs 2|s><s|-I: 0.0, 5.6e-17, 1.8e-16, 1.4e-16, 1.8e-16. `tests/test_oracles.py` (137 new lines) pins the unitary phase-insensitively and end-to-end amplification at n=2..5.
- `f1f6e3e71` **scripts/validate_runnable.py deletes any line beginning with % — including a printf-format continuation — which makes the cell unparseable and silently exempts it from the qcsim contract scan** — FIXED in 0108042 (#242). `scripts/validate_runnable.py:141` now uses `_MAGIC_LINE_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*(?:%%?|!)[A-Za-z_]")`, which requires an identifier character after the sigil, so a bare `%` printf continuation is kept as Python. The second half of the hole is closed too: `scan_notebook` at :174-181 turns a SyntaxError into a recorded violation with the message "does not parse as Python after magic-stripping ... the static qcsim contract cannot scan an unparseable cell", replacing the warn-and-continue path that let a cell exempt itself while `main()` still exited 0. `tests/test_validate_runnable.py` (86 new lines) covers both.
- `f676158b9` **The IQP feature map the browser lesson widget renders is a different unitary from the one lib.ml.feature_maps.iqp_encoding builds, and the GUIDE describes them as the same map** — FIXED in 0108042 (#242). `web/src/components/quantum/encoding.ts` was moved onto the library's product convention, and the two are now pinned cross-language by `web/src/components/quantum/__fixtures__/iqp-states.json`, generated by `scripts/gen_iqp_fixture.py`. Both sides assert it: `tests/test_feature_maps.py:114-142` (`test_iqp_encoding_matches_the_committed_cross_language_fixture`) and `web/__tests__/components/quantum/encoding.test.ts:11`. The docstring at `lib/ml/feature_maps.py:44-57` now states the convention explicitly (phi_i = x_i, phi_ij = x_i*x_j) and names it as a simplified variant of Havlicek et al. rather than the same map. Full pytest run at HEAD: 698 passed.
- `f644dc136` **test_guide_runnable_fences executes the GUIDE sandbox fences against the real Braket SDK, not qcsim, so the guarantee in its own docstring is not being tested** — FIXED in 0108042 (#242). `tests/test_guide_runnable_fences.py:127-146` now executes each fence in a FRESH subprocess that inserts `qcsim/src` on the path, imports qcsim before any braket import, and asserts `Circuit.__module__.startswith('qcsim')` before running a single line of fence source. The docstring at :20-26 names the exact cause it was blind to: `tests/conftest.py` imports `braket` at collection time, so an in-process `import qcsim` hit the `if "braket" in sys.modules: return` guard. `tests/test_notebook_contract.py:101-110` got the same alias probe.
- `f8e75412a` **Two GUIDE script inventories advertise capabilities the shipped scripts do not contain, in both locales** — FIXED in 0108042 (#242), in both locales. `03-algorithms/GUIDE.md:360` and `GUIDE.es.md:360` now describe `variational_utils.py` as "Classical optimizer wrappers (COBYLA, SPSA) with per-iteration history and callbacks" with no Adam — and `03-algorithms/scripts/variational_utils.py` does define exactly `optimize_cobyla` (:7) and `optimize_spsa` (:47), both with `callback=` parameters and a `history` list. `05-quantum-chemistry/GUIDE.md:326-328` and `GUIDE.es.md:326-328` no longer claim geometry scanning or a "custom" ansatz; `lib/chemistry/ansatz.py` exports exactly `uccsd_singles_circuit` and `hardware_efficient_ansatz`, which is what the line now says. I re-checked all seven sections' inventories in both locales against `ls */scripts/` and found no remaining overclaim.

The counts path now routes through `parse_counts` and out-of-range Hamiltonian terms are rejected at entry. `tests/test_vqe_runner.py` (110 new lines) covers the mislabeling scenarios live.

## Method

8 readers each took one dimension and were told to read the code rather than guess at it, to run anything read-only that would settle a question, and to check every finding the 2026-08-18 audit raised in their area. They raised 109 findings.

Each finding then went to two independent verifiers under different lenses — *does this reproduce?* and *is the code actually correct as written?* — for 218 verification passes. Both were told to refute, and to default to refuted when uncertain. Where the lenses disagreed, the more severe verdict is published and the finding is marked split; both raw passes are kept in the JSON twin. That rule is why 0 findings are published as refuted: a finding is refuted only when both lenses refute it, and none cleared that bar — though 13 had one lens refute them.

**What "verified" actually did.** Of 109 published verdicts, 57 rest on something observed live, 52 on something built or run locally, and 0 on the source alone. Verification was strictly read-only: no deploys, no mutations, nothing written to any live service. This command reads a system; it does not exercise one.

**Coverage bounds.** The 2,560 vendored `node_modules` files under `lambda/sync/` were not read as source; their presence in the tree was. The 45 notebooks were read for correctness of what they teach, not executed cell by cell beyond the existing contract tests. Readers recorded 218 distinct repository files opened — a measured count of what they reported, not a claim of exhaustive coverage. 0 prior findings were neither re-raised nor cleared this run and are listed above.

**Redaction.** This repository is public and a published page travels further than the repository does. Account numbers, Stripe account identifiers, deployed endpoint and user-pool identifiers, and one private individual's name and email hash are substituted for placeholders. The substitution runs through one shared module imported by both generators, which refuses to write either file if a real identifier survives it.
